components.name: AD
components.description:
Compute Accumulation/Distribution line to track cumulative money flow using close location within the high-low range.

Use to measure whether volume is flowing into (accumulating) or out of (distributing) an
asset based on where the close falls within each bar's range. Unlike OBV which only
considers close direction, AD weights volume by the close location value, giving more
nuance. Feed into ADOSC for a momentum oscillator, or into RollingZScoreTransform for
direct signal use. Requires volume data.

Output:
    Unbounded cumulative value. Rising = accumulation (buying pressure), falling =
    distribution (selling pressure). Absolute scale is in base-coin volume units —
    not comparable across assets without per-asset normalization. No NaN warmup.

Formula:
    CLV = ((close - low) - (high - close)) / (high - low)
    AD_t = AD_{t-1} + CLV * volume

Example:
    PriceDataLoader() -> AD() -> RollingZScoreTransform(window=60) -> ForecastScaler()
components.usage_hint: Use to measure whether volume is flowing into (accumulating) or out of (distributing) an asset based on where the close falls within each bar's range. Unlike OBV which only considers close direction, AD weights volume by the close location value, giving more nuance. Feed into ADOSC for a momentum oscillator, or into RollingZScoreTransform for direct signal use. Requires volume data.

components.name: ADOSC
components.description:
Compute Chaikin Accumulation/Distribution Oscillator to detect momentum shifts in money flow.

Use to identify changes in buying/selling pressure by measuring the difference between
fast and slow EMAs of the AD line. Positive ADOSC indicates accelerating accumulation,
negative indicates accelerating distribution. Unlike the raw AD line which is cumulative,
ADOSC oscillates around zero, making it easier to interpret directly — but its amplitude
is still in base-coin volume units, so raw values are not comparable across assets
(cross-asset ranking of raw ADOSC sorts by token supply, not money flow). Feed into
RollingZScoreTransform to normalize per asset before combining or ranking; do not feed
raw ADOSC into CrossSectionalZScore. Requires volume data.

Output:
    Unbounded, centered around zero, in base-coin volume units. Positive = accumulation
    momentum increasing, negative = distribution momentum increasing. NaN during warmup
    (slow_period bars).

Formula:
    ADOSC = EMA(AD, fast_period) - EMA(AD, slow_period)

Example:
    PriceDataLoader() -> ADOSC(fast_period=3, slow_period=10) -> RollingZScoreTransform(window=60)
components.usage_hint: Use to identify changes in buying/selling pressure by measuring the difference between fast and slow EMAs of the AD line. Positive ADOSC indicates accelerating accumulation, negative indicates accelerating distribution. Unlike the raw AD line which is cumulative, ADOSC oscillates around zero, making it easier to interpret directly — but its amplitude is still in base-coin volume units, so raw values are not comparable across assets (cross-asset ranking of raw ADOSC sorts by token supply, not money flow). Feed into RollingZScoreTransform to normalize per asset before combining or ranking; do not feed raw ADOSC into CrossSectionalZScore. Requires volume data.

parameters.name: fast_period
parameters.description: Short EMA period for the AD line. Shorter (2-3) captures rapid money flow shifts, longer (5-7) smooths out noise. Must be less than slow_period.

parameters.name: slow_period
parameters.description: Long EMA period for the AD line. Acts as the baseline. Standard range 8-15. Default 10 is the classic Chaikin setting. The spread between fast and slow controls oscillator sensitivity.

components.name: ADX
components.description:
Compute Average Directional Index (ADX), a trend strength indicator that measures how strongly price is trending regardless of direction.

Use as a regime filter to distinguish trending from ranging markets. ADX measures
trend strength only (not direction), so it is typically used to gate other directional
signals: enable trend-following when ADX > 25, enable mean reversion when ADX < 20.
Requires high/low/close data. Prefer ADX over ADXR when you want unsmoothed trend
strength; use ADXR for a smoother version with more lag.

Output:
    Range [0, 100]. Values > 25 = strong trend, < 20 = weak/ranging market,
    > 50 = very strong trend. Direction-agnostic (high ADX in both up and
    down trends). NaN during warmup (~2x `period` bars due to internal smoothing).

Formula:
    +DI = 100 * EMA(+DM, period) / ATR(period)
    -DI = 100 * EMA(-DM, period) / ATR(period)
    DX = 100 * |+DI - -DI| / (+DI + -DI)
    ADX = EMA(DX, period)

Example:
    ADX(period=14) -> AboveThresholdFilter(threshold=25)  # gate for trend signals
components.usage_hint: Use as a regime filter to distinguish trending from ranging markets. ADX measures trend strength only (not direction), so it is typically used to gate other directional signals: enable trend-following when ADX > 25, enable mean reversion when ADX < 20. Requires high/low/close data. Prefer ADX over ADXR when you want unsmoothed trend strength; use ADXR for a smoother version with more lag.

parameters.name: period
parameters.description: Lookback for directional movement and ATR calculations. Shorter (7-10) detects trend changes earlier but is noisier, longer (14-28) gives more reliable trend strength readings. Default 14 is standard.

components.name: ADXR
components.description:
Compute Average Directional Movement Index Rating (ADXR), a smoothed version of ADX for trend strength measurement.

Use as a smoother, laggier alternative to ADX for regime filtering. ADXR averages
the current ADX with the ADX from `period` bars ago, reducing noise in trend strength
readings. Requires high/low/close data. Prefer ADXR over ADX when you want fewer
false transitions between trending and ranging regimes at the cost of slower detection.

Output:
    Range [0, 100]. Interpretation same as ADX: > 25 = trending, < 20 = ranging.
    Smoother than ADX with more lag. NaN during warmup (~3x `period` bars
    due to ADX double-smoothing plus ADXR averaging).

Formula:
    ADXR = (ADX_today + ADX_{period_bars_ago}) / 2

Example:
    ADXR(period=14) -> AboveThresholdFilter(threshold=25)  # smooth regime gate
components.usage_hint: Use as a smoother, laggier alternative to ADX for regime filtering. ADXR averages the current ADX with the ADX from `period` bars ago, reducing noise in trend strength readings. Requires high/low/close data. Prefer ADXR over ADX when you want fewer false transitions between trending and ranging regimes at the cost of slower detection.

parameters.description: Lookback for both the underlying ADX calculation and the averaging window. Shorter (7-10) still produces a smooth output, longer (14-20) gives very stable trend strength readings. Default 14. Effective lookback is ~2x period due to internal averaging.

components.name: ATR
components.description:
Compute Average True Range to measure absolute price volatility from high-low-close range.

Use as a volatility filter or position sizing input. ATR measures absolute dollar
volatility, so it is not comparable across assets with different price levels. For
cross-asset volatility comparison, use NATR (percentage-normalized) instead. Often
fed into universe filters to exclude low-volatility assets, or used in risk managers
for stop-loss distance calculation.

Output:
    Range [0, inf), in price units. Higher = more volatile. NaN during warmup
    (period bars). Scale depends on asset price level.

Formula:
    TR = max(high - low, |high - prev_close|, |low - prev_close|)
    ATR = EMA(TR, period)  (Wilder's smoothing via TA-Lib)

Example:
    PriceDataLoader() -> ATR(period=14) -> RollingZScoreTransform(window=60)
components.usage_hint: Use as a volatility filter or position sizing input. ATR measures absolute dollar volatility, so it is not comparable across assets with different price levels. For cross-asset volatility comparison, use NATR (percentage-normalized) instead. Often fed into universe filters to exclude low-volatility assets, or used in risk managers for stop-loss distance calculation.

parameters.name: period
parameters.description: Lookback window in bars for ATR smoothing. Shorter (5-10) reacts faster to volatility spikes, longer (14-30) gives a smoother baseline. Default 14 is Wilder's standard period.

components.name: AboveThresholdFilter
components.description:
Filter for values above a threshold, converting continuous scores to a binary mask.

Use to gate signals by minimum strength, e.g., only trade momentum when return
exceeds a meaningful level. Works on raw (unnormalized) values. For range-based
filtering use RangeSelector; for below-threshold filtering use BelowThresholdFilter.

Output:
    0/1 float mask (1.0 where value exceeds threshold, 0.0 otherwise).
    NaN values produce 0.0.

Note: On a trade return, the threshold is a fraction: -0.05 is a 5% loss; inclusive=True compares at-or-beyond.

Example:
    ROC(period=10) -> AboveThresholdFilter(threshold=1.0) -> ApplyMask()
components.usage_hint: Use to gate signals by minimum strength, e.g., only trade momentum when return exceeds a meaningful level. Works on raw (unnormalized) values. For range-based filtering use RangeSelector; for below-threshold filtering use BelowThresholdFilter.

parameters.name: threshold
parameters.description: Minimum value to pass the filter. Any real number. For percentage returns: 1.0 = 1%. For z-scores: 1.0 = 1 sigma.

parameters.name: inclusive
parameters.description: If True, use >= (include exact threshold). If False (default), use > (strictly above).

components.name: Abs
components.description:
Compute absolute value to measure signal magnitude regardless of direction.

Use when only the strength of a move matters, not its direction. Common for
volatility proxies (absolute returns), regime detection (magnitude of momentum),
or as input to filters that threshold on signal strength. Often placed after
Difference or SimpleReturn.

Output:
    Range [0, inf). NaN values preserved. Zero = no signal.

Example:
    SimpleReturn(periods=4) -> Abs() -> EWMA(window=20)
components.usage_hint: Use when only the strength of a move matters, not its direction. Common for volatility proxies (absolute returns), regime detection (magnitude of momentum), or as input to filters that threshold on signal strength. Often placed after Difference or SimpleReturn.

components.name: AddCount
components.description:
Number of ScaleIn adds this trade has made, as of the start of the bar: the reader for
"once I have added" rules, such as a trail once every add is in.

Position layer: TradeManager turns entry signals into a Position; each rule is a reader, then
ordinary components, then an action (Exit, Reduce, ScaleIn, AllowEntry). It needs a ScaleIn
in a stage above it.

Example:
    TradeManager(entries="entries", prices="ohlcv") ->
      {"add": [ReturnSinceLastFill(), AboveThresholdFilter(threshold=0.05, inclusive=True), ScaleIn(units=1.0, times=2)]} ->
      {"trail_when_full": [{"full": [AddCount(), AboveThresholdFilter(threshold=2.0, inclusive=True)],
        "gave_back": [DrawdownFromPeak(), BelowThresholdFilter(threshold=-0.06)]}, MaskAnd(), Exit()]} ->
      Exposure() -> FixedWeightSizer(weight_per_position=0.1)

Note: put it in a stage below the one that adds.
components.usage_hint: Position layer: TradeManager turns entry signals into a Position; each rule is a reader, then ordinary components, then an action (Exit, Reduce, ScaleIn, AllowEntry). It needs a ScaleIn in a stage above it.

components.name: AdverseVolCap
components.description:
Cap weights by worst-case adverse-direction portfolio vol (market-neutral).

Computes the adverse-case scenario where every position's σ moves AGAINST
the position direction simultaneously. For market-neutral books this is
larger than Carver's classic "everything correlates to 1" worst case
(which is small for market-neutral since longs cancel shorts).

Formula:
    worst_adverse[t] = Σ |w_i[t] × σ_i[t]| × √bars_per_year      (the STATISTIC)
    k[t]             = target_vol × ratio      (default)         (the KNOT)
                     | threshold               (fixed pin)
                     | trailing causal quantile of worst_adverse (self-calibrating)
    M[t]             = clip((k[t] / worst_adverse[t]) ** γ, 0, 1)  (the RESPONSE)
    capped           = weights × M

γ (``response_exponent``) defaults to UNSET (``None``), which means the
identity exponent: the exponentiation is skipped entirely, so every
strategy that does not name γ is bit-identical to the pre-γ component AND
serializes to a parameter dict that omits ``response_exponent`` — a stored
blob minted before this parameter existed still round-trips (the default
is ``None``, and ``None``-valued params at a ``None`` declared default are
omitted from the compiled spec). An explicit ``response_exponent=1.0`` is
numerically the same identity path; it merely appears in the blob.

Adapted from Carver's M_corr cap (qoppac.blogspot.com/2020/05) for the
market-neutral case where the worst case is "longs and shorts move
OPPOSITE." Each asset's σ is annualized (already, by convention of the
return_vol slot).

Use as a final risk overlay alongside RealizedVolCap when you want
protection against ADVERSE-DIRECTION scenarios as well as recent
realized vol exceedance. The two caps are complementary:
  - RealizedVolCap responds to actual recent vol (slow, lagging).
  - AdverseVolCap responds to current σ × position structure
    (fast, forward-looking under adverse assumption).

Knot modes — the limit the statistic is judged against. EXACTLY ONE of
the two explicit forms may be declared; declaring NEITHER keeps the
historical default:

* (default) ``target_vol × ratio`` — the implicit Carver form. Unchanged;
  this is what every pre-existing deployment uses.
* ``threshold=`` — a frozen scalar knot, typically a percentile of the
  measure's own backtest distribution pinned in the strategy. Reproducible
  and warmup-free, but must be RE-STAMPED whenever the universe changes
  (the q90 of the intraday statistic is 3.760 on the pinned-49 flagship,
  3.757 at n50, 3.823 at n60, 3.786 at n80 — that drift is what motivated
  the quantile mode).
* ``threshold_quantile=`` + ``threshold_window=`` — the knot is a strictly
  CAUSAL trailing quantile of the statistic itself, so it self-calibrates
  to whatever universe/breadth the book actually runs and never needs a
  re-stamp. Costs a warmup: M = 1 until ``threshold_min_periods`` live
  bars exist behind the bar.

``threshold`` and ``threshold_quantile`` together RAISE — there is no
precedence rule, because silently sizing on a knot the caller did not mean
to declare is exactly the quiet mis-configuration this cap must not have.
``threshold_window`` / ``threshold_min_periods`` handed to a non-quantile
mode also RAISE rather than being ignored.

Response shape (γ = ``response_exponent``, unset ≡ 1.0):
    ``clip(x, ≤1) ** γ == clip(x ** γ, ≤1)`` for x > 0 and γ > 0, so the
    convex response is the classic kink raised to γ: it never LOOSENS the
    cap (M ≤ the γ=1 M wherever the kink binds), it only starts acting
    earlier and harder. γ=1 is the kink; γ=2–3 is the evidence-supported
    zone (the micro-checks 2026-08-02 SHAPE-REPORT frontier is monotone in
    γ with no interior optimum, but the bootstrap z falls monotonically
    past γ=3 and the binary limit's worst day gets WORSE — do not chase the
    frontier). A ramp also bounds the POST-response statistic at
    ``k^γ / fs^(γ−1) ≤ k``, which is why a hard kink stacked behind a ramp
    at the same knot is structurally inert (declared insurance, 0 binds).

Causality:
    worst_adverse[t] uses bar-t weights and bar-t σ. Both observable at
    close[t] under right-labeled bars / decision-at-close[t].

    Quantile knot: k[t] = quantile_p({ fs[s] : s < t, s live, t−window ≤ s })
      - STRICTLY EARLIER bars (``< t``, not ``≤ t``): ``shift(1)`` runs
        BEFORE the rolling window, so bar t never sees its own statistic.
        ``≤ t`` would also be defensible (fs[t] is observable at the
        decision stamp — it is built from bar-t weights and bar-t σ, both
        of which the cap already uses), but it makes the knot move with the
        very bar it is judging, which both damps the response exactly when
        it should fire and makes the multiplier a non-monotone function of
        today's fs. ``< t`` is the conservative choice, and it matches the
        offline function lab (`workspaces/micro-checks/sh_extra.py`) bar
        for bar so in-pipeline results stay comparable to the lab's.
      - The window is ``threshold_window`` INDEX POSITIONS back; non-live
        bars inside it (the book holds nothing) contribute nothing — they
        are masked to NaN before the roll — so warmup/flat stretches cannot
        drag the knot down.
      - Fewer than ``threshold_min_periods`` live observations ⇒ knot is
        NaN ⇒ M = 1 (no cap) for that bar. That is a warmup, reported at
        INFO.

Statistic seam:
    ``_worst_measure`` is the ONE place the statistic is produced, and the
    knot/response machinery below never inspects what it is made of. It is
    currently Σ|w·σ|·√bars_per_year, unchanged. SHAPE-REPORT §9.3 identifies
    the dimensionless RATIO ``fs_intra / fs_daily`` ("intraday vol has
    caught up with the daily estimate the sizer is using") as the most
    promising next form of the same signal; it is untested and deliberately
    NOT built here. Adding it is an override of ``_worst_measure`` plus a
    second σ slot — nothing else moves.

Gap semantics (σ missing where the book holds weight):
    σ is REINDEXED to the weights book (never joined) — the output book
    keeps exactly the input index/columns and weight cells are never
    mutated, densified, or zeroed (preserve_sparse contract). All gap
    handling touches σ only:
      - Missing σ is carried forward per asset for at most
        `max_stale_bars` bars (bounded stale-carry). Carried σ under a
        held position logs one WARNING per run.
      - σ missing BEYOND the bound while the asset had valid σ earlier
        is treated by WHERE the gap sits, because the DECISION row and
        the history behind it ask different questions:
          · DECISION row (the LAST row of the book — the newest bar, the
            one a live run trades) holding weight → raise (fail closed:
            sizing today's bar blind on vanished σ is a live risk
            decision, not a data observation).
          · HISTORICAL rows → substitute the carried row-max σ and log
            one WARNING per run (SIGMA_SUBSTITUTE_STALE). An interior
            hole is a data-quality event, not a reason to refuse to
            trade today: the live eval recomputes the whole lookback
            window every run, so raising on an interior hole would
            strand the strategy for as long as the hole stays in the
            window (up to the full lookback). Leaving those cells NaN is
            not an option either — NaN σ contributes 0 to the
            worst-measure, which would silently re-open the fail-open
            this policy exists to close. The cap therefore stays armed
            conservatively over the hole and the book still computes.
      - An asset that has NEVER had valid σ (warmup composition) under a
        held position substitutes the row-max of that stamp's valid σ
        and logs one WARNING per run (SIGMA_SUBSTITUTE_ROWMAX). Both
        substitutes are deliberately conservative, not neutral — for an
        adverse-scenario cap a missing σ must not shrink the worst-case
        measure — and data-dependent (they move with the cross-section's
        widest σ). If the whole row has no valid σ to substitute from
        and any weight is nonzero → raise.
      - Missing σ under ZERO weight contributes |w|·σ = 0 to the
        worst-measure and passes silently (flat/warmup gaps are honest
        NaN).
    On gap-free dense σ the output is identical to the pre-gap-fix
    behavior.

Tuning:
    ratio is the load-bearing parameter. ratio=2.0 fires when adverse-vol
    exceeds 2× target (e.g., 100% annualized at vt=0.50). ratio=6.5
    (Carver default) is very loose — fires only when adverse exceeds 325%.
    For tight risk control, try ratio in [1.5, 3.0].

Example:
    ... → RealizedVolCap(target_vol=0.50, ratio=2.0)
        → AdverseVolCap(target_vol=0.50, ratio=6.5)
        → LeverageCap(max_leverage=5)
components.usage_hint: Computes the adverse-case scenario where every position's σ moves AGAINST the position direction simultaneously. For market-neutral books this is larger than Carver's classic "everything correlates to 1" worst case (which is small for market-neutral since longs cancel shorts).

parameters.name: return_vol_slot
parameters.description: Slot name for per-asset annualized return vol.

parameters.name: target_vol
parameters.description: Target portfolio realized vol (annualized). Ignored when `threshold` or `threshold_quantile` is set.

parameters.name: ratio
parameters.description: Cap ratio. Threshold = target_vol × ratio. Higher = looser. Ignored when `threshold` or `threshold_quantile` is set.

parameters.name: bars_per_year
parameters.description: Annualization factor. Default 365 (daily perp bars).

parameters.name: threshold
parameters.description: Optional ABSOLUTE threshold override (annualized worst-case vol). When set, replaces target_vol × ratio. Use for limits calibrated to a percentile of the measure's own backtest distribution and pinned in the strategy (the Carver risk-overlay calibration procedure). Mutually exclusive with `threshold_quantile`.

parameters.name: threshold_quantile
parameters.description: Optional SELF-CALIBRATING knot — a quantile in (0, 1) of the statistic's own strictly-causal trailing distribution (0.60 = the SHAPE-REPORT winner). Requires `threshold_window`. Mutually exclusive with `threshold`; it also replaces target_vol × ratio. Costs a warmup.

parameters.name: threshold_window
parameters.description: Trailing window in BARS for the quantile knot (180 = the winner). Quantile mode only.

parameters.name: threshold_min_periods
parameters.description: Minimum LIVE observations inside the window before the knot exists; bars below it run uncapped (M = 1). Defaults to `threshold_window // 2`. Quantile mode only.

parameters.name: response_exponent
parameters.description: γ, the convexity of the response. UNSET (None, the default) means the identity exponent: the exponentiation is SKIPPED entirely, so an un-named γ is bit-identical to the pre-γ component and — because the declared default is None — does not enter the compiled blob at all, keeping blobs minted before this parameter existed loadable. An explicit 1.0 takes the same identity path and only differs by appearing in the blob. >1 makes the response convex so it acts across the whole range of the statistic instead of only its tail; 2.0 is the SHAPE-REPORT recommendation. Values < 1 are rejected: they would make the cap LOOSER than the classic kink (a risk overlay may only tighten).

parameters.name: max_stale_bars
parameters.description: Maximum bars to forward-fill stale σ before failing closed for held positions. Default 5. Set to None to disable the staleness limit (unbounded carry). Protects against capping on outdated σ. See "Gap semantics" in the class docstring.

parameters.name: log_fires
parameters.description: Log fire count + avg M at INFO when True.

components.name: AlignToFrequency
components.description:
Project a coarse signal onto a finer execution-frequency grid (ffill of completed bars).

Use when upstream signals are computed at a coarser timeframe (e.g., 12h or 1d
rebalance) and need placing on a finer execution timeframe grid (e.g., 30min or
1h). Prefer TargetSignalProjector (tracks Globals) or SignalProjector for new
multi-timeframe strategies — this component remains for existing pipelines.
Projection is the coarse-to-fine direction with one semantics: each fine bar
carries the last COMPLETED coarse bar's value (no partial-bar reads, no
lookahead); the grid derives from the declared timeframe, never from the data.

Output:
    Same value range as input, on the target frequency completed-bar grid.
    Forward-filled from completed coarse bars only. NaN only at the head,
    per column (NaN means HOLD — never filled with 0). Empty input returns
    empty output. Lookback params are bars, not time — projection never
    rescales a period parameter.

Example:
    EqualWeightSizer() -> AlignToFrequency(frequency="30min")
components.usage_hint: Use when upstream signals are computed at a coarser timeframe (e.g., 12h or 1d rebalance) and need placing on a finer execution timeframe grid (e.g., 30min or 1h). Prefer TargetSignalProjector (tracks Globals) or SignalProjector for new multi-timeframe strategies — this component remains for existing pipelines. Projection is the coarse-to-fine direction with one semantics: each fine bar carries the last COMPLETED coarse bar's value (no partial-bar reads, no lookahead); the grid derives from the declared timeframe, never from the data.

parameters.name: frequency

components.name: AllowEntry
components.description:
An entry gate: a new trade may open only on bars where this mask is 1, in addition to the
default wait for the entry signal to reset (cooldowns, trades per day, loss limits).

Position layer: TradeManager turns entry signals into a Position; each rule is a reader, then
ordinary components, then an action (Exit, Reduce, ScaleIn, AllowEntry). It is evaluated on
flat bars only; adding a gate only ever makes entry stricter.

Example:
    TradeManager(entries="entries", prices="ohlcv", reentry="any_bar") ->
      {"cooldown": [BarsSinceExit(), AboveThresholdFilter(threshold=2.0), AllowEntry()]} ->
      Exposure() -> FixedWeightSizer(weight_per_position=0.1)

Note: stops, targets, trails and other price-level rules are checked and filled at the bar's close, with no intra-bar measurement or execution, so a fill can be well past the level.
Note: gates AND with each other and with the reset.
Note: it reads between-trade readers only.

components.name: AnalyticalFDM
components.description:
Apply the Forecast Diversification Multiplier to restore combined forecast magnitude after diversification.

.. deprecated::
    Use AnalyticalFDMCombiner instead. It combines forecasts and applies
    analytical FDM in one step with a single weights parameter, eliminating
    the duplication between ForecastCombiner and AnalyticalFDM.

Place after ForecastCombiner to compensate for diversification drag (combined
forecasts are smaller than individual ones due to cancellation). Receives the
combined forecast and a correlation matrix from CorrelationEstimator via a
Parallel step. Weights must match the upstream ForecastCombiner weights exactly.

Output:
    Range [-20, 20] (hard-clipped). FDM scalar is in [fdm_min, fdm_max].
    With uncorrelated rules, FDM approaches 1/sqrt(1/N). With perfectly
    correlated rules, FDM = 1.0 (no diversification benefit).

Formula:
    FDM = 1 / sqrt(w' R w)
    scaled_forecast = clip(forecast * FDM, -20, 20)
    where w = weight vector, R = correlation matrix

Example:
    Use AnalyticalFDMCombiner instead:
    AnalyticalFDMCombiner(weights={"mr": 0.5, "mom": 0.5}, correlation_window="90d")
components.usage_hint: .. deprecated:: Use AnalyticalFDMCombiner instead. It combines forecasts and applies analytical FDM in one step with a single weights parameter, eliminating the duplication between ForecastCombiner and AnalyticalFDM.

parameters.description: Minimum FDM value. Default 1.0 (no amplification below this).

parameters.description: Maximum FDM value. Default 2.5. Caps the diversification benefit to prevent over-amplification with very low correlations.

components.name: AnalyticalFDMCombiner
components.description:
Combine forecast rules and apply analytical FDM correction in one step.

Replaces the three-component pattern (ForecastCombiner + CorrelationEstimator
+ the deprecated AnalyticalFDM) with a single Composer. Weights are specified once and used for
both combination and FDM calculation — no duplication, no mismatch risk.

Place directly after a Parallel step whose branches produce individual
ForecastSeries DataFrames. Branch names must match the weights keys.

Output:
    ForecastSeries (DataFrame). Range [-20, 20] (hard-clipped). FDM scalar
    is in [fdm_min, fdm_max]. With uncorrelated rules, FDM approaches
    1/sqrt(1/N). With perfectly correlated rules, FDM = 1.0.

Formula:
    combined = sum(w_i * forecast_i)
    FDM = 1 / sqrt(w' R w)
    result = clip(combined * FDM, -20, 20)

Example:
    {
        'fast': [EWMA(window=8), ForecastScaler()],
        'medium': [EWMA(window=16), ForecastScaler()],
        'slow': [EWMA(window=32), ForecastScaler()],
    },
    AnalyticalFDMCombiner(
        weights={'fast': 0.33, 'medium': 0.34, 'slow': 0.33},
        correlation_window='90d',
    ),

components.name: AnchoredReturn
components.description:
Return of price from the close of the bar where a market signal turned on, for up to
`within` bars: "buy the first 3.5% dip after the signal candle" entries.

Position layer: TradeManager turns entry signals into a Position; each rule is a reader, then
ordinary components, then an action (Exit, Reduce, ScaleIn, AllowEntry). AnchoredReturn
builds an ENTRY signal on the market side; it never measures a trade.

Example:
    PriceDataLoader() -> Store("ohlcv") -> RSI(period=14) -> BelowThresholdFilter(threshold=25.0) -> Store("signal") ->
      Load("ohlcv") -> ExtractSeries(series_name="close") -> AnchoredReturn(anchor_slot="signal", within=24) ->
      BelowThresholdFilter(threshold=-0.035, inclusive=True) -> Store("entries")

Note: a market value: it never measures a trade.

Output:
    A fraction (input / onset value - 1) on bars 1..within after each onset while the
    anchor stays 1; NaN elsewhere, the onset bar included.

components.name: AndCombinator
components.description:
Combine multiple boolean filter masks with AND logic so all conditions must be True.

Use after a Parallel step producing multiple filter signals (e.g., volume, liquidity,
time filters) to require all conditions are met before trading. For OR logic where
any condition is sufficient, use OrCombinator instead. NaN values are treated as False.

Every branch must carry the same timestamps and the same symbols; branches
are matched by symbol name, not column position, and a mismatch raises.

Output:
    Float mask DataFrame, values 0.0/1.0 (never bool dtype). 1.0 only where ALL input masks are True.
    Same shape as input masks, in the first branch's row and column order.

Example:
    {"vol": [VolatilityFilter(...)], "liq": [MarketVolumeRegimeFilter(...)]}
    -> AndCombinator(signals_list=["vol", "liq"])

components.name: Aroon
components.description:
Compute Aroon Oscillator, a trend direction indicator measuring recency of highs versus lows over a lookback period.

Use as a trend direction signal that responds to where the most recent high and low
occurred within the lookback window. High positive values mean a recent high (uptrend),
high negative values mean a recent low (downtrend). Requires high/low data only.
Typically followed by CrossSectionalZScore or ForecastScaler. Prefer Aroon over MACD
when you want a bounded trend signal that is purely based on high/low recency
rather than moving average convergence.

Output:
    Range [-100, +100]. Positive = uptrend (recent high closer than recent low),
    negative = downtrend. Values near zero = no clear trend.
    NaN during warmup (`period` bars).

Formula:
    Aroon_Up = 100 * (period - bars_since_highest_high) / period
    Aroon_Down = 100 * (period - bars_since_lowest_low) / period
    Aroon_Oscillator = Aroon_Up - Aroon_Down

Example:
    Aroon(period=14) -> CrossSectionalZScore() -> ForecastScaler()

High positive values mean a recent high (uptrend), high negative values mean a recent low (downtrend). Requires high/low data only. Typically followed by CrossSectionalZScore or ForecastScaler. Prefer Aroon over MACD when you want a bounded trend signal that is purely based on high/low recency rather than moving average convergence.

components.name: AssetAligner
components.description:
Cut a signal's columns down to the assets a stored OHLCV slot carries — no ranking, no scoring.

Use for "make the funding series cover the same names as the prices",
"line this secondary feed up with the universe I already chose", "these
two frames disagree about which assets exist". A second loader
(``FundingDataLoader``, ``OpenInterestLoader``) rarely returns exactly
the symbols the price loader did, and a cross-sectional step over
mismatched columns is a silent bug. This makes one frame follow the
other.

It only INTERSECTS — the asset set comes entirely from the reference
slot. If that slot was itself produced by a whole-window reducer, this
component inherits that reducer's window dependence; it adds none of its
own. Use ``RollingVolumeUniverseMask`` + ``ApplyUniverseMask`` when the
point is to RANK by liquidity (causally, keeping the frame's width), or
``Universe(mode="top_volume", top_n=N)`` to declare it.

Column ORDER comes from the reference, not the input:
    Surviving columns are emitted in the reference slot's key order, so
    ``AssetAligner`` reorders as well as filters. Nothing in the registry
    reads column order, but do not be surprised by it in a debug dump.

Row alignment (``align_rows``, default True — the same wart as the
deprecated VolumeUniverseReducerAny):
    The index is intersected with the index of the FIRST symbol in the
    reference dict — one arbitrary asset, not the union or the
    intersection of all of them — and only when that intersection is
    SHORTER than the signal's own index. On a dense panel where every
    symbol shares one index this is a no-op; on a ragged one it silently
    truncates to whichever symbol the dict happens to list first. Set it
    False to keep the signal's full time range.

Errors and NaN discipline:
    No overlap at all between the reference's symbols and the signal's
    columns RAISES, naming both sides — it never returns an empty frame.
    Otherwise nothing is computed: surviving cells are carried through
    exactly as they arrive, NaN included, with no fill, no reindex onto
    missing columns, and no alignment of values.

Causality / invariance:
    This step performs no time-axis computation of its own: it selects
    columns, and (optionally) trims the index. It cannot introduce
    lookahead — but it cannot remove one either, so whatever produced
    ``reference_slot`` owns that question.

Output:
    The input DataFrame with columns narrowed to the reference's symbols
    and ordered by them, same values, same index unless ``align_rows``
    trimmed it. Type is preserved (SignalSeries in, SignalSeries out).

Example:
    # Globals(target_timeframe="1h"): PriceDataLoader() serves the 1h bars itself — no resampler
    PriceDataLoader() -> Store("ohlcv_1h") ->
      ROC(period=24) -> Store("momentum")

    FundingDataLoader() -> AssetAligner(reference_slot="ohlcv_1h") ->
      NegateTransform() -> ForecastScaler()
components.usage_hint: Use for "make the funding series cover the same names as the prices", "line this secondary feed up with the universe I already chose", "these two frames disagree about which assets exist". A second loader (``FundingDataLoader``, ``OpenInterestLoader``) rarely returns exactly the symbols the price loader did, and a cross-sectional step over mismatched columns is a silent bug. This makes one frame follow the other.

components.name: AssetSelect
components.description:
Keep only a hard-coded list of assets, dropping every other column or key.

Use for "just trade BTC and ETH", "the DeFi basket", "long HYPE against
short BNB", "run this leg on one name". The asset set is fixed at
authoring time and never changes over the backtest.

A REDUCER, not a mask — this is the distinction that decides which
component you want:
    - ``AssetSelect`` DROPS columns, so the frame gets narrower and every
      downstream step sees only the kept assets. Cross-sectional
      operations (z-score, rank, top-N) are then computed over the
      reduced set, which is usually the point of using it inside a
      ``Parallel`` leg.
    - ``ApplyUniverseMask`` keeps the frame's width and NaNs out the
      excluded assets instead, so the full universe stays visible for
      ranking. Use that one whenever the selection is time-varying
      (rolling top-N, regime gating).
    - ``GroupAssetFilter`` is this component with the list moved into the
      ``Universe(groups={...})`` declaration, so one named group can be
      reused across branches and edited in one place.

Type-preserving:
    Runs on either shape, at any point in the pipeline: an OHLCV dict
    before any indicator (keys are filtered) or a DataFrame after one
    (columns are selected). The output is the same kind as the input.
    Anything else raises ``TypeError``.

Column order differs by input shape (both are deliberate):
    On a DataFrame the columns come out in the order of ``symbols`` —
    ``AssetSelect(symbols=["C", "A"])`` yields ``["C", "A"]``. On an
    OHLCV dict the keys keep their ORIGINAL order and ``symbols`` acts
    as set membership. Nothing downstream in the registry depends on
    column order, but do not read the DataFrame path's ordering as a
    reordering tool.

Missing symbols:
    A symbol not present in the data is silently skipped — a universe
    that legitimately lacks a listing for part of the backtest should not
    fail. Selecting NONE of them raises ``ValueError`` listing what was
    available, so a typo'd or renamed ticker fails loudly rather than
    producing an empty book.

NaN discipline:
    None to speak of — no value is read. Cells are carried through
    exactly as they arrive, NaN included, with no reindexing, alignment
    or fill.

Causality / invariance:
    Selection is on the COLUMN axis only; the time index is untouched, so
    no bar can influence another and appending or removing bars changes
    nothing about which assets are kept.

Output:
    The same type as the input (dict or DataFrame) with only the listed
    assets, identical index, identical values.

Example:
    # Pair trade: one leg per asset, recombined into a single book. Each
    # leg sizes to half the book so the two sum to 1.0x (M-29).
    # Globals(target_timeframe="1d", bar_offset="12h"): PriceDataLoader() serves 1d on the 12h grid — no resampler
    Pipeline([
        PriceDataLoader(), Store("ohlcv"),
        {
            "long_leg": [Load("ohlcv"), AssetSelect(symbols=["HYPE"]),
                         ROC(period=20), ForecastScaler(),
                         ForecastWeightNormalizer(target_leverage=0.5)],
            "short_leg": [Load("ohlcv"), AssetSelect(symbols=["BNB"]),
                          ROC(period=20), ForecastScaler(),
                          ForecastWeightNormalizer(target_leverage=0.5)],
        },
        WeightConcatenator(),
    ])

    # Multi-asset basket, inline
    AssetSelect(symbols=["AAVE", "UNI", "COMP", "MKR", "SNX"])

This list is the strategy's fixed universe for this branch: to vary the set over time use a mask (``RollingVolumeUniverseMask`` + ``ApplyUniverseMask``), and to share one list across branches declare it as a ``Universe`` group and use ``GroupAssetFilter``.

components.name: AtEntry
components.description:
A market value sampled at this trade's entry bar and held for the trade (ATR at entry, the
range low at entry): the 1R of an R multiple and the frozen stop or target level.

Position layer: TradeManager turns entry signals into a Position; each rule is a reader, then
ordinary components, then an action (Exit, Reduce, ScaleIn, AllowEntry). The slot is read
when this step runs, so a later Store of the slot changes nothing.

Example:
    ATR(period=14) -> Scale(by=2.0) -> Store("one_r") ->
      TradeManager(entries="entries", prices="ohlcv") ->
      {"numerator": [TradePnL()], "denominator": [AtEntry(slot="one_r")]} -> SignalRatio() ->
      {"stop": [BelowThresholdFilter(threshold=-1.0, inclusive=True), Exit()]} ->
      Exposure() -> FixedWeightSizer(weight_per_position=0.1)

Note: stops, targets, trails and other price-level rules are checked and filled at the bar's close, with no intra-bar measurement or execution, so a fill can be well past the level.
Note: a missing value at entry refuses that entry (required=True).

components.name: AveragePairwiseCorrelationRegime
components.description:
Compute average pairwise correlation of log returns across the universe as a correlation regime indicator.

Use to detect crowded or highly correlated market regimes where
cross-sectional signals lose their edge. Feed into RegimeGate to disable
mean reversion or relative value strategies during high-correlation periods,
or into RegimeScale to reduce forecast intensity. Pairs well with
CrossSectionalDispersionRegime for complementary regime views.

Output:
    Scalar GlobalSeries in range [-1, 1]. Values near 1 indicate all assets
    moving in lockstep (risk-off, correlated selloff), values near 0 indicate
    low correlation (idiosyncratic returns, favorable for cross-sectional
    strategies). NaN during the first lookback bars.

Formula:
    R = rolling pairwise correlation matrix of log returns
    signal = mean of upper-triangular elements of R

Example:
    PriceDataLoader() -> Store('ohlcv') -> {
        "corr": [ExtractSeries(series_name='close'),
                 AveragePairwiseCorrelationRegime(ohlcv_slot='ohlcv', lookback=20)],
        "momentum": [ROC(period=20), ForecastScaler()],
    } -> RegimeGate(index_key='corr', signal_key='momentum', condition='index < 0.5')

Feed into RegimeGate to disable mean reversion or relative value strategies during high-correlation periods, or into RegimeScale to reduce forecast intensity. Pairs well with CrossSectionalDispersionRegime for complementary regime views.

components.name: AveragePrice
components.description:
The size-weighted average entry price after adds (ScaleIn); equal to the entry close until
the first add.

Position layer: TradeManager turns entry signals into a Position; each rule is a reader, then
ordinary components, then an action (Exit, Reduce, ScaleIn, AllowEntry). Sells leave the
average unchanged; it updates on the bar after an add.

Note: stops, targets, trails and other price-level rules are checked and filled at the bar's close, with no intra-bar measurement or execution, so a fill can be well past the level.

Example:
    EWMA(window=50) -> Store("ema50") ->
      TradeManager(entries="entries", prices="ohlcv") ->
      {"ema_below_avg": [{"fast": [Load("ema50")], "slow": [AveragePrice()]}, Crossover(),
        BelowThresholdFilter(threshold=0.0), Exit()]} ->
      Exposure() -> FixedWeightSizer(weight_per_position=0.1)

components.name: BarsHeld
components.description:
Bars since this trade's entry (0 on the entry bar): the reader for a max hold, a time exit,
a stale-trade cut or any "after N bars" rule.

Position layer: TradeManager turns entry signals into a Position; each rule is a reader, then
ordinary components, then an action (Exit, Reduce, ScaleIn, AllowEntry). Bars with no price
are counted.

Example:
    TradeManager(entries="entries", prices="ohlcv") ->
      {"max_hold": [BarsHeld(), AboveThresholdFilter(threshold=48, inclusive=True), Exit()]} ->
      Exposure() -> FixedWeightSizer(weight_per_position=0.1)

Note: counts from the trade's open, not from the signal.

components.name: BarsSinceExit
components.description:
Bars since the last exit on this asset: the reader for a cooldown before re-entry, ending in
AllowEntry().

Position layer: TradeManager turns entry signals into a Position; each rule is a reader, then
ordinary components, then an action (Exit, Reduce, ScaleIn, AllowEntry). It counts from the
latest close by a rule (a flip is not an exit); before the first exit it is +inf.

Example:

      {"cooldown": [BarsSinceExit(), AboveThresholdFilter(threshold=2.0), AllowEntry()]} ->
      Exposure() -> FixedWeightSizer(weight_per_position=0.1)

components.name: BelowThresholdFilter
components.description:
Filter for values below a threshold, converting continuous scores to a binary mask.

Use to detect weakness or negative conditions, e.g., identify assets with
negative momentum or below-average funding. Works on raw (unnormalized) values.
For above-threshold filtering use AboveThresholdFilter; for range-based filtering
use RangeSelector.

    NaN values produce 0.0.

Note: On a trade return, the threshold is a fraction: -0.05 is a 5% loss; inclusive=True compares at-or-beyond.

Example:
    ROC(period=10) -> BelowThresholdFilter(threshold=-1.0) -> ApplyMask()

components.name: BenchmarkDemean
components.description:
Subtract the per-bar mean signal of named benchmark symbols from every asset.

Signal-level approximation of beta-neutralization. For a small set of
"benchmark" symbols (e.g., BTC/ETH/SOL representing the systematic
crypto factor), subtract the per-bar equal-weighted mean of their
signals from every asset's signal. Biases the resulting positions
away from the common-factor direction the benchmarks represent.

Use after a signal transform when you want positions that are net-short
the systematic factor without doing per-asset β regression at signal
time. Cheaper than full position-level β hedging and produces
equivalent first-order behavior when benchmarks span the factor.

Output:
    Same shape as input. Per-bar mean across all columns is shifted
    toward zero (exactly zero only if all benchmarks are present and
    not NaN that bar). NaN values are preserved.

Formula:
    bench_mean[t] = mean(signal[t, b] for b in benchmarks if not NaN)
    result[t, a]  = signal[t, a] - bench_mean[t]

Example:
    ROC(period=14) -> CrossSectionalZScore() -> BenchmarkDemean(benchmarks=["BTC", "ETH"]) -> ForecastScaler()

See also:
    CrossSectionalZScore — subtracts mean across ALL assets, not just
    named benchmarks (and divides by std).

components.name: BetaEstimator
components.description:
Compute rolling beta of each asset relative to a benchmark for risk analysis and hedging.

Use to measure how each asset co-moves with a benchmark (BTC or universe average).
Reads OHLCV data from the slot named by ohlcv_slot. Pipe the output to Store(MARKET_BETA)
to make betas available for BetaHedgeAllocator or other downstream components.
Useful for building beta-neutral or beta-hedged portfolios.

Output:
    Unbounded, typically [0.5, 2.0] for crypto assets. Beta > 1 means the asset
    amplifies benchmark moves, < 1 means it's more defensive. NaN during warmup
    (window // 2 bars).

Formula:
    beta_i = cov(r_i, r_benchmark, window) / var(r_benchmark, window)
    where r = percentage returns from close prices

Example:
    PriceDataLoader() -> Store("ohlcv_1d") -> BetaEstimator(ohlcv_slot="ohlcv_1d", benchmark="BTC", window=60)

components.name: BetaHedgeAllocator
components.description:
Adjust portfolio weights to neutralize market beta exposure for beta-neutral hedging.

Use to reduce directional market risk from a portfolio. Self-contained: reads OHLCV
from a caller-specified OHLCV slot, computes rolling betas internally, then adjusts incoming
weights. Place after weight allocation (e.g., EqualWeightAllocator or VolTargetWeightConverter).
For a specific-asset benchmark (e.g., "BTC"), overlays a hedge position on that asset.
For "universe", applies proportional beta reduction across all positions.

Output:
    Adjusted portfolio weights (DataFrame). Same shape as input weights. The
    benchmark asset may have a negative weight if hedging a long-biased portfolio.
    Universe mode preserves GROSS exposure (sum of |weights|) per bar, so it
    never sizes the book above the leverage it was given. Because the universe
    benchmark is built from the same assets, their betas average exactly 1:
    at hedge_ratio=1.0 an equal-weight book becomes dollar-neutral (long the
    low-beta names, short the high-beta ones) at the input's gross. A bar the
    hedge leaves (numerically) flat emits zeros.

Formula:
    Specific asset: hedge = -hedge_ratio * sum(weights * betas)
                    weights[benchmark] += hedge
    Universe:       hedged = weights * (1 - hedge_ratio * betas)
                    weights = hedged * sum(|weights|) / sum(|hedged|)

Example:
    EqualWeightAllocator() -> BetaHedgeAllocator(ohlcv_slot="ohlcv_1d", benchmark="BTC", hedge_ratio=0.8)
components.usage_hint: Use to reduce directional market risk from a portfolio. Place after weight allocation (e.g., EqualWeightAllocator or VolTargetWeightConverter). For a specific-asset benchmark (e.g., "BTC"), overlays a hedge position on that asset. For "universe", applies proportional beta reduction across all positions.

components.name: BinaryToWeight
components.description:
DEPRECATED — convert a binary signal to weights; use EqualWeightSizer or FixedWeightSizer instead.

Do not compose new strategies with this component. It is registered with
``status = "deprecated"`` and kept only so pipelines compiled before the
split still load. Both of its modes have an exact, verified replacement:

    BinaryToWeight()                → EqualWeightSizer(target_leverage=1.0)
    BinaryToWeight(fixed_weight=w)  → FixedWeightSizer(weight_per_position=w)

The replacements are bit-identical on the same input and add what this one
lacks: ``target_leverage`` (this component is hardwired to a gross of 1.0)
and ``max_weight`` (this component cannot cap a position, so a bar with one
open name puts 100% of equity into it).

Formula (per bar t, per asset i):
    fixed_weight is None:  out_i[t] = signal_i[t] / Σ_j |signal_j[t]|
    fixed_weight = w:      out_i[t] = signal_i[t] × w

Input contract: ``ensure_binary_signal`` RAISES on any value outside
{-1, 0, +1} (NaN allowed). This is stricter than either replacement, which
accept continuous input — so migrating cannot break a strategy this
component already accepted, but moving BACK to it can.

NaN discipline:
    A NaN signal cell yields a NaN weight and is EXCLUDED from the
    equal-weight denominator (the row sum skips it), so the names that do
    have a signal absorb the whole 1.0 gross between them. Nothing is
    filled or densified. An all-zero row yields zeros rather than dividing
    by zero (the denominator's 0 is replaced by 1).

Causality / invariance:
    Each bar is computed from that bar's signal row alone — no window, no
    shift, no state — so appending or removing FUTURE bars cannot change a
    past weight.

Output:
    TargetWeights with the input's index and columns. Direction from the
    signal. Gross is exactly 1.0 in equal-weight mode when anything is
    open, and ``fixed_weight × Σ|signal|`` in fixed mode.

Example:
    # Deprecated — this is the migration, not a pattern to copy:
    CrossSectionalZScore() -> ThresholdCross(upper=0.5, lower=-0.5) ->
      EqualWeightSizer(target_leverage=1.0, max_weight=0.3)

A number = that weight per open position, in units of equity, with gross floating as the count changes (0.1 = 10% per name). Direction comes from the input signal in both modes. New strategies should declare the replacement sizer instead of either mode.

components.name: BollingerBands
components.description:
Compute normalized price position within Bollinger Bands for volatility breakout and mean reversion detection.

Use to measure where price sits relative to its recent volatility envelope. Values near
0 or 1 indicate price at the lower or upper band (potential mean reversion entries), while
values outside [0, 1] signal breakouts. Feed into CrossSectionalZScore for cross-asset
comparison or WingsTransform to trade extreme band positions.

Output:
    Range approximately [0, 1] but can exceed on breakouts. 0 = price at lower band,
    0.5 = price at SMA midline, 1 = price at upper band. NaN during warmup (period bars).

Formula:
    middle = SMA(close, period)
    upper = middle + num_std * StdDev(close, period)
    lower = middle - num_std * StdDev(close, period)
    output = (close - lower) / (upper - lower)

Example:
    PriceDataLoader() -> BollingerBands(period=20, num_std=2.0) -> CrossSectionalZScore()
components.usage_hint: Use to measure where price sits relative to its recent volatility envelope. Values near 0 or 1 indicate price at the lower or upper band (potential mean reversion entries), while values outside [0, 1] signal breakouts. Feed into CrossSectionalZScore for cross-asset comparison or WingsTransform to trade extreme band positions.

parameters.name: period
parameters.description: Lookback window in bars for SMA and standard deviation. Shorter (10-15) captures fast volatility shifts, longer (20-50) gives smoother bands. Default 20 is the standard Bollinger Band period.

parameters.name: num_std
parameters.description: Number of standard deviations for band width. 2.0 = standard (captures ~95% of price action), 1.5 = tighter bands (more signals, more noise), 2.5-3.0 = wider bands (fewer but more extreme signals).

components.name: BoxCox
components.description:
Apply Box-Cox power transform to stabilize variance and reduce skewness in positive-valued signals.

Use on strictly positive signals (e.g., ATR, volume, realized volatility) to make
their distribution more Gaussian before normalization. Helps downstream z-score
transforms perform better on heavy-tailed data. Requires all input values > 0;
apply an upstream shift if needed. Pick lambda: 0 = log, 0.5 = square root.
There is no auto-fit: a lambda fitted on the run window makes each bar depend
on later bars, so lambda_param is required.

Output:
    Unbounded, transformed scale. When lambda_param != 0: (x^lambda - 1) / lambda.
    When lambda_param = 0: ln(x). NaN preserved from input; inf replaced with NaN.

Formula:
    y = (x^lambda - 1) / lambda   if lambda != 0
    y = ln(x)                      if lambda == 0

Example:
    ATR(period=14) -> BoxCox(lambda_param=0.5) -> RollingZScoreTransform(window=60)
components.usage_hint: Use on strictly positive signals (e.g., ATR, volume, realized volatility) to make their distribution more Gaussian before normalization. Helps downstream z-score transforms perform better on heavy-tailed data. Requires all input values > 0; apply an upstream shift if needed. Pick lambda: 0 = log, 0.5 = square root. There is no auto-fit: a lambda fitted on the run window makes each bar depend on later bars, so lambda_param is required.

parameters.name: lambda_param
parameters.description: Power parameter (required). Pick lambda: 0.0 = log transform, 0.5 = square root, 1.0 = linear (no-op minus shift). Typical values: 0.0-0.5 for heavy-tailed distributions.

parameters.name: lambda_param
parameters.description: Power parameter (required). Pick lambda: 0.0 = log transform, 0.5 = square root, 1.0 = linear (no-op minus shift). Typical values: 0.0-0.5 for heavy-tailed distributions.

components.name: BreakOfStructure
components.description:
Fire a signed {-1, 0, +1} pulse on the bar that BREAKS the last confirmed swing level.

Use as the SMC "structure shifted" event: +1 when price takes the last
confirmed swing HIGH (upward break), -1 when it undercuts the last
confirmed swing LOW, 0 on every other observed bar. Gate a zone entry on
it, sequence it before an order-block retest, or multiply it by a flow
confirmation (`TakerFlowLoader` CVD slope) — the spec 01 §4 "confirmed
BOS" recipe. Every contested clause is a parameter pinned to the school
that uses it (smc-trader-cohort research/05 §1, §3); Keel does not
adjudicate whose break definition is correct.

THIS COMPONENT FIRES ON EVERY BREAK of the last confirmed swing level.
Whether a particular break is a CONTINUATION (a BOS proper) or a REVERSAL
(a CHoCH) is a separate classification, and it is `ChangeOfCharacter`'s
job — under the LuxAlgo/smc.py school the two labels describe the SAME
event, so the honest split is "all breaks here, the reversal subset
there". Pure continuation is the recipe `BreakOfStructure` minus
`ChangeOfCharacter` (both on the same axes), never a hidden default.

The R4 identity (spec 01 §2, research/05 §5 V2): a WICK-trigger break and
a liquidity sweep are ONE event split by what the close does next.
`BreakOfStructure(trigger="wick")` IS the penetration set `LiquiditySweep`
evaluates — both read `structure.level_breaks`, the one owner of trigger
semantics — and a penetration becomes a SWEEP when price closes back
inside within `reclaim_bars`, or stays a BREAK when it closes beyond.

Axes (sourced defaults, spec 01 contract 3):
    detector: "fractal" (default) = the symmetric shape ICT teaches and
        smc.py implements; "leg_flip" = LuxAlgo's rolling-extreme state
        flip, which is NOT a fractal (research/05 §1 V3). See `SwingPivot`
        for the full detector contract — the same one owner produces the
        levels this component breaks.
    width: swing width in bars (default 5). The sourced ladder is 1 (ICT's
        short-term high), 5 and 50 — LuxAlgo maintains BOTH 5 and 50 as
        two parallel structures and labels breaks on each, which educators
        call INTERNAL vs SWING (external) structure; smc.py's
        `swing_length` default is 50. `structure.TIER_WIDTHS` is that
        named pair. The default follows the internal tier: a width-50
        fractal confirms only a handful of levels per 500 bars, so its
        break pulse is too sparse to be a default. Two instances at
        width 5 and width 50 give you both tiers, which is what LuxAlgo
        itself runs.
    trigger: what price has to do to take the level. "close" (default) =
        the body closes beyond it — the dominant educator rule ("a wick
        alone does not confirm a structure break… a wick through a level
        is treated as a liquidity sweep"), smc.py's `close_break=True`,
        and the only thing LuxAlgo offers (`ta.crossover(close, level)`).
        "wick" = the high/low alone is enough — smc.py's
        `close_break=False`, and the sweep-detection half of the R4
        identity above.
    expiry_bars: safety bound — an untaken level stops being breakable
        `expiry_bars` bars after its confirmation (default 200). A KEEL
        CONVENTION, not a practitioner one: no surveyed source expires a
        level by bar count. It is what keeps lookback bounded.

UNITS — none; a dimensionless direction. Scale-invariant (doubling every
price leaves the pulse unchanged), so it pools across assets directly.

Output:
    SignalSeries (timestamps x symbols) holding exactly {-1.0, 0.0, +1.0}
    or NaN (`output_domain` Binary, hard-guarded at run time). Causal, no
    repaint: a level exists only from its confirmation bar, and the pulse
    marks the break bar itself. A level is CONSUMED by its break — the
    same level never fires twice; the side is silent until a newer pivot
    confirms. On an outside bar that takes BOTH levels the two pulses sum
    and clip to 0 — one scalar per bar, never a stack, and 0 there means
    "both ways at once", not "nothing happened".

NaN semantics:
    The first `width` bars (leg_flip) / `2 * width` bars (fractal) hold no
    confirmed level, so no break is possible — but the bars are OBSERVED,
    so they emit 0.0, not NaN. NaN appears only on bars with a NaN in
    high/low/close: such a bar can neither break a level nor be broken
    (tracker state persists across it, so a level survives the gap and is
    still breakable afterwards). Never zero-filled where undefined: NaN
    means "unobserved bar", 0.0 means "observed, no break".

Caveats (research/06 §2.1, R5): the closest thing to evidence here is
Osler (2003/2005) — stop-loss orders cluster just beyond prior extremes
and their triggering produces price cascades, which is a documented reason
breaks ACCELERATE. That is evidence about order clustering, not a Keel
claim that trading a structure break pays; no controlled test of the BOS
construct itself has been published. Execution is bar-close: the pulse is
known at the break bar's close, so the earliest fill is the next bar.

Note: stops, targets, trails and other price-level rules are checked and filled at the bar's close, with no intra-bar measurement or execution, so a fill can be well past the level.

Example:
    # Globals(target_timeframe="1h"): PriceDataLoader() serves the 1h bars itself — no resampler
    Pipeline([
        {
            "bos": [PriceDataLoader(),
                    BreakOfStructure(width=5, trigger="close")],
            "flow": [TakerFlowLoader(side="net"), CumulativeSum(), ROC(period=6)],
        },
        # a break the flow agrees with (spec 01 §4 "confirmed BOS")
        ...
    ])

components.name: BreakerBlock
components.description:
Track ICT breaker and mitigation blocks — a failed block whose role flips — and emit the signed ATR distance to the nearest active one.

Use for the "the level that failed now holds" family of SMC entries.
The sequence, bullish, is fixed and agreed by every source
(smc-trader-cohort research/05 §9): a swing low, then a swing high,
then a leg that FAILS to continue down, then a close back above that
swing high (the structure shift). The zone is the down-closing candle
inside the failed leg — the failed bearish block — and it is expected to
act as demand on the way back. The component keeps every unmitigated
one as an active zone and reports the signed ATR distance from the close
to the nearest, exactly as `OrderBlock` and `FairValueGap` do.

THE `mode` AXIS IS A CLASSIFIER, NOT A VARIANT (R4, research/05 §9). In
ICT canon the raid is what NAMES the pattern: a BREAKER is the flip
where the failing leg first took out the prior extreme (the swing low,
for a bullish breaker) — "find the raid, wait for the failure to
confirm, mark the breaker" (LuxAlgo). A MITIGATION BLOCK is "the same
role-flip without that raid": the failing leg did NOT take the prior
extreme (LuxAlgo, howtotrade, opofinance, TFlab all agree). They are two
named things sharing one machine, which is why this is `mode` and not
`require_sweep: bool`. Breakers are graded higher-probability BY
PRACTITIONERS because of the raid (TFlab) — a folk grading, not a
measured one (see the caveat).

TAXONOMY CONFLICT, RECORDED AS FOUND: one educator (theicttrader) uses
"mitigation block" for a HELD order-block retest in trend continuation
instead — a minority reading. This component implements the role-flip
consensus above; the held-retest reading is `OrderBlock` with
mitigation="touch", not this component.

Axes (sourced defaults, spec 01 contract 3):
    mode: "breaker" (default) = the failing leg RAIDED the prior extreme;
        "mitigation" = it did not. The classifier above. When no prior
        opposite pivot has been confirmed yet the raid is undecidable
        and NO zone is born under either mode — never a default verdict.
    direction: "bullish" | "bearish" | "both" (default). A bullish
        breaker is demand below price, a bearish one supply above it.
    candle_select: which candle of the failed leg is the block.
        "extreme_in_leg" (default — LuxAlgo, smc.py: the candidate at
        the top of the failed move) or "last_opposite" (the candle of
        the "series" nearest the failure). BOTH are restricted to
        candles that closed against the breaker's direction, which is
        LuxAlgo's own wording for a breaker and is the one way this
        differs from `OrderBlock`'s selection.
    zone: "full_range" (default — LuxAlgo, smc.py) or "body" (the ICT
        mirrors). Contested exactly as for order blocks: "some traders
        use bodies only, others the full range" (LuxAlgo).
    mitigation: "touch" (default — smc.py), "midpoint" (the ICT mean
        threshold, 50%) or "close_through" (LuxAlgo's invalidation, "a
        clean trade back through the whole zone"). Tested from the bar
        AFTER birth.
    max_range_atr: LuxAlgo's volatility filter — a candle whose own
        range reaches this many ATR is not eligible. Default 0.0 = OFF;
        2.0 reproduces LuxAlgo's `range < threshold * 2`.
    expiry_bars: the single bound on EVERY piece of state (default 200) —
        an unbroken swing level stops being breakable `expiry_bars` bars
        after confirmation, AND a block is dropped `expiry_bars` bars
        after birth. A KEEL CONVENTION, not a practitioner one.
    output: "distance" (default) = signed ATR distance (below); "edge" =
        the nearest active block's invalidation boundary PRICE, for an AtEntry(slot=...) structure stop and RiskSizer(distance=...).
    detector: pivot rule — "fractal" (default) or "leg_flip" (LuxAlgo).
    width: swing width in bars for the pivots whose break confirms the
        role flip (default 5) — the SAME axis the structure family
        takes, spelled the same way. The sourced ladder is 1 (ICT's
        short-term high), 5 (LuxAlgo's hardcoded INTERNAL structure)
        and 50 (its SWING structure, and smc.py's `swing_length`
        default); `structure.TIER_WIDTHS` is that named pair. It is ONE
        CONTINUOUS AXIS (>= 1, typically 1..100), not two rungs: the
        two named readings remain reachable as the values 5 and 50, and
        every width between and beyond them is now available too. The default
        follows the internal reading — a width-50 fractal confirms only
        a handful of levels per 500 bars, too sparse to birth blocks on
        a normal backtest window. research/05 §1, §3.
    atr_period: bars in the ATR reference (default 14) — the simple mean
        true range of the bars ENDING AT t-1.

Note there is NO `confirm` axis: unlike an order block, the confirmation
of a breaker is fixed at "close beyond the broken extreme plus the
structure shift" in ALL sources (research/05 §9), so it is machinery,
not an interpretation.

UNITS — "distance" is in ATR multiples (unit-free, comparable across
assets); "edge" is in price units. `max_range_atr` is an ATR multiple.

Output:
    SignalSeries (timestamps x symbols), causal, no repaint. "distance":
    > 0 outside every active block, 0 exactly on an edge, < 0 inside
    (minus the depth to the nearest edge / ATR). Nearest = smallest such
    value across active blocks (an enclosing block wins; ties go to the
    older one). NaN when none is active.
    THE BAR THAT REACHES A BLOCK REPORTS IT (Q-1020): the output at bar
    t is computed over every block alive at t's close, including the
    one(s) bar t mitigates — so under the default "touch" the first bar
    whose low reaches a bullish block emits its distance (<= 0 when the
    close is inside), and the block is gone from the NEXT bar on. That
    touch bar is the bar-close entry ("price is in the block"); a
    durable in-block mask over several bars needs mitigation="midpoint"
    or "close_through".
    A block is BORN at the close of the CONFIRMING bar — the bar whose
    close completes the structure shift, never at the block candle's own
    (earlier) bar — and is tested for mitigation from the next bar on.

NaN semantics:
    A bar with NaN in open/high/low/close emits NaN and neither births
    nor mitigates a block (state untouched; it still ages toward
    expiry), and can never BE the block candle. A NaN inside the ATR
    window blanks the reference for `atr_period` bars: "distance" is NaN
    over those bars even with active blocks ("edge" still reports). A
    flat tape (ATR 0) has no reference — NaN, never a division by zero.
    A failed leg with no qualifying candle, or an undecidable raid,
    births NO block. Never zero-filled.

Caveats (research/05 §9, research/06, R5): no controlled test of breaker
or mitigation blocks has ever been published; the practitioner grading
that breakers beat mitigation blocks rests on the raid narrative, not on
measurement, and the two dominant zone conventions disagree. Offered as
an interpretation of the tape, NEVER as a Keel claim. Execution is
bar-close.

Note: stops, targets, trails and other price-level rules are checked and filled at the bar's close, with no intra-bar measurement or execution, so a fill can be well past the level.

Example:
    # Globals(target_timeframe="1h"): PriceDataLoader() serves the 1h bars itself — no resampler
    Pipeline([
        PriceDataLoader(),
        BreakerBlock(mode="breaker", direction="bullish",
                     mitigation="close_through"),
        RangeSelector(low_threshold=-10.0, high_threshold=0.0),   # close inside a live breaker
        EqualWeightSizer(target_leverage=1.0),
    ])

components.name: BreakoutDistance
components.description:
Compute continuous breakout distance from rolling channel midpoint as a trend-following signal.

Use after VolatilityAdjustedPriceSeries to measure how far price has broken
beyond its recent range, producing a continuous (not binary) breakout strength
signal already in vol-normalized units. Feed into ForecastScaler for
standardized forecasts. Prefer over binary breakout flags when signal
magnitude matters for position sizing.

Output:
    Unbounded, already vol-normalized. Positive = price above channel midpoint
    (uptrend/long breakout), negative = below (downtrend/short breakout).
    Zero = price at exact channel midpoint. NaN during warmup (lookback bars).

Formula:
    net = 2 * adj_price - (rolling_high + rolling_low)
    where rolling_high/low are computed over lookback bars
    (shifted by 1 bar when exclude_current=True to avoid lookahead)

Example:
    VolatilityAdjustedPriceSeries(vol_span=32) -> BreakoutDistance(lookback=20) -> ForecastScaler()

components.name: CCI
components.description:
Compute Commodity Channel Index (CCI), an unbounded momentum oscillator measuring deviation from the statistical mean price.

Use for trend-following or mean reversion signals. CCI measures how far the typical
price deviates from its moving average in terms of mean deviation units. Values beyond
+/-100 indicate strong trend; extreme values (+/-200) suggest overbought/oversold.
Requires high/low/close data. Prefer CCI over RSI when you want an unbounded indicator
that can distinguish between moderate and extreme momentum.

Output:
    Unbounded, centered around 0. Typically [-200, +200] but can exceed during
    strong trends. Positive = bullish momentum, negative = bearish.
    NaN during warmup (`period` bars).

Formula:
    TP = (high + low + close) / 3
    CCI = (TP - SMA(TP, period)) / (0.015 * mean_deviation(TP, period))

Example:
    CCI(period=20) -> CrossSectionalZScore() -> WingsTransform(threshold=1.5)

components.name: CDFTransform
components.description:
Compute empirical CDF percentile rank over a rolling window for distribution-free normalization.

Use when you want to know where the current value sits relative to its own recent
history without assuming normality. Similar to RollingPercentile but semantically
framed as a CDF transform. Good for regime detection (e.g., "is volatility in the
top 10% of recent history?"). Place before threshold-based filters or regime gates.

Output:
    Range [0, 1]. 0 = at rolling minimum, 1 = at rolling maximum. 0.5 = median
    of rolling window. NaN during warmup period.

Formula:
    output = rolling_rank(x, window, pct=True)

Example:
    ATR(period=14) -> CDFTransform(window=120) -> ThresholdCross(upper=0.9, mode="long_only")

components.name: CMO
components.description:
Compute Chande Momentum Oscillator (CMO), a bounded momentum indicator using the ratio of up and down price movement.

Use as a momentum or mean reversion signal similar to RSI but on a symmetric [-100, +100]
scale centered at zero. Only requires close prices. CMO differs from RSI by being
symmetric around zero (no 50-midline bias), making it easier to use with threshold-based
transforms. Prefer CMO over RSI when you want a zero-centered oscillator for cleaner
signal processing with WingsTransform or similar dead-zone filters.

Output:
    Range [-100, +100]. Positive = bullish momentum (up moves dominate),
    negative = bearish (down moves dominate). Zero = equal up/down movement.
    NaN during warmup (`period` bars).

Formula:
    CMO = ((sum_up - sum_down) / (sum_up + sum_down)) * 100
    where sum_up = sum of positive price changes over period
          sum_down = sum of absolute negative price changes over period

Example:
    CMO(period=14) -> CrossSectionalZScore() -> ForecastScaler()

Prefer CMO over RSI when you want a zero-centered oscillator for cleaner signal processing with WingsTransform or similar dead-zone filters.

components.name: ChangeOfCharacter
components.description:
Fire a signed {-1, 0, +1} pulse only on the structure breaks that REVERSE the trend (CHoCH).

Use as the SMC "the trend just turned" event — the entry trigger most
educator playbooks hang a reversal setup on: +1 when an upward break ends
a down-structure, -1 when a downward break ends an up-structure, 0 on
every other observed bar. `BreakOfStructure` is the same detector without
the classification: it fires on EVERY break of the last confirmed swing
level, and this component is the reversal SUBSET of that set, so
`BreakOfStructure - ChangeOfCharacter` is the pure-continuation (BOS
proper) recipe. Both read the same one owner of trigger semantics
(`structure.structure_events` / `structure.level_breaks`), so the two can
never drift apart. Every contested clause is a parameter pinned to the
school that uses it (smc-trader-cohort research/05 §1, §3, §4).

Axes (sourced defaults, spec 01 contract 3):
    which_pivot: WHICH break counts as the turn — the genuinely contested
        clause, and the one that changes when you get filled.
        "last_swing" (default) = the trend-state flip: a break of the last
        confirmed swing level AGAINST the prevailing direction is a CHoCH,
        with the trend set by the previous break. Same level as a BOS,
        different label — this is LuxAlgo's rule, and smc.py's 4-pivot
        inequality pattern is its equivalent. It is the default because
        BOTH deployed implementations run it.
        "bos_origin" = the educator school: "a valid CHoCH must break the
        swing that produced the last BOS" (quantum-algo, justwolves). The
        BOS records its ORIGIN — the most recently confirmed opposite-side
        pivot at the break bar — and only taking THAT level turns the
        trend. Strictly later and rarer; a counter-trend break of a mere
        last swing that never reaches the origin is NEITHER a BOS nor a
        CHoCH under this school, and is dropped rather than relabelled.
        The valid-pullback filter (>= 3 opposing candles / >= 50%
        retracement, the structure-mapping school) is a documented later
        widening, not a v1 option.
    detector: "fractal" (default, ICT's symmetric shape / smc.py) or
        "leg_flip" (LuxAlgo's rolling-extreme state flip, NOT a fractal —
        research/05 §1 V3). See `SwingPivot` for the full contract.
    width: swing width in bars (default 5). The sourced ladder is 1 (ICT's
        short-term high), 5 and 50; LuxAlgo runs 5 (internal) and 50
        (swing) as two parallel structures and labels breaks on each
        (`structure.TIER_WIDTHS` is that named pair), and smc.py's
        `swing_length` default is 50. The default follows the internal
        tier — a width-50 fractal confirms only a handful of levels per
        500 bars, so its reversal pulse is too sparse to be a default.
    trigger: "close" (default) = the body must close beyond the level, the
        dominant educator rule ("a wick alone does not confirm a structure
        break") and smc.py's `close_break=True`; "wick" = the high/low
        alone (smc.py `close_break=False`).
    expiry_bars: safety bound — an untaken level stops being breakable
        `expiry_bars` bars after its confirmation (default 200), and the
        PREVAILING TREND set by a break expires the same number of bars
        after that break (Q-1023): with no confirming break inside the
        span the structure is unknown again and the next break is a BOS.
        Under "bos_origin" the recorded ORIGIN expires with the trend
        that recorded it. A KEEL CONVENTION, not a practitioner one: no
        surveyed source expires a level or a trend by bar count; it is
        what makes the state BOUNDED (spec 01 contract 4) — a run
        started at any bar agrees with the full history after
        `2 * width + 2 * expiry_bars` bars.

UNITS — none; a dimensionless direction. Scale-invariant (doubling every
price leaves the pulse unchanged), so it pools across assets directly.

Output:
    SignalSeries (timestamps x symbols) holding exactly {-1.0, 0.0, +1.0}
    or NaN (`output_domain` Binary, hard-guarded at run time). Causal, no
    repaint: levels exist only from their confirmation bar and the pulse
    marks the turning bar itself. The FIRST break of a series has no trend
    to oppose, so it is never a CHoCH under either school. On a bar
    carrying reversals both ways the pulses sum and clip to 0 — one scalar
    per bar, never a stack.

NaN semantics:
    The warmup bars carry no confirmed level, so no turn is possible — but
    they are OBSERVED and emit 0.0, not NaN. NaN appears only on bars with
    a NaN in high/low/close: such a bar can neither turn the structure nor
    be turned (state persists across it). Never zero-filled where
    undefined: NaN means "unobserved bar", 0.0 means "observed, no turn".

Caveats (research/06 §2.1/§2.5, R5): no controlled test of the CHoCH
construct has been published — the surveyed evidence reaches only as far
as Osler (2003/2005) on stop clustering beyond prior extremes, which
explains why breaks accelerate, not that trading a labelled reversal pays.
The two `which_pivot` schools disagree about roughly when a turn exists at
all, which is itself the honest reason this is a parameter and not a
constant. Execution is bar-close: the pulse is known at the turning bar's
close, so the earliest fill is the next bar.

Note: stops, targets, trails and other price-level rules are checked and filled at the bar's close, with no intra-bar measurement or execution, so a fill can be well past the level.

Example:
    # Globals(target_timeframe="1h"): PriceDataLoader() serves the 1h bars itself — no resampler
    Pipeline([
        {
            "turn": [PriceDataLoader(),
                     ChangeOfCharacter(which_pivot="bos_origin", width=5)],
            "zone": [PriceDataLoader(),
                     FairValueGap(direction="bullish")],
        },
        # a turn, then a retrace into the imbalance it left
        ...
    ])
components.usage_hint: Use as the SMC "the trend just turned" event — the entry trigger most educator playbooks hang a reversal setup on: +1 when an upward break ends a down-structure, -1 when a downward break ends an up-structure, 0 on every other observed bar. `BreakOfStructure` is the same detector without the classification: it fires on EVERY break of the last confirmed swing level, and this component is the reversal SUBSET of that set, so `BreakOfStructure - ChangeOfCharacter` is the pure-continuation (BOS proper) recipe. Both read the same one owner of trigger semantics (`structure.structure_events` / `structure.level_breaks`), so the two can never drift apart. Every contested clause is a parameter pinned to the school that uses it (smc-trader-cohort research/05 §1, §3, §4).
