components.name: ConstantForecast
components.description:
Emit a fixed forecast value for every loaded asset and timestamp — the hold / index-basket entry: a basket held at constant conviction, sized by the normalizer after it.

Accepts either OHLCVDict (raw loader output) or an existing
ForecastSeries / DataFrame. Both produce a ForecastSeries with every
non-NaN cell set to ``value`` and NaN cells preserved (no position for
missing data). The two input forms cover the two natural usage patterns:

1. Index / basket entry — buy the basket and hold it at constant
   conviction: PriceDataLoader → ConstantForecast(value=10) →
   ForecastWeightNormalizer.
   Emits a constant forecast for every asset the loader returned. The
   canonical entry point for index strategies that do not need a signal
   in front.

2. Directional pair / basket leg: after AssetSelect or GroupAssetFilter
   inside a Parallel branch, ConstantForecast fixes the leg's direction
   and magnitude. NaN cells from the upstream selector mark assets the
   leg should ignore.

Not for use after signal, ranking, or filtering components
(QuantileRangeSelector, CrossSectionalZScore, QuantileRankTransform,
etc.): those carry direction and magnitude in their output values, and
ConstantForecast would overwrite them (including 0.0, which represents
"no position" in BinarySignal/mask outputs).

Output:
    Same shape as input. All non-NaN cells set to ``value``.
    NaN cells preserved (no position for missing data).

Examples:
    # Index basket entry — no signal needed
    # Globals(target_timeframe="1d", bar_offset="12h"): PriceDataLoader() serves 1d on the 12h grid — no resampler
    PriceDataLoader(symbols=["VVV", "RENDER", "IO", "TAO"])
    -> ConstantForecast(value=10)
    -> ForecastWeightNormalizer(target_leverage=1.0)

    # Dollar-balanced pair — direction set per leg; each leg sizes to
    # WeightSeries before WeightConcatenator, and the book's gross
    # leverage is the sum of the leg targets (0.5 + 0.5)
    {
        "long": [AssetSelect(symbols=["BTC"]), ConstantForecast(value=10),
                 ForecastWeightNormalizer(target_leverage=0.5)],
        "short": [AssetSelect(symbols=["ZK"]), ConstantForecast(value=-10),
                  ForecastWeightNormalizer(target_leverage=0.5)],
    } -> WeightConcatenator()

    # WRONG — QuantileRangeSelector outputs 1.0/0.0, not NaN.
    # ConstantForecast will overwrite both, destroying the mask:
    # QuantileRangeSelector() -> ConstantForecast(value=10)  # BUG: all assets get 10

Estimate the correlation matrix between forecast rules.

Computes inter-rule correlations from a dict of forecast DataFrames.
Uses delta-forecasts (first differences) for correlation estimation.

components.name: CrossSectionalDemedian
components.description:
Demedian each row and scale by a SLOW time-series normalizer — a dispersion-PRESERVING cross-section.

The deliberate opposite of CrossSectionalZScore: rank-z forces the same
N(0,1) shape every bar, so a day with tiny cross-sectional spread
produces the same forecast magnitudes as a day with huge spread —
"leveraging up on weak information" (Carver's warning against
dispersion-normalized carry). This transform subtracts the row median,
then divides by a slow ROLLING MEAN of the row std, so day-to-day
dispersion passes through to signal size: wide days produce big
forecasts, thin days produce small ones.

Use where the cross-sectional spread IS information — e.g. funding-carry
sleeves, where a 200bps funding-spread day genuinely warrants more risk
than a 5bps day. Keep CrossSectionalZScore where only ranking matters
(trend/momentum cross-sections; measured worse with this transform).

Output:
    Row-demedianed values divided by the slow scale; approximately
    zero-median per row, magnitude proportional to current dispersion
    relative to its recent average. NaN preserved from input.

Formula:
    y_i(t) = x_i(t) - median_j(x_j(t))
    s(t)   = rolling_mean(std_j(y_j(t)), slow_window)   [warmup: same-day std]
    z_i(t) = y_i(t) / s(t)

Population scoping (optional, ``population_mask_slot``):
    With a mask slot wired, BOTH the median and the dispersion are taken
    over the masked cells only and applied to everyone::

        m(t)   = median_j { x_j(t) : member }
        y_i(t) = x_i(t) - m(t)                            (all i)
        s(t)   = rolling_mean( std_j { y_j(t) : member }, slow_window )
        z_i(t) = y_i(t) / s(t)

    A MEMBER cell is therefore bit-identical to running this component
    unscoped on the member-only panel (same median, same std, same slow
    scale, same warmup fallback).

    THE BOUND THAT DISAPPEARS. Unscoped, an outlier inflates the very
    dispersion it is divided by, so the transform is self-limiting.
    Scoped, a non-member is divided by the MEMBER dispersion, which it
    does not enter: ``|x_i - m| / s`` is UNBOUNDED (measured z of 1385
    on a two-name member panel). Containment is external and mandatory —
    follow every scoped use with ``ForecastCapper``; see
    ``components.population_scoping``. A one-name member population
    yields an all-NaN row (ddof=1 std of one value), so a book cannot
    trade on a single-member cross-section.

Example:
    EWMATransform(window=30) -> CrossSectionalDemedian(slow_window=60) -> BenchmarkDemean() -> ForecastScaler()

This transform subtracts the row median, then divides by a slow ROLLING MEAN of the row std, so day-to-day dispersion passes through to signal size: wide days produce big forecasts, thin days produce small ones.

components.name: CrossSectionalDispersionRegime
components.description:
Measure cross-sectional return dispersion to detect high-differentiation regimes.

Use to identify periods where asset returns diverge, indicating opportunities for
cross-sectional strategies like relative value and momentum. Feed into RegimeGate
to enable cross-sectional signals only during high-dispersion periods, or into
RegimeScale to modulate forecast intensity. Complements
AveragePairwiseCorrelationRegime -- high dispersion with low correlation is the
ideal regime for cross-sectional alpha.

Output:
    Scalar GlobalSeries, non-negative (std of returns). Higher values indicate
    wider return spread across assets. Smoothed by rolling mean over lookback.
    NaN where fewer than 2 valid instrument returns are available, including
    missing-price observations and the return immediately following them.

Formula:
    raw = std(return_i) across instruments per timestamp
    signal = rolling_mean(raw, lookback)

Example:
    PriceDataLoader() -> Store('ohlcv') -> {
        "dispersion": [ExtractSeries(series_name='close'),
                       CrossSectionalDispersionRegime(ohlcv_slot='ohlcv', lookback=10)],
        "momentum": [ROC(period=20), ForecastScaler()],
    } -> RegimeScale(index_key='dispersion', signal_key='momentum')

components.name: CrossSectionalZScore
components.description:
Normalize signals by cross-sectional z-score relative to other assets at each timestamp for delta-neutral ranking.

Use for strategies where asset-relative ranking matters more than absolute levels
(e.g., long/short, delta-neutral). Placed after any indicator and before ForecastScaler
and ForecastCapper. Creates approximately zero-sum signals across assets. Prefer
RollingZScoreTransform when absolute deviation from historical norm matters instead.

Output:
    Unbounded, centered around 0 with mean ~ 0 across assets at each bar.
    Positive = strong vs peers, negative = weak vs peers. NaN preserved from input.

Formula:
    rank_i(t) = rank(x_i(t)) across N assets
    u_i(t) = rank_i(t) / (N + 1)
    z_i(t) = inverse_normal_cdf(u_i(t))

Population scoping (optional, ``population_mask_slot``):
    With a mask slot wired, the RANK POPULATION narrows to the masked
    cells while every cell — masked or not — is still scored::

        P(t)    = { x_j(t) : mask_j(t) == 1.0 and x_j(t) is not NaN }
        N(t)    = |P(t)|
        r_i(t)  = #{p in P : p < x_i} + 0.5 * #{p in P : p == x_i} + 0.5
        u_i(t)  = r_i(t) / (N(t) + 1)

    ``r`` is algebraically pandas' ``rank(method="average")`` over
    ``P(t)`` and ``N(t) + 1`` is the same denominator as above, so a
    MEMBER cell's z-score is bit-identical to running this component
    unscoped on the member-only panel: admitting or removing a
    non-member cannot move it. A non-member gets the mid-insertion rank
    it would occupy without displacing anyone — interior by
    construction (``Phi^-1`` never sees 0 or 1), but NOT inside the
    member panel's own extremes: a non-member above every member value
    lands at ``(N+0.5)/(N+1) > N/(N+1)``. Bound the result downstream
    (``ForecastCapper``); see ``components.population_scoping``.

    A row whose member population is EMPTY produces all-NaN, exactly as
    an unscoped row with no valid data does — never a fabricated score.

Example:
    ROC(period=10) -> CrossSectionalZScore() -> ForecastScaler(method="mean") -> ForecastCapper()

components.name: Crossover
components.description:
Compute the difference between two parallel signals (fast minus slow) — the crossover signal of trend-following and momentum strategies.

Use after a Parallel block that produces "fast" and "slow" branches (e.g.,
two EWMA smoothers with different spans). The canonical EWMAC pattern — a
moving average crossover — is
{"fast": [EWMA(window=2)], "slow": [EWMA(window=8)]} -> Crossover(). Feed
the output into ForecastScaler or CrossSectionalZScore for normalization.
Also the natural spread operator for pairs/basket intents — but ONLY when
both branches carry the same assets on the same clock (see the shape
contract below); a pair built from two disjoint AssetSelect legs is a
different component's job.

Output:
    Unbounded (fast - slow). Positive = fast signal above slow (bullish
    momentum), negative = fast below slow (bearish). Magnitude reflects
    divergence strength. NaN where either input is NaN — NaN in, NaN out,
    never a fill. Both branches must have exactly the same index and the
    same columns (same order); any mismatch raises ValueError naming the
    branches and the offending rows/columns — no silent alignment, no
    reindex, no forward-fill (v2; v1 NaN-aligned to an all-NaN frame).
    Inputs are float-coerced (see run()), so boolean branches are
    supported.

Note: "same length, different timestamps" with both branches on one clock
    is a SPAN difference (M-34) — report it, do not re-clock the branch;
    only a CLOCK difference is fixed by TargetSignalProjector() /
    TargetSignalResampler(). A projected or resampled branch already carries
    the run window's grid a native branch has (Q-1580).

Example:
    {"fast": [EWMA(window=4)], "slow": [EWMA(window=16)]} -> Crossover() -> ForecastScaler()

Also valid as a directional combiner of two boolean/binary entry
conditions: {"fast": [<long entry>], "slow": [<short entry>]} -> Crossover() yields +1
where only the long condition fires, -1 where only the short fires, and 0
otherwise (both/neither). Pair with ThresholdCross(upper=0.5, lower=-0.5)
to formalize as a BinarySignal.

Feed the output into ForecastScaler or CrossSectionalZScore for normalization. Also the natural spread operator for pairs/basket intents — but ONLY when both branches carry the same assets on the same clock (see the shape contract below); a pair built from two disjoint AssetSelect legs is a different component's job.

components.name: CrossoverCombinator
components.description:
Generate binary regime signals from a fast/slow crossover for trend detection and regime switching.

Use after computing two moving averages (fast and slow) to create a regime signal
that switches between bull and bear states. Input must be a DataFrame with columns
matching fast_key and slow_key. Commonly used with EWMA at different periods fed
through a Parallel step, then combined here for regime-based signal gating.

    (default 1) and bear_value (default -1). NaN when either crossover input
    is missing because the relative ordering is then unknown.

components.name: CumulativeReturnTransform
components.description:
Convert price series to cumulative returns for equity curve analysis and relative performance.

Use to transform raw prices into growth-factor curves (normalized, starting at 1.0)
or total-return percentages. Commonly used in regime detection pipelines to compare
asset performance over time, or as input to CrossSectionalAggregator for
market-wide return indices.

Output:
    When normalize=True: starts at 1.0, unbounded above 0. Value of 1.5 = +50% return.
    When normalize=False: starts at 0.0, unbounded. Value of 0.5 = +50% return.
    First row is always 1.0 (normalized) or 0.0 (raw).

Formula:
    pct = (P_t - P_{t-1}) / P_{t-1}
    normalized: cumprod(1 + pct)
    raw: cumprod(1 + pct) - 1

Example:
    PriceDataLoader() -> CumulativeReturnTransform(normalize=True) -> CrossSectionalAggregator()
components.usage_hint: Use to transform raw prices into growth-factor curves (normalized, starting at 1.0) or total-return percentages. Commonly used in regime detection pipelines to compare asset performance over time, or as input to CrossSectionalAggregator for market-wide return indices.

components.name: CumulativeSum
components.description:
Compute per-column running total (cumulative sum), over all history or reset each session.

Use to accumulate a flow-like series into a running total — the CVD
(cumulative volume delta) carrier: net taker flow in, CVD out. This is an
expanding-window operation, not rolling. NaN semantics are fixed (no knob,
one behavior): a NaN input cell yields NaN at that cell and accumulation
continues after it — the gap stays visible, is never treated as 0, and
never poisons the rest of the series. It supersedes
the deprecated CumulativeTransform(method="sum") as the cumsum owner.

Axes:
    reset: "none" (default) accumulates over the whole loaded window.
        "session" restarts the total at every session open, for
        session-anchored CVD and the exact session-VWAP recipe.
    session_mask_slot: REQUIRED when reset="session", and refused
        otherwise (a slot that could never be read is a wiring bug, not a
        default). Names the slot holding an in-session mask — values in
        {0.0, 1.0}, e.g. Store()d SessionMask output. CumulativeSum owns
        no calendar: every timezone/DST/weekend decision stays in the
        session family, and this component only reads where the mask
        says a session is running (component-expansion spec 02 D12).

Session semantics (reset="session"): a SESSION is a maximal run of
consecutive mask==1 bars, per column. The total restarts on each such
run's first bar and is NaN on every out-of-session bar — nothing carries
across a boundary. The mask must be a frame on the same index whose
columns cover the input's, and its values must be exactly {0.0, 1.0}: a
NaN or a 0.7 raises rather than being rounded, since a wrong boundary
silently mixes two sessions' totals.

Output:
    Running total, same units as input. With reset="none" the level is
    relative to the loaded window's start — a cumulative sum has no
    absolute level (CVD has no absolute level); honest uses are slopes,
    divergences, and window-local z-scores, and comparing levels across
    different windows is a category error. With reset="session" the level
    is relative to that session's open, which makes levels comparable
    ACROSS sessions (the point of the mode). NaN cells preserved.

Example:
    TakerFlowLoader(side="net") -> CumulativeSum()
    (any SignalSeries branch works today; TakerFlowLoader ships with the
    flow-loader family, W1 S3)

    # session-anchored CVD:
    {
        "session": [SessionMask(timezone="America/New_York"), Store("session")],
        "cvd": [TakerFlowLoader(side="net"),
                CumulativeSum(reset="session", session_mask_slot="session")],
    }
components.usage_hint: Use to accumulate a flow-like series into a running total — the CVD (cumulative volume delta) carrier: net taker flow in, CVD out. This is an expanding-window operation, not rolling. NaN semantics are fixed (no knob, one behavior): a NaN input cell yields NaN at that cell and accumulation continues after it — the gap stays visible, is never treated as 0, and never poisons the rest of the series. It supersedes the deprecated CumulativeTransform(method="sum") as the cumsum owner.

components.name: DEMA
components.description:
Compute Double Exponential Moving Average (DEMA), a reduced-lag trend-following moving average.

Use as a faster-responding alternative to EWMA for trend following. DEMA reduces the
inherent lag of a standard EMA by applying a double-smoothing correction. Output is in
price units, so it must be combined with another moving average for crossover signals
or normalized before cross-asset comparison. Prefer DEMA over EWMA when lag reduction
matters; use TEMA for even less lag at the cost of potential overshoot.

Output:
    In price units, tracks the smoothed close price. Responds faster to price
    changes than a standard EMA of the same period. NaN during warmup
    (`period` bars).

Formula:
    DEMA = 2 * EMA(close, period) - EMA(EMA(close, period), period)

Example:
    DEMA(period=20) -> Store("fast_ma")
    EWMA(window=60) -> Store("slow_ma")
components.usage_hint: Use as a faster-responding alternative to EWMA for trend following. DEMA reduces the inherent lag of a standard EMA by applying a double-smoothing correction. Output is in price units, so it must be combined with another moving average for crossover signals or normalized before cross-asset comparison. Prefer DEMA over EWMA when lag reduction matters; use TEMA for even less lag at the cost of potential overshoot.

parameters.description: EMA span for both smoothing passes. Shorter (10-20) closely tracks price, longer (30-60) captures broader trend. Default 30. Equivalent DEMA has roughly half the lag of a standard EMA at the same period.

Use when you need raw level changes rather than percentage returns. Useful for

percentage change is meaningless. Also serves as a simple derivative or
rate-of-change in absolute terms.

Formula:
    diff = x_t - x_{t-n}

Example:

components.name: DispersionWeightMapper
components.description:
Map cross-sectional return dispersion to dynamic time-series vs cross-sectional weight allocations.

Use to produce a weight DataFrame (w_ts, w_xs) that can be consumed by downstream
blending logic. High dispersion favors directional (TS) bets; low dispersion favors
relative-value (XS) ranking. For a single-step combine-and-blend, use
DispersionWeightedCombinator instead.

Output:
    DataFrame with columns [w_ts, w_xs]. Both in [min_weight, max_weight],
    summing to 1.0 at each timestamp. NaN during burn-in (~20 bars).

Formula:
    z = expanding_zscore(dispersion)
    w_ts = sigmoid(disp_coeff * z) * (max_w - min_w) + min_w
    w_xs = 1 - w_ts
    Smooth (EWMA half_life) then clip.

Example:
    {"dispersion": ...} -> DispersionWeightMapper(disp_coeff=1.0) -> ...

components.name: DispersionWeightedCombinator
components.description:
Blend time-series and cross-sectional forecasts with dynamic weights driven by return dispersion.

Use to combine a directional (TS) and a relative-value (XS) signal in a single
step, automatically allocating more to TS during high-dispersion regimes and more
to XS during low-dispersion regimes. For weight output only (without blending),
use DispersionWeightMapper.

The TS and XS branches must cover the same symbols; they are matched by
symbol name, not column position, and a different symbol set raises.

Output:
    Same scale as input forecasts (weighted blend). NaN during dispersion
    burn-in (~20 bars). Values reflect the TS/XS mix at each timestamp.

Formula:
    z = expanding_zscore(dispersion)
    w_ts = sigmoid(disp_coeff * z) * (max_w - min_w) + min_w
    w_xs = 1 - w_ts
    blended = w_ts * ts_signal + w_xs * xs_signal

Example:
    {"ts": ..., "xs": ..., "dispersion": ...} -> DispersionWeightedCombinator(ts_key="ts", xs_key="xs")

components.name: Displacement
components.description:
Flag ICT displacement candles — bars whose body dwarfs the recent range — as a signed {-1, 0, +1} pulse.

Use as the "strong push" confirmation the SMC vocabulary hangs on: the
impulse that validates a fair value gap ("valid FVG"), the leg an order
block is the origin of, the displacement half of a market structure
shift. Positive = an up impulse (close well above open), negative = a
down impulse, 0 = an ordinary bar. Gate or sequence it with the zone
components (e.g. an FVG touch AFTER a displacement) via RegimeGate, or
as the entry of a TradeManager; it is not a standalone forecast.

Axes (sourced, research/05 §7):
    body_atr_mult: body threshold in ATR multiples (default 1.5). Sources
        state magnitude relative to the surrounding tape, not in ATR:
        ictkillzone — body >= 1.5x the average preceding candle (the
        default's source; ATR is that average range), wicks < 25% of the
        range; backtrex — body >= 60-70% of the bar's own range;
        howtotrade — "no fixed threshold". The ATR denomination is a Keel
        normalization; the wick-share and body/range metrics are fixture
        material and candidate options, not v1 params.
    require_fvg: True = the impulse counts only if it leaves a fair value
        gap — the 3-bar core completing on the NEXT bar in the same
        direction (backtrex: "without a gap there is no displacement");
        False (default) = the FVG confirms, it does not define
        (ictkillzone). Genuinely contested; both truth values have named
        users. With True the pulse is emitted one bar LATER (at the bar
        that completes the gap), because that is when the gap is known —
        never at the impulse bar itself.
    atr_period: bars in the ATR reference (default 14): the simple mean
        true range of the `atr_period` bars ENDING AT t-1, so the impulse
        is never measured against a range it inflated.

Output:
    SignalSeries with values exactly in {-1.0, 0.0, +1.0} (output_domain
    Binary, hard-guarded at run time) or NaN; +1/-1 at displacement bars
    (or, with require_fvg, at the bar completing the gap the impulse
    left), 0 elsewhere. Unit-free — a body/ATR ratio test — so the pulse
    is identical at any price scale. Causal, no repaint: a bar's verdict
    reads bars <= t only and never changes.

NaN semantics:
    The first `atr_period + 1` bars are NaN (no ATR reference); with
    require_fvg the first `atr_period + 2`. A bar with NaN open/close
    (or a NaN inside its ATR window, which blanks the reference for
    `atr_period` bars) is NaN, never 0 — 0 means "measured, not an
    impulse". A flat tape (ATR 0) has no reference → NaN. With
    require_fvg, a NaN at the impulse bar or in either gap bar yields NaN
    at the completing bar.

Caveat (research/06): flow-backed moves are distinguishable from drift in
the order-flow-imbalance literature, but the candle-body construct itself
is untested; the measurable neighbor is TakerFlowLoader (a displacement
coinciding with taker imbalance). Offered as interpretation, not claim.

Example:
    # Globals(target_timeframe="1h"): PriceDataLoader() serves the 1h bars itself — no resampler
    Pipeline([
        {
            "impulse": [PriceDataLoader(), Displacement(body_atr_mult=1.5)],
            "gap": [PriceDataLoader(), FairValueGap(direction="bullish")],
        },
        ...  # sequence: an up impulse, then a return into the gap it left
    ])

Positive = an up impulse (close well above open), negative = a down impulse, 0 = an ordinary bar. Gate or sequence it with the zone components (e.g. an FVG touch AFTER a displacement) via RegimeGate, or as the entry of a TradeManager; it is not a standalone forecast.

components.name: DollarVolumeLoader
components.description:
Load dollar volume per bar (USDC): exact traded notional from trades, the 15m candle proxy before the trades era.

Use for dollar volume / notional turnover signals: liquidity floors
(e.g. an exact $10M/24h screen via a rolling sum), dollar-volume
regimes, notional-weighted universes, relative dollar volume, and as
the numerator of a rolling VWAP recipe. Unlike base-coin volume this IS
comparable across assets — it is the cross-sectional volume measure, and
the input every dollar-volume component version takes.

Exact vs proxy, spliced in ONE place: from the trades era (market_flow's
ARCHIVE_SERVABLE_START, the archive's first full UTC day) each bar is
sum(price × size) over
its trades (`pv_sum`); before it — where no trade-level notional exists —
each bar is the 15m capture's volume × close summed per 15m bar (the
`NotionalVolumeExtractor` quantity, back to each coin's first capture
bar, read through PriceDataLoader v3 at 15min). A bar
that straddles the boundary is the sum of its two parts. The provenance
block `dollar_volume_splice` names the boundary and every spliced bar,
so the approximation is always named, never silent.

UNITS — USDC notional. Sums are exact at every timeframe and offset.

Output:
    DollarVolumeSeries (a StreamSeries DataFrame, bar close labels x
    symbols). Zero means no trades in the bar; NaN means unobserved
    (pre-listing, a named archive gap, a capture bar the price path does
    not serve, past the observed frontier, or before the trades era on a
    clock finer than 15min) — never zero-filled.

Timeframe: omit `timeframe` to serve Globals.target_timeframe (and its
bar_offset); pass a literal for an explicit MTF branch.

Example:
    DollarVolumeLoader() -> RollingZScoreTransform(window=96)  # 24h window on 15m
    DollarVolumeLoader(timeframe="1d")

Unlike base-coin volume this IS comparable across assets — it is the cross-sectional volume measure, and the input every dollar-volume component version takes.

components.name: DonchianChannel
components.description:
Compute normalized price position within Donchian Channels for trend breakout detection.

Use to identify breakout and trend-following setups. The channel is defined by the highest
high and lowest low over the lookback period, making it purely price-range based (no
averaging). Values near 1 indicate price at period highs (bullish breakout), near 0 at
period lows (bearish breakout). Unlike BollingerBands and KeltnerChannel, Donchian uses
raw extremes rather than volatility-adjusted bands.

Output:
    Range [0, 1]. 0 = price at period low, 1 = price at period high, 0.5 = midrange.
    NaN during warmup (min_periods bars) or when channel width is zero.

Formula:
    upper = max(high, period)
    lower = min(low, period)
    output = (close - lower) / (upper - lower)

Example:
    PriceDataLoader() -> DonchianChannel(period=20) -> CrossSectionalZScore()

The channel is defined by the highest high and lowest low over the lookback period, making it purely price-range based (no averaging). Values near 1 indicate price at period highs (bullish breakout), near 0 at period lows (bearish breakout). Unlike BollingerBands and KeltnerChannel, Donchian uses raw extremes rather than volatility-adjusted bands.

components.name: DynamicEqualWeightAllocator
components.description:
Allocate equal weight (1/n_active) that dynamically adapts to the number of active positions.

Use when the number of concurrent positions varies over time and you want all active
positions to share capital equally. Automatically rebalances all active positions when
the portfolio composition changes (entry or exit). Placed after SelectionToSignalConverter
or InertiaManager. Prefer over FixedWeightAllocator when you don't know max positions in advance.

Output:
    Range [0, 1]. Entries get 1/n_active weight, exits get 0.0, holds get NaN
    (sparse). All active positions are rebalanced on any composition change
    (e.g., 9 to 8 assets: weights shift from 0.111 to 0.125).

Formula:
    weight = 1 / n_active_positions  (for all active assets on rebalance)

Example:
    SelectionToSignalConverter(hold_periods=5) -> DynamicEqualWeightAllocator()

components.name: EWMA
components.description:
Compute exponential weighted moving average (EWMA) of close prices for trend following and smoothing.

Use as a building block for trend-following strategies, typically paired with another
EWMA of different span to form a crossover signal (EWMAC). Output is in price units,
so not directly comparable across assets. For a crossover signal, use two EWMA
components and subtract via a signal composer. Prefer EWMA over DEMA/TEMA when you
want standard exponential smoothing without reduced-lag corrections.

Output:
    In price units, tracks the smoothed close price. NaN for the first
    `min_periods` bars (defaults to `window`). Always positive for positive
    price assets.

Formula:
    EWMA_t = alpha * close_t + (1 - alpha) * EWMA_{t-1}
    where alpha = 2 / (window + 1)

Example:
    EWMA(window=8) -> Store("fast_ma")
    EWMA(window=32) -> Store("slow_ma")
components.usage_hint: Use as a building block for trend-following strategies, typically paired with another EWMA of different span to form a crossover signal (EWMAC). Output is in price units, so not directly comparable across assets. For a crossover signal, use two EWMA components and subtract via a signal composer. Prefer EWMA over DEMA/TEMA when you want standard exponential smoothing without reduced-lag corrections.

parameters.description: EWMA span controlling smoothing weight. Shorter (4-16) = responsive (tracks price closely), longer (32-128) = smooth (captures macro trend). Common pairs for EWMAC crossover: (8, 32), (16, 64), (32, 128).

parameters.name: min_periods
parameters.description: Minimum observations before producing output. Defaults to `window`. Lower values start output earlier but with less stable estimates. Set to 1 for earliest possible output.

components.name: EWMATransform
components.description:
Apply exponential moving average smoothing to reduce noise while preserving signal trends.

Use as a generic noise filter between any indicator and downstream transforms.
Works on scores, normalized signals, or forecasts. Place after noisy indicators
(e.g., ROC, RSI) and before threshold or forecast scaling components. Prefer over
SMA when recent observations should carry more weight. Introduces minimal lag
compared to simple rolling mean of equivalent smoothness.

Output:
    Same scale and range as input, smoothed. No NaN introduced beyond input NaN
    (EWMA handles partial windows gracefully). Preserves polarity and magnitude.

Formula:
    s_t = alpha * x_t + (1 - alpha) * s_{t-1}
    where alpha = 2 / (window + 1)

Example:
    ROC(period=10) -> EWMATransform(window=5) -> CrossSectionalZScore()

Place after noisy indicators (e.g., ROC, RSI) and before threshold or forecast scaling components. Prefer over SMA when recent observations should carry more weight. Introduces minimal lag compared to simple rolling mean of equivalent smoothness.

components.name: EmpiricalFDM
components.description:
Rescale combined forecast to restore target volatility.

Standalone step in sequential flow: ForecastSeries -> ForecastSeries.
Uses target/rolling_avg rescaling (empirical approach).

Production parameters preserved from the original combined FDM implementation:
- Cross-asset sum/count rolling approach (pools across all instruments)
- shift(1) prevents look-ahead bias
- EWMA smoothing with adjust=False
- First window_bars values set to NaN

Population scoping (optional, ``population_mask_slot``):
    The FDM is one number the whole panel is multiplied by, pooled over
    every instrument in the window — so one cell moves every established
    name's forecast. With a mask slot wired, the rolling sum and count
    run over the MASKED cells only; the resulting FDM series still
    multiplies the FULL frame. With no non-member cell in the panel the
    result is the unscoped FDM bit-for-bit.

    The pool is masked BEFORE ``shift(1)``, not after: ``member[t]`` is
    membership AT t, while the value at row t after the shift is ``|f|``
    from t-1, so masking after the shift admits each name's last
    pre-membership observation into the pool (measured max dFDM 0.0161).

    An EMPTY member pool yields NaN, never the neutral ``1.0`` the
    unscoped path substitutes — see ``components.population_scoping``.
components.usage_hint: Standalone step in sequential flow: ForecastSeries -> ForecastSeries. Uses target/rolling_avg rescaling (empirical approach).

components.name: EqualWeightAllocator
components.description:
Allocate equal weight (1/N) to each instrument for uniform risk distribution.

Use as the simplest instrument weighting scheme where each asset gets the same
allocation regardless of volatility or conviction. Placed after VolTargetWeightConverter
and before IDMPortfolioAggregator or LeverageCap. Prefer RiskParityAllocator
when assets have meaningfully different volatility profiles.

Output:
    Weighted blocks (DataFrame, same shape as input). Each instrument's blocks
    are multiplied by 1/N where N is the number of assets. Weights sum to 1.0
    unless ``min_weight``/``max_weight`` bind — the bounds are applied LAST
    and are hard, so a binding cap leaves gross below 1.0 (excess to cash)
    and a binding floor leaves it above.

Formula:
    weighted_blocks[asset] = subsystem_blocks[asset] * (1 / N)

Example:
    VolTargetWeightConverter(return_vol_slot="return_vol")
    -> EqualWeightAllocator() -> IDMPortfolioAggregator(...)

Placed after VolTargetWeightConverter and before IDMPortfolioAggregator or LeverageCap. Prefer RiskParityAllocator when assets have meaningfully different volatility profiles.

parameters.description: Hard floor on each instrument's weight, applied AFTER normalization. Default 0.0 (no floor). 0.05 guarantees at least 5% in each asset — and note the floor is FUNDED, so with N assets and min_weight * N > 1 the book's gross rises above 1.0. Only ever binds here when 1/N is below it.

Assign equal weight (1/n_active) to all active assets on rebalance dates for passive portfolio construction.

Use after CalendarRebalance or any component producing rebalance flags (1.0 on
rebalance dates, NaN elsewhere). Also accepts binary universe masks (1.0 = included,
0.0 = excluded). On rebalance rows, active assets get 1/n_active weight. Non-rebalance
rows produce NaN (sparse convention). Ideal for index-tracking or passive strategies.

    other finite flag (0.0 = excluded) gets 0.0, so an excluded asset is
    exited and an all-zero mask goes flat. NaN flags stay NaN, and
    non-rebalance rows are NaN (sparse convention: NaN = hold). Weights sum

components.name: EqualWeightSizer
components.description:
Split a fixed gross leverage evenly across open positions, keeping partial exits and adds in the size.

Version 2 of the default entry/exit sizer ("equal weight", "1/n", "split
the book evenly"). On a signal it is v1 exactly: ``signal × target_leverage
/ Σ|signal|`` per bar, clipped to ±``max_weight``. After a
``TradeManager``'s ``Exposure()`` it sizes UNITS: each open name gets one
unit's weight (the 1/n split over the names that are open), multiplied by
the units it holds, so a trade that took half off (``Reduce(fraction=0.5)``)
holds half the weight and a trade that added a unit (``ScaleIn``) holds
twice. v1 would size 0.5 and 2 units exactly like 1.

Formula, after Exposure() (per bar t, per asset i, X = units held × direction):
    unit_i[t] = sign(X_i[t]);  out_i[t] = v1(unit)_i[t] × |X_i[t]|

so ``max_weight`` caps ONE UNIT; a name holding two units can hold twice
the cap. On a ternary exposure (no partials or adds) the output equals
v1's bit for bit. Opening or closing a name re-prices every open name
(the 1/n term, see v1); adding to one does not.

The units path is taken only for the exact frame ``Exposure()`` returned.
A transformed exposure (``Clip``, a combiner, a scale) is a signal again
and is sized by v1's rule.

Example:
    TradeManager(entries="entries", prices="ohlcv") ->
      {"tp": [TakeProfit(pct=0.10, fraction=0.5)], "stop": [StopLoss(pct=0.05)]} ->
      Exposure() -> EqualWeightSizer(target_leverage=1.0, max_weight=0.3)

parameters.description: Gross exposure to divide among the open positions, in units of equity. 1.0 (default) = fully invested, 0.5 = half the book in cash, 2.0 = 2x leveraged. Each open name gets ``target_leverage / Σ|signal|`` of that bar's row, so the level is set here and nowhere else. Lower it when a downstream risk overlay should have room to work; raise it only against a venue's real margin limit.

The excess goes to CASH — gross exposure falls below target_leverage — it is not redistributed to the other names. Set it whenever the strategy can plausibly narrow to one or two names; leave it None only for a book with a reliably wide active set.

components.name: Exit
components.description:
Closes the whole trade on the first bar its 0/1 mask is 1; the branch name is the exit
reason: the action for stop loss, take profit, trailing stop, time and signal exits.

Position layer: TradeManager turns entry signals into a Position; each rule is a reader, then
ordinary components, then an action (Exit, Reduce, ScaleIn, AllowEntry). Several exits on one
bar close the trade once; the reason is their names, sorted, joined with "+".

Example:
    TradeManager(entries="entries", prices="ohlcv") ->
      {"stop": [TradeReturn(), BelowThresholdFilter(threshold=-0.05, inclusive=True), Exit()],
       "target": [TradeReturn(), AboveThresholdFilter(threshold=0.10, inclusive=True), Exit()]} ->
      Exposure() -> FixedWeightSizer(weight_per_position=0.1)

Note: stops, targets, trails and other price-level rules are checked and filled at the bar's close, with no intra-bar measurement or execution, so a fill can be well past the level.
Note: a ±1 signal is not a mask: test it with a filter first.
Note: a market exit's bar also refuses a new entry.
components.usage_hint: Position layer: TradeManager turns entry signals into a Position; each rule is a reader, then ordinary components, then an action (Exit, Reduce, ScaleIn, AllowEntry). Several exits on one bar close the trade once; the reason is their names, sorted, joined with "+".

components.name: Exposure
components.description:
Turns a Position into its exposure (units held, signed) as an ordinary signal, for books that are combined before sizing (ForecastCombiner across several TradeManagers).

Position layer: TradeManager turns entry signals into a Position; each rule is a reader, then
ordinary components, then an action (Exit, Reduce, ScaleIn, AllowEntry). Exposure() ends the
rules: every rule above it is evaluated here jointly, trade by trade, and an ordinary sizer or a
combiner follows it (RiskSizer takes the Position instead).

Nothing turns a Position into numbers implicitly: a sizer, a combiner or
any other step that receives the Position itself refuses it
(``POSITION_NEEDS_EXPOSURE``).

Output:
    A frame on the entries grid: +1 / -1 × units held after each bar's
    events (1 unit per trade unless ``Reduce``/``ScaleIn`` change it), 0
    when flat, NaN before an asset's first entry value. With no
    ``Reduce``/``ScaleIn`` rule the values are in {-1, 0, 1}.

Sizing after it:
    A unit is the sizer's weight per position: ``FixedWeightSizer`` keeps
    partials and adds as they are; size-preserving versions of the other
    binary sizers do the same. A sizer that sizes by sign would erase a
    partial and is refused (``SIZER_ERASES_SIZE``). Transforming the
    exposure first (a Clip, a combiner) makes it an ordinary signal again.

Diagnostics:
    Each realisation publishes its trades table, legs and report (entries
    blocked per gate, refused by reason, per-rule fire counts) for the
    run summary.

Note: it goes between the rules and every sizer except RiskSizer, and before a combiner.
Note: a transformed exposure (Clip, ...) is sized as a signal.

components.name: ExtractSeries
components.description:
Extract a single price field (close, open, high, low, volume) from an OHLCV dict into a flat DataFrame.

Use as the first step in a pipeline branch when you need a specific price field
rather than the full OHLCV structure. Produces a DataFrame with symbols as columns
and timestamps as index. Case-insensitive column matching.

This is how you use the raw price itself as a signal: extract the close
price series, then compare it against an indicator — e.g. price minus
moving average (spot price vs EMA distance), price relative to a rolling
high/low, or feeding close prices directly into any signal transform.

Volume caution: series_name="volume" extracts raw BASE-COIN volume, whose
unit differs per asset. Do not feed it into cross-sectional selectors or
rankers (TopNAssetSelector, CrossSectionalZScore, quantile selectors)
directly — "top N by volume" would select the highest-supply tokens, not
the most-traded ones. Use DollarVolumeLoader (traded notional) — or
NotionalVolumeExtractor, the candle volume × close proxy — for liquidity
or dollar-volume ranking; extracted base volume is fine for per-asset use
(e.g. RollingZScoreTransform, RelativeVolume-style ratios).

Output:
    DataFrame (timestamps x symbols). Values match the original price field.
    No NaN introduced beyond what exists in the source data.

Example:
    PriceDataLoader() -> ExtractSeries(series_name="close") -> ROC(period=10)
components.usage_hint: Use as the first step in a pipeline branch when you need a specific price field rather than the full OHLCV structure. Produces a DataFrame with symbols as columns and timestamps as index. Case-insensitive column matching.

components.name: FairValueGap
components.description:
Track ICT fair value gaps (3-bar imbalance zones) and emit the signed ATR distance to the nearest active gap.

Use for SMC "imbalance" entries and gap-fill logic: a fair value gap
(FVG, also "imbalance" / "inefficiency") is the price range a fast
three-bar move skipped — the third bar's low sits above the first bar's
high (bullish) or its high below the first bar's low (bearish). The
component keeps every unfilled gap as an ACTIVE zone and reports how far
the close is from the nearest one, in ATR units, so "price is inside /
returning to an FVG" is a threshold recipe on this scalar (RangeSelector
/ AboveThresholdFilter): inside <= 0, approaching from outside is a
small positive number. Every interpretation axis below is a parameter
with each option pinned to the school that uses it (smc-trader-cohort
research/05 §2); Keel does not adjudicate whose FVG is correct.

Axes (sourced defaults, spec 01 contract 3):
    direction: "bullish" | "bearish" | "both" (default). Which gaps are
        tracked. A bullish gap is demand below price, a bearish gap supply
        above it.
    min_size_atr: minimum gap height in ATR units (default 0.0 = no size
        filter, the smc.py convention). LuxAlgo's "auto threshold" filters
        small gaps by a running-average size; ICT canon has no size rule.
        ATR denomination is a Keel normalization (no source states one).
    middle_candle: qualifier on the middle bar. "none" (default) = the pure
        3-bar core all sources agree on; "direction" = the middle bar must
        close in the gap's direction (smc.py); "close_beyond" = the middle
        bar must CLOSE beyond the first bar's extreme (LuxAlgo).
    fill: when a gap stops being active. "touch" (default) = first bar
        whose low reaches the gap top / high reaches the gap bottom
        (smc.py mitigation); "midpoint" = price reaches the 50% level
        (ICT "consequent encroachment"); "full" = price traverses the
        whole gap (LuxAlgo deletes the box). Tested from the bar AFTER
        the gap is born.
    expiry_bars: safety bound — a gap is dropped `expiry_bars` bars after
        its birth whether or not it filled (default 200). A KEEL
        CONVENTION, not a practitioner one: no surveyed source uses
        bar-count expiry (they fill or cap the displayed count); it is
        what keeps state bounded and warmup finite.
    require_displacement: True = the middle bar must also be a
        displacement candle (body >= 1.5x the ATR reference — ICT's
        "valid FVG" grading; the same test `Displacement` runs). Default
        False.
    output: "distance" (default) = signed ATR distance (below); "edge" =
        the nearest active gap's invalidation boundary PRICE (bottom of a
        bullish gap, top of a bearish one) for an AtEntry(slot=...) structure stop and RiskSizer(distance=...).
        One scalar series either
        way; "edge" carries price units and is not cross-asset comparable.
    atr_period: bars in the ATR reference (default 14). The reference at
        bar t is the simple mean true range of the `atr_period` bars ENDING
        AT t-1, so a pattern is never measured against its own range.

UNITS — "distance" is in ATR multiples (unit-free, comparable across
assets); "edge" is in price units.

Output:
    SignalSeries (timestamps x symbols), causal, no repaint. "distance":
    > 0 outside every active gap (price distance to the nearest gap's
    nearest edge / ATR), 0 exactly on an edge, < 0 inside (minus the depth
    to the nearest edge / ATR) — so `<= 0` is the in-gap mask. Nearest =
    smallest such value across active gaps (an enclosing gap wins; ties go
    to the older gap). NaN when no gap is active.
    THE BAR THAT REACHES A GAP REPORTS IT (Q-1020): the output at bar t
    is computed over every gap alive at t's close, including the one(s)
    bar t fills — so under the default "touch" the FIRST bar whose low
    reaches a bullish gap emits its distance (< 0 when the close is
    inside), and the gap is gone from the NEXT bar on. That touch bar is
    the bar-close entry ("price is in the gap"). A durable in-gap mask
    over several bars needs fill="midpoint" (price may sit between the
    50% level and the near edge) or fill="full" (anywhere above the far
    edge) — the Example below uses "midpoint".
    A gap is BORN at the
    close of the bar that completes the 3-bar pattern and is reflected in
    that bar's output; it is tested for fill from the next bar on.

NaN semantics:
    The first `atr_period + 1` bars are NaN (ATR warmup: the reference at
    bar t averages the `atr_period` true ranges ending at t-1 and the
    first true range is undefined for want of a previous close, so the
    earliest defined reference — and hence the earliest possible birth —
    is at bar `atr_period + 1`). A bar with NaN in open/high/low/
    close emits NaN and neither births nor fills a gap (state untouched;
    it still ages toward expiry); a NaN inside the ATR window blanks the
    reference for `atr_period` bars — no gap is born and "distance" is
    NaN over those bars even with active gaps ("edge" still reports). A
    flat tape (ATR 0) has no reference — NaN, never a division by zero.
    Never zero-filled: NaN means "no active gap / undefined", not 0.

Caveats (research/06 §2.2, R5): the FVG construct has never been tested
in a controlled study; the academic gap-fill literature is mostly
negative on exploitability and the vendor "70% fill" figures carry no
matched-control baseline. Offered as an interpretation, never as a Keel
claim. Execution is bar-close: "in the gap" means the CLOSE is in the
gap.

Note: stops, targets, trails and other price-level rules are checked and filled at the bar's close, with no intra-bar measurement or execution, so a fill can be well past the level.

Example:
    # Globals(target_timeframe="1h"): PriceDataLoader() serves the 1h bars itself — no resampler
    Pipeline([
        PriceDataLoader(),
        FairValueGap(direction="bullish", fill="midpoint", middle_candle="direction"),
        RangeSelector(low_threshold=-10.0, high_threshold=0.0),   # close inside an unfilled bullish gap
        EqualWeightSizer(target_leverage=1.0),
    ])
components.usage_hint: Use for SMC "imbalance" entries and gap-fill logic: a fair value gap (FVG, also "imbalance" / "inefficiency") is the price range a fast three-bar move skipped — the third bar's low sits above the first bar's high (bullish) or its high below the first bar's low (bearish). The component keeps every unfilled gap as an ACTIVE zone and reports how far the close is from the nearest one, in ATR units, so "price is inside / returning to an FVG" is a threshold recipe on this scalar (RangeSelector / AboveThresholdFilter): inside <= 0, approaching from outside is a small positive number. Every interpretation axis below is a parameter with each option pinned to the school that uses it (smc-trader-cohort research/05 §2); Keel does not adjudicate whose FVG is correct.

components.name: FixedWeightAllocator
components.description:
Assign fixed equal weight (1/max_positions) to each entry signal for static position sizing.

Use for simple equal-weight strategies where the maximum number of concurrent
positions is known in advance. Placed after SelectionToSignalConverter or any
component producing entry/exit signals (+1/-1). Produces sparse weight output
(NaN = hold). Prefer DynamicEqualWeightAllocator when position count varies
and you need automatic rebalancing.

Output:
    Range [0, 1/max_positions]. Entries get fixed weight, exits get 0.0,
    holds get NaN (sparse convention meaning "no change"). Weights are
    constant regardless of how many positions are actually active.

Formula:
    weight = 1 / max_positions  (for entries)

Example:
    SelectionToSignalConverter(hold_periods=5) -> FixedWeightAllocator(max_positions=10)

components.name: FixedWeightSizer
components.description:
Give every open position the same fixed weight, letting gross exposure float with position count.

Use for "10% per trade", "fixed size", "same clip every time", "one unit
per name" — the sizing rule where each position's size is decided on its
own and the book's total exposure is whatever the sum comes to. The
trade-off against ``EqualWeightSizer`` is exact: this pins the POSITION and
lets gross float; that one pins GROSS and lets the position float.

Formula (per bar t, per asset i):
    out_i[t] = signal_i[t] × weight_per_position

That is the whole computation — one elementwise multiply, no row
normalization and no cross-asset term. Consequences worth stating:

- Gross exposure is ``weight_per_position × Σ|signal|``: 5 open names at
  0.1 = 0.5x, 10 = 1.0x, 30 = 3.0x. Nothing here bounds it. Put
  ``LeverageCap`` downstream if the book must not exceed a limit.
- Opening or closing a name does NOT move any other name's weight, so
  there is no 1/n rebalancing turnover — the fee term that dominates a
  clustered-entry EqualWeightSizer book is simply absent here.
- On a level-valued input (the units a Position holds after ``ScaleIn``
  adds, realised by ``Exposure()``) the weight scales linearly with the
  level: 3 units at 0.1 is a 0.3 weight. That is the intended pyramiding
  behaviour, not an accident.

Pairing with Execution:
    Under the DEFAULT ``Execution(rebalance='every_bar')`` the engine
    computes ``target_position = weight × portfolio_value / price`` for
    every name on every bar and trades any non-zero delta — with
    ``min_trade_size`` defaulting to 0.0 there is no floor — so a position
    held at a constant weight is re-trued, and traded, on every bar of its
    life as equity and price move. ``Execution(rebalance='on_change')``
    skips a name whose target weight moved by less than
    ``on_change_tolerance`` (default 1e-8). With this sizer the weight is
    genuinely constant while a position is held, so on_change reduces the
    lifecycle to exactly one trade in and one trade out.

NaN discipline:
    NaN signal ⇒ NaN weight, cell for cell. Nothing is filled, dropped or
    densified, and no other cell is affected (there is no shared
    denominator to poison). The output keeps the input's index and columns
    exactly.

Causality / invariance:
    Elementwise on the signal, with no window, shift, state or cross-bar
    term, so appending or removing FUTURE bars cannot change a past weight
    and any sub-window is bit-identical to the same span of the full run.

Output:
    WeightSeries with the input's index and columns. Direction from the
    signal (+1 → +weight_per_position, -1 → -weight_per_position, 0 → 0.0).
    Unbounded gross by construction.

Example:
    TradeManager(entries="entries", prices="ohlcv") ->
      {"stop": [StopLoss(pct=0.05)]} -> Exposure() ->
      FixedWeightSizer(weight_per_position=0.1)

    ... -> Exposure() -> FixedWeightSizer(weight_per_position=0.05)
      -> LeverageCap(max_leverage=1.0)
components.usage_hint: Use for "10% per trade", "fixed size", "same clip every time", "one unit per name" — the sizing rule where each position's size is decided on its own and the book's total exposure is whatever the sum comes to. The trade-off against ``EqualWeightSizer`` is exact: this pins the POSITION and lets gross float; that one pins GROSS and lets the position float.

parameters.name: weight_per_position
parameters.description: Weight given to each open position, in units of equity. 0.1 (default) = 10% of capital per name. Direction comes from the input signal (long → positive, short → negative), and on a level-valued input the weight is multiplied by the level. Because gross exposure is this number times the number of open names, choose it against the strategy's TYPICAL active count — 0.1 is a 1.0x book at ten names and a 3.0x book at thirty. Nothing here caps the result; add LeverageCap downstream if that matters.

components.name: ForecastCapper
components.description:
Clip forecast values to a symmetric hard cap to prevent extreme position sizes.

Place after ForecastScaler to limit outlier forecasts that would otherwise
dominate portfolio positions. Standard cap is +/-20 (2x the target magnitude
of 10). For a version with dead-zone filtering, use LinearForecastMapper instead.

Output:
    Range [-limit, +limit]. Values within the cap pass through unchanged.
    NaN values are preserved.

Formula:
    capped = clip(forecast, -limit, +limit)

Example:
    ForecastScaler() -> ForecastCapper(limit=20) -> EqualForecastCombiner()
components.usage_hint: Place after ForecastScaler to limit outlier forecasts that would otherwise dominate portfolio positions. Standard cap is +/-20 (2x the target magnitude of 10). For a version with dead-zone filtering, use LinearForecastMapper instead.

parameters.description: Maximum absolute forecast value. Standard is 20 (2x the target avg|f|=10). Lower values (e.g., 15) constrain outliers more aggressively, reducing tail risk but dampening high-conviction signals.

components.name: ForecastClipper
components.description:
Clip forecast values with asymmetric bounds for directional constraints.

Use to enforce long-only or short-only strategies on continuous forecasts.
Values outside [lower, upper] are clamped to the bound. Values inside
pass through unchanged. NaN values are preserved.

Unlike ForecastCapper (symmetric ±limit), this supports asymmetric bounds.
Unlike ForecastRemap (linear rescale), this is a hard clamp — no rescaling,
no shifting. A forecast of +5 stays +5; a forecast of -5 becomes 0
(with lower=0).

Output:
    Range [lower, upper]. Values within bounds are unchanged.
    NaN preserved. Same shape as input.

Examples:
    # Long-only: keep positive forecasts, zero out negative (flat when bearish)
    ForecastClipper(lower=0)
    # -15 → 0, -1 → 0, 0 → 0, +5 → +5, +20 → +20

    # Short-only: keep negative forecasts, zero out positive (flat when bullish)
    ForecastClipper(upper=0)
    # -20 → -20, -5 → -5, 0 → 0, +5 → 0, +15 → 0

    # Asymmetric bounds: tighter on shorts
    ForecastClipper(lower=-10, upper=20)

components.name: ForecastCombiner
components.description:
Combine forecast branches with explicit per-branch weights.

Use after a Parallel step to combine multiple forecast rules with custom
weights. Weights are keyed by branch name and must sum to 1.0. For equal
weighting, use EqualForecastCombiner instead.

Output:
    Same scale as input forecasts (weighted sum). NaN propagates from any
    input branch (intersection semantics). Typically followed by EmpiricalFDM.
    For analytical FDM, use AnalyticalFDMCombiner instead (combine+FDM in one step).

Formula:
    combined = sum(w_i * forecast_i)  for each branch i

Example:
    {"mr": ..., "momentum": ...} -> ForecastCombiner(weights={"mr": 0.6, "momentum": 0.4})

components.name: ForecastMapperConvex
components.description:
Apply power-law mapping to disproportionately amplify or compress extreme forecast values.

Use when you want non-linear treatment of forecast magnitude. Power > 1 amplifies
extremes (convex/aggressive), power < 1 compresses extremes (concave/conservative).
At power=1.0 this is equivalent to ForecastCapper. Prefer over piecewise mappers
when you want a smooth, continuous non-linearity.

Output:
    Range [-cap, +cap]. Preserves sign. Smooth non-linear curve.
    NaN values are preserved.

Formula:
    output = sign(x) * cap * (min(|x|, cap) / cap) ^ power

Example:
    ForecastScaler() -> ForecastMapperConvex(power=1.5) -> EqualForecastCombiner()
components.usage_hint: Use when you want non-linear treatment of forecast magnitude. Power > 1 amplifies extremes (convex/aggressive), power < 1 compresses extremes (concave/conservative). At power=1.0 this is equivalent to ForecastCapper. Prefer over piecewise mappers when you want a smooth, continuous non-linearity.

parameters.description: Exponent controlling the non-linearity. Must be > 0. 1.0 = linear (same as ForecastCapper). 1.5 = moderate convexity (amplify extremes). 2.0 = strong convexity (quadratic amplification). 0.5 = concave (sqrt, compress extremes).

parameters.description: Maximum absolute output value. Default 20.

components.name: ForecastMapperGrouped
components.description:
Apply two-slope piecewise-linear mapping to concentrate forecast distribution around a target value.

Use when you want forecasts clustered near a specific magnitude (+/- peak) rather
than uniformly spread. The steep first slope rapidly lifts signals out of the dead
zone to the target, while the gentle second slope compresses extremes. Produces a
"double hump" distribution. Prefer over LinearForecastMapper when you want explicit
control over the target forecast level.

Output:
    Range [-cap_output, +cap_output]. Zero inside dead zone. Peaks at +/- peak
    value near the breakpoint. NaN values are preserved.

Formula:
    slope1 = peak / (breakpoint - dead_zone)    (steep ramp)
    slope2 = (cap_output - peak) / (cap - breakpoint)  (gentle ramp)
    |x| < dead_zone           -> 0
    dead_zone <= |x| <= breakpoint -> slope1 * (|x| - dead_zone)
    breakpoint < |x| <= cap   -> peak + slope2 * (|x| - breakpoint)
    |x| > cap                 -> cap_output

Example:
    ForecastScaler() -> ForecastMapperGrouped(dead_zone=2, breakpoint=8, peak=12) -> EqualForecastCombiner()

components.name: ForecastMapperWinged
components.description:
Apply tent-shaped mapping that amplifies moderate forecasts and dampens extreme ones for adjusted trend following.

Use for trend strategies where moderate signals are more predictive than
extreme ones (which signal reversal risk). Output rises to a peak at the
breakpoint, then declines back toward zero at the cap. Prefer over
ForecastMapperGrouped when you want to explicitly penalize extreme forecasts.

Output:
    Range [0, peak] (magnitude). Output rises then falls in a triangle shape.
    Beyond cap, output drops to floor_output (default 0). NaN preserved.

Formula:
    dead_zone <= |x| <= breakpoint -> slope_up * (|x| - dead_zone)  (amplify)
    breakpoint < |x| <= cap -> peak - slope_down * (|x| - breakpoint)  (dampen)
    |x| > cap -> floor_output
    slope_up = peak / (breakpoint - dead_zone)
    slope_down = (peak - floor_output) / (cap - breakpoint)

Example:
    ForecastScaler() -> ForecastMapperWinged(breakpoint=10, peak=20) -> EqualForecastCombiner()

Output rises to a peak at the breakpoint, then declines back toward zero at the cap. Prefer over ForecastMapperGrouped when you want to explicitly penalize extreme forecasts.

components.name: ForecastRemap
components.description:
Linearly rescale forecast values from one bounded range to another.

Maps input values from [from_min, from_max] to [to_min, to_max] using a
linear transform. Values outside the source range are clamped to the target
range boundaries. NaN values are preserved.

Use to enforce directional constraints in pair/basket strategies:
a forecast in [-20, +20] remapped to to_min=1, to_max=20 is always positive
(long-only), while to_min=-20, to_max=-1 is always negative (short-only).
The signal shape and relative ordering are preserved — only the range shifts.

Output:
    Range [to_min, to_max]. Input values outside [from_min, from_max] are
    clamped. NaN preserved. Same shape as input.

Formula:
    y = to_min + (x - from_min) * (to_max - to_min) / (from_max - from_min)
    y = clip(y, to_min, to_max)

Examples:
    # Always-long: weakest momentum -> small long, strongest -> full long
    ForecastRemap(to_min=1, to_max=20)
    # -20 -> 1, 0 -> 10.5, +20 -> 20

    # Always-short: weakest -> small short, strongest -> full short
    ForecastRemap(to_min=-20, to_max=-1)

    # Constant forecast (passive hedge leg):
    ForecastRemap(to_min=10, to_max=10)
    # All values -> 10

    # Rescale RSI (0-100) to forecast scale:
    ForecastRemap(from_min=0, from_max=100, to_min=-20, to_max=20)

components.name: ForecastScaler
components.description:
Scale raw signals to a target average absolute forecast magnitude for comparable combination.

Use after any signal-generating component (indicators, transforms, mean reversion) to
normalize forecast magnitudes before combining with ForecastCombiner,
AnalyticalFDMCombiner, or EmpiricalFDM. Standard target is 10 (Pardo convention). Prefer rolling mode
for realistic backtesting; static mode introduces in-sample bias.

Output:
    Unbounded, centered around 0. After scaling, median|f| or mean|f| equals
    avg_abs_target (default 10). NaN values pass through unchanged.

Formula:
    scalar = target / statistic(|signal|)
    where statistic is rolling median (MAD) or mean over the window
    scaled_forecast = signal * scalar

Population scoping (optional, ``population_mask_slot``):
    The global scalar is pooled over the whole panel in the window, so
    every cell in that window moves the number every established name is
    multiplied by. With a mask slot wired, the rolling sum and count run
    over the MASKED cells only; the resulting per-bar scalar still
    multiplies the FULL frame — non-members are scaled BY the member
    panel's scalar rather than contributing TO it. With every cell a
    member the result is the unscoped scalar exactly.

    Only ``pool="global", method="mean", rolling=True`` is implemented;
    any other combination RAISES at construction rather than quietly
    scaling by an unscoped statistic. (``by_asset`` has no
    cross-sectional population to scope, and the ``MAD`` path pools a
    STACKED rolling median whose window length counts slots rather than
    observations, so masking it silently changes the estimator.)

    An EMPTY member pool yields NaN, never the neutral ``1.0`` the
    unscoped path substitutes — see ``components.population_scoping``.
    Because the scoped statistic is unbounded, follow every scoped use
    with ``ForecastCapper``.

Example:
    TimeSeriesMeanReversionForecast(k=4) -> ForecastScaler(method="MAD", window="90d") -> ForecastCapper()
components.usage_hint: Use after any signal-generating component (indicators, transforms, mean reversion) to normalize forecast magnitudes before combining with ForecastCombiner, AnalyticalFDMCombiner, or EmpiricalFDM. Standard target is 10 (Pardo convention). Prefer rolling mode for realistic backtesting; static mode introduces in-sample bias.

parameters.description: Pooling strategy for scalar calculation. "global" = single scalar across all assets (most stable), "by_asset" = per-asset scalar (captures asset-specific signal scale differences).

parameters.name: method

parameters.name: window
parameters.description: Lookback for scalar calculation. Time string ("90d", "30d") or integer bar count. Shorter = more adaptive but noisier, longer = more stable. Default "90d" is standard.

parameters.name: rolling
parameters.description: Whether to recalculate scalar at each bar. True (default) = realistic backtesting with no future information. False = static scalar from calibration window (in-sample bias).

components.name: ForecastWeightNormalizer
components.description:
Normalize forecasts to portfolio weights with target gross leverage.

Use as the simplest position sizing step for forecast-based strategies. Divides
each row of forecasts by the sum of absolute values, then scales by target_leverage.
Preserves relative conviction: stronger forecasts get proportionally larger weights.
No slots required — works purely from the pipeline value.

For production strategies needing volatility-targeted sizing, upgrade to the
ReturnVolatility → VolTargetWeightConverter chain instead.

Output:
    WeightSeries (DataFrame, timestamps x assets). Absolute values sum to
    target_leverage per row. Sign preserved from forecasts (positive = long,
    negative = short). A row whose finite forecasts are all zero is a
    deliberate flat and yields 0.0 in every finite cell (NaN cells stay
    NaN); an all-NaN row stays NaN (hold).

Zero vs NaN (Q-2369):
    In Keel weights 0.0 is a clear zero-weight target (exit/flat) and NaN
    means HOLD the prior position. An all-zero forecast row — a gated-off
    RegimeGate, an empty screen, an identical cross-section — therefore
    normalizes to 0.0, never NaN: a finite row in is a finite row out.

Formula:
    weight_i(t) = forecast_i(t) / sum(|forecast_j(t)|) * target_leverage

Example:
    ForecastCapper(limit=20.0) -> ForecastWeightNormalizer(target_leverage=1.0)
components.usage_hint: Use as the simplest position sizing step for forecast-based strategies. Divides each row of forecasts by the sum of absolute values, then scales by target_leverage. Preserves relative conviction: stronger forecasts get proportionally larger weights. No slots required — works purely from the pipeline value.

parameters.description: Target gross leverage (sum of absolute weights per row). 1.0 = fully invested (no leverage). 2.0 = 2x gross exposure. Default 1.0.

parameters.description: Maximum absolute weight per asset. None = no cap. 0.20 = no single asset exceeds 20% of portfolio. Excess goes to cash (gross leverage reduced), not redistributed.

components.name: FundingDataLoader
components.description:
Load funding rate data for all universe symbols on the strategy's clock, from cache or live database.

Use to build funding-based signals: carry / funding carry (short the
high-funded, long the low-funded), funding premium mean reversion,
funding regime detection, crowding and basis reads. Sign convention
(Hyperliquid): a positive funding rate means longs pay shorts. Synonyms:
funding rate, perp funding, funding payments, carry rate, funding
premium, settled funding, hourly funding.

Timeframe: omit `timeframe` to serve Globals.target_timeframe (the
common case — nothing else about time anywhere); pass a literal for a
branch on its OWN clock (multi-timeframe). The hourly funding partition
is the native grain: at 1h it is served as-is; at a coarser grain the
hourly rates are rolled onto the bar grid (Globals.bar_offset included)
with `agg`; a finer grain (30min, 15min, 5min) is refused — set
timeframe="1h" and end the branch with TargetSignalProjector(), which
holds the last completed hour on the fine grid, visibly.

Aggregation (`agg`, default "mean"): the average hourly rate over the
bar — the funding LEVEL, comparable across grains (a 1d mean of hourly
rates is the average hourly rate that day), which is what carry and
regime signals average anyway. "sum" is the accrual over the bar (the
total funding paid or received per unit notional — its units change
with the grain); "last" is the rate at the bar's close.

Output:
    StreamSeries (DataFrame, bar close labels x symbols). Values are
    funding rates as decimals per hour (e.g., 0.0001 = 0.01% per hour;
    typically [-0.01, 0.01]) — per bar for agg="sum". NaN where data is
    unavailable, never interpolated. This loader feeds signals only: the
    funding a perp backtest charges is loaded by the platform for every
    run, whatever this branch serves.

A funding-only (price-free) pipeline is a first-class shape: this loader
can open the pipeline with no PriceDataLoader anywhere — every backtest's
simulation prices are loaded by the platform at the strategy clock, from
the venue the data loaders name.

Example:
    # Globals(target_timeframe="1d", bar_offset="12h"): funding at 1d —
    # the common carry strategy; served 1d, the mean of the hourly rates
    # on the 12h grid the declaration names
    FundingDataLoader() -> NegateTransform() -> CrossSectionalZScore()

    # Globals(target_timeframe="1d"): 1h funding with your own smoothing —
    # the explicit timeframe is the override; the resampler puts the
    # smoothed 1h series on the 1d clock
    FundingDataLoader(timeframe="1h") -> EWMATransform(window=24) -> TargetSignalResampler(method="last")

    # Globals(target_timeframe="1d"): accrued funding per day
    FundingDataLoader(agg="sum")

    # Globals(target_timeframe="15min"): the only legal shape under a
    # clock finer than the 1h native grain — serve the hour, project it
    FundingDataLoader(timeframe="1h") -> TargetSignalProjector()

    # 15min price for one thing beside 1d price for another: combine at
    # the terminal clock (PriceDataLoader(timeframe="15min") -> ... ->
    # TargetSignalResampler(method=...) beside PriceDataLoader() -> ...)

Sign convention (Hyperliquid): a positive funding rate means longs pay shorts. Synonyms: funding rate, perp funding, funding payments, carry rate, funding premium, settled funding, hourly funding.

components.name: FundingDispersionRegime
components.description:
Measure cross-sectional dispersion of funding rates to detect carry differentiation regimes.

Use to gate or scale carry-based signals when funding rates diverge across
instruments. High dispersion indicates that carry signals can better differentiate
between long and short candidates. Feed into RegimeGate to enable carry strategies
only during high-dispersion periods, or into RegimeScale to modulate carry forecast
intensity.

Output:
    Scalar GlobalSeries, non-negative (std of funding rates). Higher values
    indicate more divergent funding across instruments. NaN during warmup
    (lookback // 2 bars) and on bars where fewer than two instruments
    report. The output sits on the clock of the funding frame it reads,
    label for label: FundingDataLoader() serves Globals.target_timeframe on
    the Globals.bar_offset grid, so by default the regime is on the
    strategy's clock. The component never re-clocks — a different clock is
    declared on the loader and re-clocked by a projector or resampler.

Formula:
    raw = std(funding_rate_i) across instruments per bar
    signal = rolling_mean(raw, lookback)   # lookback in bars of that clock

Example:
    FundingDataLoader() -> Store("funding_disp_funding_data") -> {
        "dispersion": [FundingDispersionRegime(lookback=20)],
        "carry": [NegateTransform(), ForecastScaler()],
    } -> RegimeGate(index_key="dispersion", signal_key="carry", condition="index > 0.5")

    The Store is required: this component reads the funding frame from the
    slot 'funding_disp_funding_data' (implicit slot read), not from its
    flow input. Without the Store the pipeline fails validation with
    SLOT_REF_NOT_FOUND.

    # Globals(target_timeframe="4h"): a DAILY dispersion regime on a 4h
    # strategy — declare the daily clock on the loader, then hold the last
    # completed day on the 4h grid
    FundingDataLoader(timeframe="1d") -> Store("funding_disp_funding_data") -> FundingDispersionRegime(lookback=20) -> TargetSignalProjector()

components.name: FundingLevelRegime
components.description:
Detect extreme funding regimes by averaging absolute funding rates across the universe.

Use to gate or scale carry and mean reversion strategies based on overall funding
intensity. High funding levels indicate large carry opportunities where
funding-based signals are most profitable. Feed into RegimeGate to enable/disable
strategy legs, or into RegimeScale to modulate forecast intensity.

Output:
    Scalar GlobalSeries, non-negative (absolute funding rates). Higher values
    indicate more extreme funding across the universe. NaN during warmup
    (lookback // 2 bars) and on bars where no instrument reports. The
    output sits on the clock of the funding frame it reads, label for
    label: FundingDataLoader() serves Globals.target_timeframe on the
    Globals.bar_offset grid, so by default the regime is on the strategy's
    clock. The component never re-clocks — a different clock is declared on
    the loader and re-clocked by a projector or resampler.

Formula:
    raw = mean(|funding_rate_i|) across instruments per bar
    signal = rolling_mean(raw, lookback)   # lookback in bars of that clock

Example:
    FundingDataLoader() -> Store("funding_level_funding_data") -> {
        "level": [FundingLevelRegime(lookback=20)],
        "carry": [NegateTransform(), ForecastScaler()],
    } -> RegimeScale(index_key="level", signal_key="carry")

    The Store is required: this component reads the funding frame from the
    slot 'funding_level_funding_data' (implicit slot read), not from its
    flow input. Without the Store the pipeline fails validation with
    SLOT_REF_NOT_FOUND.

    # Globals(target_timeframe="4h"): a DAILY funding-level regime on a 4h
    # strategy — declare the daily clock on the loader, then hold the last
    # completed day on the 4h grid
    FundingDataLoader(timeframe="1d") -> Store("funding_level_funding_data") -> FundingLevelRegime(lookback=20) -> TargetSignalProjector()

components.name: GarmanKlassVolatility
components.description:
Compute annualized Garman-Klass volatility from OHLC data for efficient variance estimation.

Use when you need a more statistically efficient volatility estimate than close-to-close
HistoricalVolatility. Garman-Klass uses all four OHLC prices per bar, extracting more
information and producing lower-variance estimates. Ideal for volatility regime detection
and risk management. Requires OHLC data (not just close prices).

Output:
    Range [0, inf), annualized volatility as a decimal (e.g., 0.80 = 80% annualized vol).
    NaN during warmup (min_periods bars) or where any OHLC price is zero.

Formula:
    per_bar_var = 0.5 * ln(H/L)^2 - (2*ln(2) - 1) * ln(C/O)^2
    GK_vol = sqrt(rolling_mean(per_bar_var, window) * annualization_factor)

Example:
    PriceDataLoader() -> GarmanKlassVolatility(window=20) -> CrossSectionalZScore()
components.usage_hint: Use when you need a more statistically efficient volatility estimate than close-to-close HistoricalVolatility. Garman-Klass uses all four OHLC prices per bar, extracting more information and producing lower-variance estimates. Ideal for volatility regime detection and risk management. Requires OHLC data (not just close prices).

components.name: GiveBack
components.description:
How far price has come back from this trade's best close, in price units (≥ 0): compare it
with an ATR distance for a chandelier or ATR trailing stop.

Position layer: TradeManager turns entry signals into a Position; each rule is a reader, then
ordinary components, then an action (Exit, Reduce, ScaleIn, AllowEntry). Value at row k:
direction × (best close − close).

Example:
    ATR(period=14) -> Scale(by=2.5) -> Store("trail_dist") ->
      TradeManager(entries="entries", prices="ohlcv") ->
      {"trail": [{"fast": [GiveBack()], "slow": [Load("trail_dist")]}, Crossover(),
        AboveThresholdFilter(threshold=0.0), Exit()]} ->
      Exposure() -> FixedWeightSizer(weight_per_position=0.1)

Note: stops, targets, trails and other price-level rules are checked and filled at the bar's close, with no intra-bar measurement or execution, so a fill can be well past the level.
Note: compare by difference with the ATR distance; a ratio never fires on a zero-ATR bar.
