components.name: GroupAssetFilter
components.description:
Keep only the assets of one named group from the Universe declaration.

Use for "run this leg on the DeFi names", "sector buckets", "split the
book into groups and size each one separately", "the majors branch". It
is ``AssetSelect`` with the symbol list lifted out of the pipeline and
into the strategy's ``Universe(groups={...})`` declaration — so one list
is edited in one place, several branches can name it, and the group
membership is visible to the editor and the validator instead of being
buried in a step's parameters.

Compile-time resolution, not a slot:
    ``group`` is a DECLARATION REFERENCE (``universe.groups``). The
    resolver looks the name up in ``Universe.groups`` and injects the
    symbol list before the pipeline runs, so nothing is read from
    ``Context`` and no ``Store``/``Load`` is involved. A group name that
    the ``Universe`` block does not define raises at run time, naming the
    group.

Reducer, not a mask:
    Columns/keys are DROPPED, so the frame gets narrower and every
    downstream step — including cross-sectional ones — sees only this
    group. For a selection that varies over time, keep the frame's width
    and use a mask (``RollingVolumeUniverseMask`` + ``ApplyUniverseMask``)
    instead. For a one-off list that no other branch shares,
    ``AssetSelect`` says the same thing inline.

Empty result is NOT an error (the trap in this component):
    Unlike ``AssetSelect``, which raises when none of its symbols are
    present, this returns an EMPTY dict or a zero-column DataFrame and
    lets the pipeline continue. A group whose members are all absent
    from the loaded universe — a typo in ``Universe.groups``, or symbols
    outside the declared ``Universe.symbols`` — therefore produces a
    branch that trades nothing, quietly. Check that every group's
    members are in the universe the loader actually returns.

Type-preserving:
    Runs on either shape: an OHLCV dict before any indicator (keys are
    filtered) or a DataFrame after one (columns are selected). Output is
    the same kind as the input; anything else raises ``TypeError``. On
    both shapes the surviving entries keep the INPUT's order — unlike
    ``AssetSelect``'s DataFrame path, this never reorders.

NaN discipline:
    None to speak of — no value is read. Cells are carried through
    exactly as they arrive, NaN included, with no reindexing or fill.

Causality / invariance:
    Selection is on the COLUMN axis only and the membership is fixed at
    compile time; the time index is untouched, so no bar can influence
    another.

Output:
    The same type as the input (dict or DataFrame) with only the group's
    assets, identical index, identical values.

Example:
    Universe(mode="manual", symbols=["AAVE", "UNI", "BTC", "ETH"],
             groups={"defi": ["AAVE", "UNI"], "majors": ["BTC", "ETH"]})

    # Each group sleeve sizes to half the book so the two sum to 1.0x (M-29).
    # Globals(target_timeframe="1d", bar_offset="12h"): PriceDataLoader() serves 1d on the 12h grid — no resampler
    Pipeline([
        PriceDataLoader(), Store("ohlcv"),
        {
            "defi": [Load("ohlcv"), GroupAssetFilter(group="defi"),
                     ROC(period=20), ForecastScaler(),
                     ForecastWeightNormalizer(target_leverage=0.5)],
            "majors": [Load("ohlcv"), GroupAssetFilter(group="majors"),
                       ROC(period=20), ForecastScaler(),
                       ForecastWeightNormalizer(target_leverage=0.5)],
        },
        WeightConcatenator(),
    ])

It is ``AssetSelect`` with the symbol list lifted out of the pipeline and into the strategy's ``Universe(groups={...})`` declaration — so one list is edited in one place, several branches can name it, and the group membership is visible to the editor and the validator instead of being buried in a step's parameters.

components.name: HeikinAshi
components.description:
Convert OHLCV candles to Heikin-Ashi smoothed bars that reduce price noise and highlight trends.

Use as an early pipeline step before indicators when you want smoother price action
for trend-following strategies. Heikin-Ashi candles suppress intra-bar whipsaws,
making momentum and trend indicators (EWMA, ROC) less noisy. Not recommended for
mean reversion strategies that rely on exact price levels.

Output:
    Same OHLCV dict structure with modified open/high/low/close columns.
    Volume is unchanged. First bar uses simple average for ha_open.

Formula:
    ha_close = (O + H + L + C) / 4
    ha_open[i] = (ha_open[i-1] + ha_close[i-1]) / 2
    ha_high = max(H, ha_open, ha_close)
    ha_low = min(L, ha_open, ha_close)

Example:
    PriceDataLoader() -> HeikinAshi() -> EWMA(window=20)
components.usage_hint: Use as an early pipeline step before indicators when you want smoother price action for trend-following strategies. Heikin-Ashi candles suppress intra-bar whipsaws, making momentum and trend indicators (EWMA, ROC) less noisy. Not recommended for mean reversion strategies that rely on exact price levels.

components.name: HistoricalVolatility
components.description:
Compute annualized close-to-close realized volatility for risk measurement and regime detection.

Use to estimate historical volatility from log returns. Suitable for volatility targeting,
regime filtering (high-vol vs low-vol environments), and risk-adjusted signal scaling.
For a more efficient estimator that uses OHLC data, consider GarmanKlassVolatility instead.
Often fed into slot stores for regime-based strategy switching.

Output:
    Range [0, inf), annualized volatility as a decimal (e.g., 0.80 = 80% annualized vol).
    NaN during warmup (min_periods bars). Higher = more volatile.

Formula:
    r = ln(close_t / close_{t-1})
    HV = std(r, window) * sqrt(annualization_factor)

Example:
    PriceDataLoader() -> HistoricalVolatility(window=20) -> RollingZScoreTransform(window=120)

Suitable for volatility targeting, regime filtering (high-vol vs low-vol environments), and risk-adjusted signal scaling. For a more efficient estimator that uses OHLC data, consider GarmanKlassVolatility instead. Often fed into slot stores for regime-based strategy switching.

components.name: Hurst
components.description:
Compute rolling Hurst exponent via Rescaled Range analysis to classify trending vs mean-reverting regimes.

Use as a regime indicator to dynamically select strategy type. When H > 0.5 the asset
is trending (favor momentum signals), when H < 0.5 it is mean-reverting (favor mean
reversion signals), and H ~ 0.5 indicates a random walk. Typically stored in a slot
and used to gate or weight other signals. Computationally expensive due to R/S
regression over logarithmically spaced sub-windows.

Output:
    Range approximately [0, 1]. H > 0.5 = persistent/trending, H < 0.5 = anti-persistent/
    mean-reverting, H ~ 0.5 = random walk. NaN during warmup (max_window bars) and
    where standard deviation is near-zero.

Formula:
    For each sub-window size n:
      R/S = (max(cumdev) - min(cumdev)) / std(returns)
    H = slope of log(R/S) vs log(n) regression

Example:
    PriceDataLoader() -> Hurst(max_window=100) -> Store("regime")
components.usage_hint: Use as a regime indicator to dynamically select strategy type. When H > 0.5 the asset is trending (favor momentum signals), when H < 0.5 it is mean-reverting (favor mean reversion signals), and H ~ 0.5 indicates a random walk. Typically stored in a slot and used to gate or weight other signals. Computationally expensive due to R/S regression over logarithmically spaced sub-windows.

parameters.name: min_window
parameters.description: Smallest sub-window size for R/S regression. Must be >= 4 for meaningful statistics. Smaller values (4-8) add more data points to the regression but increase noise. Default 10 is a good balance.

parameters.name: max_window
parameters.description: Rolling lookback in bars and largest sub-window size. Controls how much history is used. Shorter (50-80) adapts faster to regime changes, longer (100-200) gives more stable estimates. Default 100 is ~25 hours on 15-min bars.

components.name: IDMPortfolioAggregator
components.description:
Calculate the Instrument Diversification Multiplier (IDM) and aggregate subsystem blocks into portfolio positions.

Use as the portfolio aggregation step that combines per-instrument subsystem blocks
into final portfolio positions. Reads forecast, return volatility, and OHLCV data
from slots to build a synthetic PnL, estimate instrument correlations, and compute
the diversification benefit. Place after VolTargetWeightConverter and before
LeverageCap. IDM rewards diversification: low-correlated instruments get a higher
multiplier.

Output:
    Portfolio blocks (DataFrame, same shape as input subsystem blocks). Values are
    subsystem_blocks * (1/N) * IDM. IDM typically ranges [1.0, 2.5]. Higher IDM
    means greater diversification benefit.

Formula:
    IDM = 1 / sqrt(u' R u)
    where u = [1/N, ..., 1/N] (equal weights), R = correlation matrix
    (negatives floored to 0 when floor_negative_correlations=True, the default;
    raw signed correlations when False)
    portfolio_blocks = subsystem_blocks * (1/N) * IDM

Example:
    VolTargetWeightConverter(return_vol_slot="return_vol") -> IDMPortfolioAggregator(
        forecast_slot="forecast", return_vol_slot="return_vol", ohlcv_slot="ohlcv_1d"
    ) -> LeverageCap()

components.name: IchimokuCloud
components.description:
Compute Ichimoku Cloud direction signal, a multi-component trend system that outputs discrete trend state based on cloud position.

Use as a trend direction and strength filter. The cloud (kumo) provides support/resistance
zones; price above cloud = bullish, below = bearish, inside = neutral/consolidating.
Requires high/low/close data. The discrete output (+1/0/-1) works well as a regime
gate or as input to a forecast mapper. Prefer IchimokuCloud over SuperTrend when
you want a neutral zone (inside cloud) rather than a binary trend signal.

Output:
    Discrete values: +1.0 (close above cloud top, bullish), -1.0 (close below
    cloud bottom, bearish), 0.0 (inside cloud, neutral). NaN during warmup
    (`senkou_b_period` + `kijun_period` bars due to forward displacement).

Long/cash (hold the uptrend, flat otherwise): follow with ThresholdCross(upper=0.5, mode='long_only') — it stays BinarySignal; Clip would not.

Formula:
    tenkan_sen = (highest_high(tenkan) + lowest_low(tenkan)) / 2
    kijun_sen = (highest_high(kijun) + lowest_low(kijun)) / 2
    senkou_a = ((tenkan + kijun) / 2), shifted forward by kijun_period
    senkou_b = ((HH(senkou_b_period) + LL(senkou_b_period)) / 2), shifted forward
    cloud = [min(senkou_a, senkou_b), max(senkou_a, senkou_b)]

Example:
    IchimokuCloud(tenkan_period=9, kijun_period=26) -> ForecastScaler()
components.usage_hint: Use as a trend direction and strength filter. The cloud (kumo) provides support/resistance zones; price above cloud = bullish, below = bearish, inside = neutral/consolidating. Requires high/low/close data. The discrete output (+1/0/-1) works well as a regime gate or as input to a forecast mapper. Prefer IchimokuCloud over SuperTrend when you want a neutral zone (inside cloud) rather than a binary trend signal.

components.name: IndexShiftTransform
components.description:
DEPRECATED: use Lag(periods=N) to delay execution. Shifts signal timestamps forward.

Deprecated (Q-2489): moving the TIMESTAMPS forward pushes a strategy's last
held bar past the end of the price data, and the engine refuses weights it
has no price for, so a strategy holding on its last bar cannot run. Lag
shifts the values and keeps the timestamps — the same execution delay with
nothing past the data. Pinned strategies keep loading and running
unchanged; new strategies should use Lag.

Output:
    Same scale and values as input, with timestamps moved forward by
    ``bars`` bar durations. No bars are dropped; the index is simply
    offset. No NaN introduced.

    A nonzero shift needs a known bar duration. Two or more timestamps use
    the first observed interval; a single timestamp uses its index
    frequency metadata. A single timestamp without frequency metadata
    raises an explicit error instead of guessing an execution interval.

Example:
    ROC(period=10) -> CrossSectionalZScore() -> IndexShiftTransform(bars=1)
components.usage_hint: Deprecated (Q-2489): moving the TIMESTAMPS forward pushes a strategy's last held bar past the end of the price data, and the engine refuses weights it has no price for, so a strategy holding on its last bar cannot run. Lag shifts the values and keeps the timestamps — the same execution delay with nothing past the data. Pinned strategies keep loading and running unchanged; new strategies should use Lag.

parameters.name: bars
parameters.description: Number of bars to shift the index FORWARD in time (delay the signal). 0 = no shift (pass-through). Typical use: bars=1 to execute on the next bar after signal generation. Negative values are rejected at v2 — they read a bar that has not closed yet.

changelog.2: bars constrained to >= 0 (dsl-mtf-clocks spec 02 §8.2, R-22.3): a NEGATIVE shift moves every signal timestamp BACKWARD, so a value computed from a bar that closes at t is stamped before t and traded on data that has not happened yet — the registered lookahead injector (measured R3 LA-6: bars=-1 ships today with zero warnings). The negative surface is tombstoned; pinned v1 instances keep loading and running unchanged.

parameters.description: Number of bars to shift the index. Positive = forward in time (delay signal), negative = backward. 0 = no shift (pass-through). Typical use: bars=1 to execute on the next bar after signal generation.

components.name: InertiaManager
components.description:
Reduce a repeating selection signal to one entry EVENT and one exit EVENT per position.

Use for "deduplicate my entries", "only trade the first bar of the signal",
"stop re-entering while I'm already in", "turn a selection mask into
entry/exit events". A selector such as ``SelectionToSignalConverter``
repeats +1 for every bar a name is selected; this collapses that run to a
single +1 on the first bar and a single -1 on the closing bar, so a
downstream allocator that acts on EVENTS (``DynamicEqualWeightAllocator``)
trades once per position instead of once per bar.

The output is an EVENT stream, not a position state. +1 means "open here",
-1 means "close here", and 0 means "nothing happens on this bar" — which
covers both holding an open position and being flat. Reading the output as
a state would say the book is flat on every bar between entry and exit. Use
``TradeManager`` when you want a held STATE instead, and pair the
output of this component only with consumers documented to read events.

Sequential rule (per asset, one forward pass):
    +1 while flat  → emit +1 and open
    +1 while open  → emit 0 (the entry is absorbed — this is the "inertia")
    -1 while open  → emit -1 and close
    -1 while flat  → emit 0 (ignored; there is nothing to close)
    anything else  → emit 0
So each lifecycle carries exactly one +1 and at most one -1, and a run
``1,1,1,0,0,-1,0,1,0,-1`` becomes ``1,0,0,0,0,-1,0,1,0,-1``.

Long-only by construction. Entries are recognised as +1 ONLY; a -1 in the
entry slot is folded into the exit channel and closes an open position. There
is no short lifecycle here — for signed entries use ``TradeManager``.

Two input modes:
    - AUTO-DETECT (neither slot named, the default): the pipeline input is
      read as one COMBINED signal, +1 = entry and -1 = exit.
    - NAMED SLOTS (``entry_slot`` and ``exit_slot``, both or neither —
      naming one raises): the two frames are read separately. Note that in
      this mode ANY non-zero value in the exit slot forces an exit, so the
      exit channel is direction-blind and magnitude-blind.

NaN discipline (the two modes differ, and the difference is a real trap):
    - AUTO-DETECT / identical frames: NaN matches neither the ``== 1`` nor
      the ``== -1`` mask, so it is a no-op — the position is held through
      the gap and no event is emitted.
    - NAMED SLOTS: a NaN in the EXIT slot satisfies ``!= 0`` and therefore
      FIRES AN EXIT. Missing exit data closes the position rather than
      holding it. Fill the exit slot before this component if that is not
      what you want. A NaN in the entry slot is a no-op in both modes.
    - The output is dense in every case: it is built from a zero frame and
      only ever written with +1/-1, so a NaN input yields 0.0 and the
      output is never NaN.

Parameters this component REFUSES rather than ignores:
    ``combination_method``, ``max_position_size`` and
    ``allow_multiple_entries`` are still in the signature — stored blobs
    and locks reference them forever — but any value other than the
    default now RAISES at construction. Each was validated, stored and
    never consulted by ``run``, so setting one silently produced the
    default strategy; an ignored parameter reads as a declared behaviour,
    so it is rejected instead (Q-1085). Size limits belong to a sizer
    downstream (``EqualWeightSizer(max_weight=...)``, ``LeverageCap``);
    adding to a position is a ``ScaleIn`` rule under ``TradeManager``,
    whose units this component's {+1, 0, -1} event stream cannot express.

Causality / invariance:
    One forward pass per asset carrying a single boolean (in position or
    not), read strictly in index order, with no lookahead and no full-frame
    statistic — so appending or removing FUTURE bars cannot change a past
    event. Assets are independent of one another. The state is NOT
    trade-bounded: a run that begins mid-position starts flat and will emit
    its first +1 at the first entry bar it sees, so two runs agree only from
    the first bar on which both are flat.

Output:
    DataFrame with the input's index and columns, values in {+1.0, 0.0,
    -1.0} (the declared ``output_domain``). Dense — never NaN.

Example:
    SelectionToSignalConverter(hold_periods=5) -> InertiaManager() ->
      DynamicEqualWeightAllocator()

    # Separate entry and exit channels
    ... -> Store("z") -> ThresholdCross(upper=0.5, lower=-0.5, mode="long_only") -> Store("entries")
    ... -> Load("z") -> BelowThresholdFilter(threshold=0.0) -> Store("exits")
    ... -> InertiaManager(entry_slot="entries", exit_slot="exits")

parameters.name: entry_slot
parameters.description: Slot holding the entry channel, where +1 opens a position. None (default) selects AUTO-DETECT mode: the pipeline input is read as one combined signal with +1 = entry and -1 = exit. Must be given together with ``exit_slot`` — naming exactly one of the two raises.

parameters.name: exit_slot
parameters.description: Slot holding the exit channel. In this mode ANY non-zero value closes an open position, NaN included, so the channel is direction- and magnitude-blind and missing data reads as an exit. Must be given together with ``entry_slot``.

parameters.name: combination_method
parameters.description: REFUSED unless left at its default "sequential_cleaning", the only algorithm implemented. ``run`` never read it, so any other value produced the default behaviour with no signal that the instruction was dropped.

parameters.name: max_position_size
parameters.description: REFUSED unless left at its default 1.0. This component emits events in {+1, 0, -1} and does no sizing at all, so a size limit could never have applied here — put it on the sizer downstream (``EqualWeightSizer(max_weight=...)``, ``LeverageCap``).

parameters.name: allow_multiple_entries
parameters.description: REFUSED unless left at its default False. It promised entry stacking and did nothing: ``run`` never read it, so True produced output identical to False. Stacking is not expressible in this component's {+1, 0, -1} event stream — use ``ScalingPositionManager``, which emits an integer level per position and has a real ``max_entries``.

components.name: KeltnerChannel
components.description:
Compute normalized price position within Keltner Channels using EMA center and ATR-based bands.

Use as a volatility-adaptive trend and breakout indicator. Unlike BollingerBands which uses
standard deviation bands, KeltnerChannel uses ATR for band width, making it less sensitive
to outlier closes. Values near +1/-1 indicate price at the channel extremes. Feed into
CrossSectionalZScore or a threshold component to generate trading signals.

Output:
    Approximately [-1, +1] but can exceed on breakouts. 0 = price at EMA center,
    +1 = price at upper channel, -1 = price at lower channel. NaN during warmup
    (period bars). Values beyond +/-1 indicate a channel breakout.

Formula:
    center = EMA(close, period)
    upper = center + multiplier * ATR(period)
    lower = center - multiplier * ATR(period)
    output = (close - center) / (multiplier * ATR)

Example:
    PriceDataLoader() -> KeltnerChannel(period=20, multiplier=2.0) -> WingsTransform(threshold=0.8)
components.usage_hint: Use as a volatility-adaptive trend and breakout indicator. Unlike BollingerBands which uses standard deviation bands, KeltnerChannel uses ATR for band width, making it less sensitive to outlier closes. Values near +1/-1 indicate price at the channel extremes. Feed into CrossSectionalZScore or a threshold component to generate trading signals.

parameters.name: period
parameters.description: Lookback window in bars for both EMA and ATR calculation. Shorter (10-15) = tighter, more responsive channels; longer (20-40) = wider, smoother channels. Default 20 is the standard Keltner period.

parameters.name: multiplier
parameters.description: ATR multiplier for channel width. 2.0 = standard (captures most price action), 1.5 = narrower channels (more breakout signals), 2.5-3.0 = wider channels (fewer, stronger breakouts).

components.name: Lag
components.description:
Delay execution by N bars: the value computed at bar t is traded at bar t+N.

The execution-delay component. Put it at the end of a signal chain to trade
each bar's signal N bars later, and use it to test a signal's robustness to
delayed execution: compare Lag(periods=0) with 1, 2, 3... to see how fast
the edge decays when you cannot trade on the bar that produced it. It shifts
the VALUES and keeps the timestamps, so nothing lands past the end of the
data (unlike shifting the index). Also builds lagged copies of a signal,
e.g. for crossovers.

Output:
    Same range and index as input; each value moved N rows later. The first
    N rows become NaN.

Example:
    EWMA(window=20) -> Lag(periods=1) -> CrossoverCombinator(fast_key="fast", slow_key="slow")

components.name: LastTradeReturn
components.description:
The realized return of the previous trade on this asset: the reader for "only take the next
trade if the last one won" gates, ending in AllowEntry().

Position layer: TradeManager turns entry signals into a Position; each rule is a reader, then
ordinary components, then an action (Exit, Reduce, ScaleIn, AllowEntry). A fraction in
TradeReturn units, partial sells included; NaN before the first closed trade.

Example:

      {"last_won": [LastTradeReturn(), AboveThresholdFilter(threshold=0.0), AllowEntry()]} ->
      Exposure() -> FixedWeightSizer(weight_per_position=0.1)

components.name: LeverageCap
components.description:
Cap gross portfolio leverage by scaling down weights proportionally when exceeded.

Use as the final risk control before execution to enforce a hard leverage limit.
When sum(|weights|) exceeds max_leverage on any bar, all weights on that bar are
scaled down proportionally to hit the cap. Relative allocations are preserved.

Optionally also caps each SINGLE asset's weight at max_asset_weight
(per-asset leverage bound, e.g. 1.0 = no single name above 1x equity —
Carver's RAW_MAX_LEVERAGE production guardrail). The per-asset clip is
applied FIRST, then the gross scale, so both bounds hold on output.
Excess from the clip goes to cash; it is not redistributed.

Output:
    WeightSeries (DataFrame, same shape as input). Gross leverage per row
    is guaranteed <= max_leverage, and |w_i| <= max_asset_weight when set.
    Rows already below the caps pass through unchanged.

Formula:
    if max_asset_weight is not None:
        w_i = clip(w_i, -max_asset_weight, +max_asset_weight)
    if sum(|w_i|) > max_leverage:
        scale = max_leverage / sum(|w_i|)
        w_i = w_i * scale

Example:
    ForecastWeightNormalizer(target_leverage=2.0) -> LeverageCap(max_leverage=5.0)
components.usage_hint: Use as the final risk control before execution to enforce a hard leverage limit. When sum(|weights|) exceeds max_leverage on any bar, all weights on that bar are scaled down proportionally to hit the cap. Relative allocations are preserved.

parameters.name: max_leverage
parameters.description: Maximum allowed gross leverage (sum of absolute weights per row). Rows exceeding this are scaled down proportionally. Default 5.0, at most 10.0 (the platform's gross limit). Common values: 1.0 (no leverage), 2.0, 5.0.

parameters.name: max_asset_weight
parameters.description: Optional per-asset absolute weight cap, applied BEFORE the gross scale. None (default) disables it. E.g. 1.0 bounds every single name at 1x equity.

components.name: LinearForecastMapper
components.description:
Apply piecewise-linear mapping with dead zone and boost to eliminate weak forecasts and amplify conviction.

Drop-in replacement for ForecastCapper that adds a dead zone (zeroing weak signals)
and a boost (amplifying strong ones). Controlled by a single parameter `a_param`
that preserves forecast variance. Use after ForecastScaler when you want to filter
out noise near zero without losing the continuous signal shape.

Output:
    Range [-cap*a_param, +cap*a_param]. Zero inside the dead zone (|x| < threshold).
    NaN values are preserved. Polarity matches input.

Formula:
    threshold = -19.811 + 22.263 * a_param
    slope = (cap * a_param) / (cap - threshold)
    |x| < threshold        -> 0             (dead zone)
    threshold <= |x| <= cap -> slope * (|x| - threshold)  (linear ramp)
    |x| > cap              -> cap * a_param  (boosted cap)

Example:
    ForecastScaler() -> LinearForecastMapper(a_param=1.4) -> EqualForecastCombiner()

Controlled by a single parameter `a_param` that preserves forecast variance. Use after ForecastScaler when you want to filter out noise near zero without losing the continuous signal shape.

parameters.name: a_param
parameters.description: Controls dead zone width and boost magnitude. Must be in (1.0, 2.0). Lower (1.1-1.2) = narrow dead zone, mild boost. Higher (1.5-1.8) = wide dead zone, strong boost. Default 1.4 is a good balance for typical scaled forecasts.

parameters.name: cap
parameters.description: Input cap level (should match ForecastScaler target * 2, default 20). Rarely changed.

components.name: LinearRegressionR2
components.description:
Compute rolling R² of log-price linear regression to measure trend cleanliness.

Use to distinguish clean, linear trends from noisy, choppy price action. High R²
(near 1.0) indicates price follows a smooth trend line — ideal for trend-following
strategies. Low R² (near 0.0) indicates random or choppy movement — better for
mean reversion or range strategies. Complements Hurst for regime detection:
Hurst measures persistence (trending vs mean-reverting), R² measures linearity
(smooth vs noisy). Feed into QuantileRankTransform for screening or use as a
regime filter to gate other signals.

Output:
    Range [0, 1]. 1.0 = perfectly linear price trend, 0.0 = no linear relationship.
    NaN during warmup (window bars) and where price is constant. Values above 0.7
    indicate a strong, clean trend; below 0.3 indicates choppy/range-bound.

Formula:
    y = log(close) over rolling window
    x = [0, 1, ..., window-1]
    R² = (Σ(x-x̄)(y-ȳ))² / (Σ(x-x̄)² · Σ(y-ȳ)²)

Example:
    PriceDataLoader() -> LinearRegressionR2(window=20) -> QuantileRankTransform()

Low R² (near 0.0) indicates random or choppy movement — better for mean reversion or range strategies. Complements Hurst for regime detection: Hurst measures persistence (trending vs mean-reverting), R² measures linearity (smooth vs noisy). Feed into QuantileRankTransform for screening or use as a regime filter to gate other signals.

parameters.description: Rolling lookback in bars for the linear regression fit. Shorter (10-15) measures short-term trend quality, longer (20-40) measures medium-term. Default 20 balances sensitivity and stability. The x-axis is simply [0..window-1], so this is a fixed-length sliding window regression.

components.name: LiquiditySweep
components.description:
Fire a signed {-1, 0, +1} pulse at the RECLAIM bar of a stop hunt — price ran a level, then closed back inside.

Use as the "turtle soup" / stop-hunt reversal trigger: -1 when buy-side
liquidity above a high was taken and price CLOSED back below it (bearish),
+1 after a low was raided and price closed back above (bullish). The pulse
lands on the RECLAIM bar, not the penetration bar — a sweep is only a
sweep once price is back inside, which is the whole content of the
concept. Multiply it by a flow reversal (`TakerFlowLoader(side="net")`) for the
spec 01 §4 "confirmed sweep" recipe. Every contested clause is a parameter
pinned to the school that uses it (smc-trader-cohort research/05 §5).

The R4 identity, and why penetration is NOT here: a wick-trigger break and
a sweep are ONE event split by what the close does next. The penetration
set is `BreakOfStructure(trigger="wick")`; both components read the same
owner, `structure.level_breaks(trigger="wick")`, and this one adds only
the close-back-inside predicate. If you want penetration-only (smc.py's
`liquidity()`, research/05 §5 V2), use `BreakOfStructure(trigger="wick")`
— not `reclaim_bars=1`, which is a different thing (the strictest sweep,
not the absence of one).

A sweep and a close-break are NOT mutually exclusive above
`reclaim_bars=1` — that is the point of the window. A level can be closed
through (so `BreakOfStructure(trigger="close")` fires) and then reclaimed
a bar or two later (so this fires too); the canonical false breakout is
exactly that sequence, and both events are real. Set `reclaim_bars=1` for
the exclusive reading, where a sweep requires the penetration bar itself
to close back inside and anything that closes through is a break and
nothing else. See Q-1017: cancelling on the penetration bar's own close
made that exclusivity total and left the window unreachable.

Axes (sourced defaults, spec 01 contract 3):
    target: WHERE the resting liquidity is assumed to sit — the three
        sourced pools. "swing" (default) = a single prior swing level, the
        turtle-soup original (fxopen, ictkillzone). "equal_cluster" =
        equal highs / equal lows, where two consecutive same-side pivots
        sit within `cluster_tolerance_atr` ATRs of each other and the
        level is the OUTER extreme (LuxAlgo's ATR-scaled EQH/EQL; smc.py
        pools swing levels within 1% of the data range and requires >= 2
        members). "period_extreme" = the prior calendar period's high and
        low — PDH/PDL and previous-week H/L (smc.py `previous_high_low`;
        ICT's buy-side/sell-side liquidity "above old highs / below old
        lows"). This requires a DatetimeIndex and raises without one.
    reclaim_bars: how many bars the reclaim may take, counting the
        penetration bar itself (default 3). THE LOAD-BEARING CLAUSE — it
        is what separates a sweep from a break — and no surveyed source
        states a number; the sources say "reverses with a body close back
        inside the prior range" and leave the window to the reader. So 3
        is a KEEL CONVENTION chosen to keep the window short enough that
        the reclaim is still the same move; treat it as the parameter you
        tune first, not as a sourced constant. The sweep lands on the
        FIRST bar in the window that closes back inside; a close BEYOND
        the level does not cancel the candidate (that is the false
        breakout, not a disqualification), but the window running out
        does, and so does an unobserved close — after a NaN the sequence
        can no longer be verified, so it is abandoned rather than guessed.
        At 1 the window is the penetration bar alone (the exclusive
        reading above).
    min_penetration_atr: minimum wick penetration beyond the level, in
        ATR multiples read at the PENETRATION bar (default 0.0 = every
        penetration counts). smc.py's analogue is range-relative (1% of
        the data range); ATR denomination is a Keel normalization, so no
        source states an ATR number. At 0.0 the ATR is not consulted at
        all — deliberately, so the component has no ATR warmup when no
        depth filter was asked for.
    detector: "fractal" (default, ICT's symmetric shape / smc.py) or
        "leg_flip" (LuxAlgo's rolling-extreme state flip, NOT a fractal).
        Used by "swing" and "equal_cluster"; ignored by "period_extreme",
        whose levels are calendar-defined.
    width: swing width in bars (default 5). The sourced ladder is 1 (ICT's
        short-term high), 5 and 50 (LuxAlgo's parallel internal and swing
        tiers, `structure.TIER_WIDTHS`; smc.py's `swing_length` default is
        50). Used by "swing" and "equal_cluster"; ignored by
        "period_extreme".
    cluster_tolerance_atr: how close two same-side pivots must be to count
        as "equal", in ATR multiples at the second pivot's confirmation
        bar (default 0.25). Used ONLY by target="equal_cluster". LuxAlgo
        uses an ATR-scaled tolerance and smc.py 1% of the data range, but
        NEITHER states a multiple this maps onto, so 0.25 is a Keel choice
        — the honest reading is "a quarter of a typical bar's range" and
        it is the number to sweep if the cluster set looks wrong.
    period: "day" (default) or "week" — the calendar period whose high and
        low become levels, read off the index's OWN timezone (weeks start
        Monday). Used ONLY by target="period_extreme". Both extremes
        become KNOWN at the first bar of the NEXT period, which is the
        causality contract for a calendar level.
    expiry_bars: safety bound — an untaken level stops being sweepable
        `expiry_bars` bars after it becomes known (default 200). A KEEL
        CONVENTION, not a practitioner one.
    atr_period: bars in the Wilder ATR (default 14). Consulted only when
        `min_penetration_atr` > 0 or target="equal_cluster".

UNITS — none; a dimensionless direction. Scale-invariant (doubling every
price leaves the pulse unchanged), so it pools across assets directly.

Output:
    SignalSeries (timestamps x symbols) holding exactly {-1.0, 0.0, +1.0}
    or NaN (`output_domain` Binary, hard-guarded at run time). Causal, no
    repaint: levels exist only from the bar they become known, and the
    pulse lands on the reclaim bar itself. A level is consumed by its
    penetration — the same level is never swept twice. On a bar carrying
    reclaims both ways the pulses sum and clip to 0.

NaN semantics:
    Observed bars with no sweep emit 0.0, including the warmup where no
    level is known yet. NaN appears on (a) bars with a NaN in
    high/low/close — such a bar can neither penetrate nor reclaim, and
    state persists across it — and (b) when `min_penetration_atr` > 0 and
    the ATR is undefined at a penetration bar, the reclaim window of that
    penetration, where the answer is genuinely UNKNOWN rather than "no
    sweep" (an unjudgeable depth is not a rejected one). A bar in that
    window on which a DIFFERENT, decidable sweep fires keeps its pulse.
    Never zero-filled where undefined.

Evidence note (research/06 §2.1 / §3, R5 — BINDING): this is the
best-evidenced primitive in the family, and it is the only one where the
honest claim is about a MECHANISM rather than a pattern. Osler (2003)
read a large FX dealer's actual stop-loss and take-profit book and found
trigger prices cluster strongly at round numbers and prior levels; Osler
(2005) showed those stops fire in waves and generate price cascades;
Urquhart (2017) found the same round-number clustering in BTC. In crypto
perps the mechanism is public infrastructure — liquidations are forced,
printed and attributed (Cheng et al. 2021 measured daily forced
liquidations averaging 3.51% of open interest in longs on BitMEX). So
"stops cluster beyond prior extremes and their triggering moves price" is
a documented fact. That a sweep-and-reclaim ENTRY is profitable is NOT:
no controlled test of this trigger has been published, and Keel makes no
such claim. Execution is bar-close: the reclaim is known at that bar's
close, so the earliest fill is the next bar.

Note: stops, targets, trails and other price-level rules are checked and filled at the bar's close, with no intra-bar measurement or execution, so a fill can be well past the level.

Example:
    # Globals(target_timeframe="1h"): PriceDataLoader() serves the 1h bars itself — no resampler
    Pipeline([
        {
            "sweep": [PriceDataLoader(),
                      LiquiditySweep(target="period_extreme", period="day")],
            "flow": [TakerFlowLoader(side="net"), RollingZScoreTransform(window=48)],
        },
        # a raid of yesterday's high that taker flow flips against
        ...
    ])
components.usage_hint: Use as the "turtle soup" / stop-hunt reversal trigger: -1 when buy-side liquidity above a high was taken and price CLOSED back below it (bearish), +1 after a low was raided and price closed back above (bullish). The pulse lands on the RECLAIM bar, not the penetration bar — a sweep is only a sweep once price is back inside, which is the whole content of the concept. Multiply it by a flow reversal (`TakerFlowLoader(side="net")`) for the spec 01 §4 "confirmed sweep" recipe. Every contested clause is a parameter pinned to the school that uses it (smc-trader-cohort research/05 §5).

components.name: LogReturn
components.description:
Compute logarithmic return over N periods for additive compounding and volatility analysis.

Use when returns need to be additive across time (e.g., for volatility estimation
or cumulative return decomposition). Log returns are symmetric around zero and
better suited for statistical analysis than SimpleReturn. Prefer SimpleReturn
when interpretability as percentage change matters more.

Output:
    Unbounded log-ratio. Positive = price increase, negative = decrease.
    First N rows are NaN (warmup). Zero prices produce NaN (not inf).

Formula:
    return = log(x_t / x_{t-n})

Example:
    PriceDataLoader() -> LogReturn(periods=1) -> RollingZScoreTransform(window=60)

components.name: LongShortWeightConverter
components.description:
Force every non-zero weight in the book to the short side, or pass the book through unchanged.

Use for building the short leg of a long-short pair: run the same signal
pipeline twice, once with ``mode="long"`` and once with ``mode="short"``,
and combine the two books downstream. The trader vocabulary that should
route here is "short this basket", "make this sleeve short-only", "invert
the leg", "flip the book to the short side". It does NOT rank, select, or
decide WHICH names to short — it only sets the sign of the weights it is
handed, so the selection has to have happened upstream.

Formula (per cell):
    mode="short":  out = 0 where w == 0, otherwise out = -|w|
    mode="long":   out = w   (the input object itself, not a copy)

The short rule is ``-|w|``, NOT ``-w``. A cell that is already negative
therefore STAYS negative instead of flipping back to long, and a two-sided
book handed to ``mode="short"`` collapses to short-only. "Short" here means
"this book is a short book", not "reverse every sign" — if you want a true
sign reversal of a two-sided book, this is not the component.

NaN discipline:
    NaN passes through as NaN in both modes: ``w == 0`` is False for NaN,
    so a NaN cell takes the ``-|w|`` branch and stays NaN. Nothing is
    densified, filled, dropped or reindexed — the output carries the
    input's index and columns exactly.

Causality / invariance:
    Purely elementwise: the value at bar t is a function of the weight at
    bar t and of nothing else. There is no rolling window, no shift, and
    no cross-bar or cross-asset statistic, so appending or removing FUTURE
    bars cannot change any past value, and any sub-window of a run is
    bit-identical to the same span of the full run.

Output:
    WeightSeries with the input's index and columns. In "short" mode every
    finite cell is <= 0 and |out| == |in| cell by cell, so gross exposure
    is unchanged and net exposure becomes -gross. In "long" mode, the input
    verbatim.

Example:
    DynamicEqualWeightAllocator() -> LongShortWeightConverter(mode="short")

    # The two legs of a pair, combined downstream
    ... -> EqualWeightSizer(target_leverage=0.5) ->
      LongShortWeightConverter(mode="short") -> LeverageCap(max_leverage=1.0)

It does NOT rank, select, or decide WHICH names to short — it only sets the sign of the weights it is handed, so the selection has to have happened upstream.

parameters.description: Which side this leg trades. "short" rewrites every non-zero cell to -|w|, which makes the whole book short regardless of the sign it arrived with. Sizing and allocation are untouched in both modes: this sets signs only. Any other value raises.

components.name: LossStreak
components.description:
Consecutive losing trades in the window, newest first: the reader for "stop after two
losses in a row" gates, ending in AllowEntry().

Position layer: TradeManager turns entry signals into a Position; each rule is a reader, then
ordinary components, then an action (Exit, Reduce, ScaleIn, AllowEntry). A loss is a closed
trade whose realized return (partial sells included) is below 0; breakeven is not a loss.

Example:
    TradeManager(entries="entries", prices="ohlcv") ->
      {"pause": [LossStreak(window="1d"), BelowThresholdFilter(threshold=2.0), AllowEntry()]} ->
      Exposure() -> FixedWeightSizer(weight_per_position=0.1)

Note: counts losses, not money: a loss limit is RealizedPnL.

components.name: MACD
components.description:
MACD histogram (MACD line minus signal line; above 0 means the line is above the signal), the single-output MACD in price units — a trend-following momentum indicator from two exponential moving averages.

Use as a trend direction and momentum signal. The histogram output captures acceleration
of the trend: positive and rising = strengthening uptrend, negative and falling =
strengthening downtrend. Typically followed by CrossSectionalZScore or ForecastScaler.
Prefer MACD over simple moving average crossovers (EWMA pairs) when you want a
single-output indicator with built-in signal-line smoothing.

Output:
    Unbounded, in price units. The histogram = MACD line - signal line.
    Positive = bullish momentum, negative = bearish. Zero-crossings indicate
    trend transitions. NaN during warmup (`slow_period` + `signal_period` bars).

Formula:
    MACD_line = EMA(close, fast_period) - EMA(close, slow_period)
    signal_line = EMA(MACD_line, signal_period)
    histogram = MACD_line - signal_line

Example:
    MACD(fast_period=12, slow_period=26) -> CrossSectionalZScore() -> ForecastScaler()

Typically followed by CrossSectionalZScore or ForecastScaler. Prefer MACD over simple moving average crossovers (EWMA pairs) when you want a single-output indicator with built-in signal-line smoothing.

components.name: MFI
components.description:
Compute Money Flow Index as a volume-weighted momentum oscillator for overbought and oversold detection.

Use as a volume-confirmed version of RSI. MFI incorporates both price and volume,
making it less susceptible to false signals during low-volume moves. Values above 80
indicate overbought conditions, below 20 oversold. Feed into CrossSectionalZScore for
relative ranking or WingsTransform to trade extreme readings. Requires volume data.

Output:
    Range [0, 100]. Above 80 = overbought (selling pressure expected), below 20 =
    oversold (buying pressure expected). NaN during warmup (period bars).

Example:
    PriceDataLoader() -> MFI(period=14) -> CrossSectionalZScore() -> ForecastScaler()

components.name: MOM
components.description:
Compute raw price momentum as the absolute price difference over a lookback period.

Use as a simple momentum signal when you need absolute price change rather than
percentage (ROC). Because output is in price units, it is not directly comparable
across assets with different price levels -- always follow with CrossSectionalZScore
or RollingZScoreTransform to normalize. Prefer ROC over MOM for most strategies
unless you specifically need unnormalized price deltas.

Output:
    Unbounded, in price units. Positive = price rose over the period,
    negative = price fell. Magnitude depends on asset price level.
    NaN during warmup (`period` bars).

Formula:
    MOM = close - close[t - period]

Example:
    MOM(period=10) -> CrossSectionalZScore() -> ForecastScaler()

components.name: ManualWeightAllocator
components.description:
Scale each instrument's column by a hand-declared, time-invariant allocation weight.

Use for a fixed house view — "50% BTC, 30% ETH, 20% SOL", "overweight the
majors", "pin the sleeve weights" — where the split across instruments is a
decision, not something derived from the data. It is the constant-weight
sibling of ``EqualWeightAllocator`` (1/N) and ``RiskParityAllocator``
(inverse vol), and like both of them it MULTIPLIES the incoming per-asset
column; it does not produce weights from nothing. Place it after
``VolTargetWeightConverter`` and before ``IDMPortfolioAggregator`` or
``LeverageCap``.

Formula (per asset i, applied to every bar of that asset's column):
    w_i     = weights[i] / Σ_j weights[j]        (over EVERY key in the dict)
    w'_i    = clip(w_i, min_weight, max_weight)  (the LAST operation)
    out_i[t] = in_i[t] × w'_i

Three consequences of that expression:

- **``min_weight`` / ``max_weight`` BIND on the output.** The clip is the
  last operation, so no emitted weight is outside the declared bounds —
  ``{BTC: 0.9, ETH: 0.1}`` with ``max_weight=0.5`` emits 0.5 / 0.1, and the
  0.4 the cap removed goes to CASH rather than to ETH. Gross exposure
  therefore floats: below 1.0 when the cap binds, above 1.0 when the floor
  does (a floor of ``m`` over ``n`` names is unsatisfiable inside a sum of
  1.0 once ``m * n > 1``, and the floor is what the caller declared). This
  matches ``EqualWeightSizer(max_weight=...)`` and
  ``VolWeightSizer(max_weight=...)`` exactly. Before Q-1086 the clip ran
  BEFORE the normalization and neither bound survived it — the same call
  emitted 0.833.
- **Normalization is over every key in the dict**, not over the assets
  actually present in the input, so a key for an asset outside the current
  universe still consumes its share of the 1.0.
- **A dict key absent from the input adds a column.** The multiply aligns on
  the union of columns, so an extra key produces an all-NaN column in the
  output. The reverse — an INPUT asset with no weight — raises instead.

Authoring-time contract: the declared dict must sum to 1.0 (a ``sum_eq``
``param_constraints`` rule both validators enforce). At RUN time a dict that
does not sum to 1.0 is renormalized with a warning rather than refused, and
one summing to zero raises.

NaN discipline:
    The weight vector is a constant, so NaN can only arrive in the data.
    A NaN input cell stays NaN (a NaN times a scalar is NaN); nothing is
    filled, dropped or densified, and the index is untouched. The only NaN
    this component CREATES is the extra column described above.

Causality / invariance:
    The weight vector is a declared constant — it is never estimated from
    the data, and every bar is scaled by the same number. There is no
    window, shift, state or cross-bar term, so appending or removing FUTURE
    bars cannot change a past value and any sub-window of a run is
    bit-identical to the same span of the full run.

Output:
    WeightSeries carrying the input's index and, for the DataFrame input a
    pipeline supplies, the UNION of the input's columns with the dict's
    keys. Each present asset's column is the input column times its
    normalized weight; those weights sum to 1.0 across the dict unless a
    bound binds, in which case they sum to less (cap) or more (floor).
    (Called directly with a NAMED Series, it returns that Series scaled by
    its own weight.)

Example:
    VolTargetWeightConverter(return_vol_slot="return_vol")
    -> ManualWeightAllocator(weights={"BTC": 0.5, "ETH": 0.3, "SOL": 0.2})
components.usage_hint: Use for a fixed house view — "50% BTC, 30% ETH, 20% SOL", "overweight the majors", "pin the sleeve weights" — where the split across instruments is a decision, not something derived from the data. It is the constant-weight sibling of ``EqualWeightAllocator`` (1/N) and ``RiskParityAllocator`` (inverse vol), and like both of them it MULTIPLIES the incoming per-asset column; it does not produce weights from nothing. Place it after ``VolTargetWeightConverter`` and before ``IDMPortfolioAggregator`` or ``LeverageCap``.

parameters.name: weights
parameters.description: Asset name → allocation weight, e.g. ``{"BTC": 0.5, "ETH": 0.3, "SOL": 0.2}``. Required and must be non-empty. The authoring validators require the declared values to sum to 1.0; at run time a different sum is renormalized with a warning, and a sum of zero raises. Every asset in the input must appear here or ``run`` raises; a key with no matching input asset is legal and produces an all-NaN column. Units are fractions of the incoming allocation, not of equity — this multiplies whatever the upstream step produced.

components.name: MarketLeverageScaler
components.description:
Renormalize the book's gross exposure to a market-wide regime's leverage target.

Use for "lever up when the market is risk-on", "trade smaller when the
regime turns", "3x in a bull tape, 1x otherwise" — a single market-wide
regime label (bullish / bearish / neutral) chooses the leverage the whole
book is then rescaled to. Place after weight allocation and before any
hard cap. The regime is ONE series for the market, not one per asset;
per-asset conditioning belongs upstream in the weights themselves.

This RESCALES, it does not multiply. The book's incoming gross exposure is
divided out and replaced by the regime's target, so a book arriving at
0.2 gross and a book arriving at 2.0 gross both leave at exactly
``base_leverage`` in a neutral regime. Relative allocation is preserved
within each side; the level is set entirely by this component.

Formula (long_only=True — one target for the whole book):
    L[t]      = regime_leverage  if regime[t] == +1
              = base_leverage    otherwise (bearish, neutral, or NaN)
    G[t]      = Σ_i |w_i[t]|                       (NaN cells skipped)
    out_i[t]  = w_i[t] × L[t] / G[t],   and 0 where G[t] == 0

Formula (long_only=False — the two sides are rescaled independently):
    bullish → longs to regime_leverage, shorts to base_leverage
    bearish → longs to base_leverage,   shorts to regime_leverage
    neutral/NaN → both sides to base_leverage
    out_i[t] = w_i[t] × target_side[t] / Σ(that side's |w|)

Regime input contract:
    A Series, or a SINGLE-column DataFrame (extracted as the series). A
    multi-column DataFrame RAISES — it means per-asset regimes, which this
    component cannot honour, and there is no per-asset leverage scaler to
    forward to: either collapse the frame to one market-wide series
    upstream (``MarketVolumeRegimeFilter`` / ``MarketTrendRegimeFilter``,
    or ``Extract`` a single column), or apply the per-asset regime to the
    WEIGHTS upstream instead of routing it through leverage. A zero-ROW
    DataFrame is read as "no regime data" and becomes an all-neutral
    series aligned to the weights. Only exactly +1 (within 1e-6) counts as
    bullish and exactly -1 as bearish; every other value, NaN included, is
    neutral.

Alignment: when the regime index differs from the weights index the regime
is reindexed onto the weights with a forward fill and NO staleness bound —
the last known regime is carried forward indefinitely. Use
``RegimeLeverageScaler`` when a stale regime must decay back to neutral.

NaN discipline (the two modes differ, and the difference is load-bearing):
    - Regime NaN ⇒ neutral ⇒ ``base_leverage``. Never a refusal, never a
      carry beyond what the ffill above already did.
    - long_only=True: a NaN weight cell stays NaN in the output and is
      skipped by the gross sum, so the REMAINING names absorb the entire
      leverage target. Two names at 0.5 each with one NaN leaves the other
      holding the full ``L[t]`` on its own.
    - long_only=False: a NaN weight cell becomes 0.0 (the side masks send
      NaN to zero), i.e. the output is densified. The surviving names again
      absorb the whole side target.
    - An all-zero (or all-NaN) row scales to 0.0 rather than dividing by
      zero.

Causality / invariance:
    Every step is per-bar — a row-wise gross sum, a row-wise regime lookup,
    and a multiply — and the only cross-bar operation is a BACKWARD forward
    fill of the regime. Bar t therefore reads bars <= t only, so appending
    or removing FUTURE bars cannot change a past value. (Removing PAST bars
    can, if the dropped bars held the regime observation the ffill was
    carrying.)

Output:
    WeightSeries with the input's index and columns. Gross exposure per bar
    is exactly ``base_leverage`` or ``regime_leverage`` (per side when
    ``long_only=False``), or 0.0 on a flat row. Signs are preserved.

Example:
    # Globals(target_timeframe="1h"): PriceDataLoader() serves the 1h bars itself — no resampler
    DollarVolumeLoader() -> Store("dollar_volume") -> PriceDataLoader() ->
      MarketVolumeRegimeFilter(dollar_volume_slot="dollar_volume", threshold=2.0)
      -> Store("volume_regime")

    # MarketVolumeRegimeFilter emits 1.0 / 0.0, so 1.0 is the boosted
    # regime and 0.0 falls through to base_leverage.
    ... -> EqualWeightSizer(target_leverage=1.0) ->
      MarketLeverageScaler(base_leverage=1.0, regime_leverage=3.0,

components.name: MarketRiskScaler
components.description:
Multiply the whole book by one of three scale factors, chosen by a market-wide risk metric.

Use for "size down when market vol is high", "press when the tape is calm",
"risk-off haircut" — a single market-wide risk number (realized vol, a
stress index, a dispersion measure) is compared to one threshold and the
entire book is multiplied by the matching factor. The metric is continuous,
but the RESPONSE is a three-valued step, not a ramp: everything below the
threshold gets the same treatment, and so does everything above it.

This MULTIPLIES, unlike ``MarketLeverageScaler`` / ``RegimeLeverageScaler``,
which renormalize the book to an absolute gross target. Incoming gross is
preserved up to the factor, so a book arriving at 0.4 gross with
``low_risk_scale=1.5`` leaves at 0.6 gross, not at 1.5.

Formula (per bar t, applied to every cell of the row):
    s[t] = low_risk_scale   if risk[t] <  risk_threshold
         = high_risk_scale  if risk[t] >  risk_threshold
         = base_scale       if risk[t] == risk_threshold, or risk[t] is NaN
    out_i[t] = w_i[t] × s[t]

Risk input contract:
    A Series only. ANY DataFrame raises, including a single-column one —
    this is stricter than ``MarketLeverageScaler``, which unwraps a
    one-column frame. Extract the column upstream if that is what you have.
    When the risk index differs from the weights index it is reindexed onto
    the weights with a forward fill and NO staleness bound.

NaN discipline:
    NaN risk lands on neither side of a strict comparison, so it takes the
    ``base_scale`` default — the book is neither pressed nor cut, and no
    warning is raised. NaN weight cells stay NaN (a NaN times a scalar is
    NaN); nothing is densified, filled or dropped, and the output keeps the
    input's index and columns exactly. Zero weights stay zero.

Causality / invariance:
    Per-bar throughout: one comparison and one multiply per row, with the
    only cross-bar step a BACKWARD forward fill of the risk series. Bar t
    reads bars <= t, so appending or removing FUTURE bars cannot change a
    past value.

Output:
    WeightSeries with the input's index and columns. Every cell is the
    input cell times one of exactly three scalars, so signs are preserved
    and gross exposure is the input's gross times that scalar. Nothing
    bounds the result — put ``LeverageCap`` downstream if a hard ceiling
    matters.

``risk_threshold`` is an ABSOLUTE level, so it means something only if the
index feeding ``risk_slot`` is on a known scale. Feeding it
``RealizedVolatilityRegime`` from v2 on, that scale is annualized vol taken
off the declared ``Globals(target_timeframe)``: 1.0 is 100% annualized vol
on every clock, so a threshold picked at 1d keeps its meaning at 4h or
15min. Under that component's v1 the same threshold did NOT transfer — a
15min index read 9.80x low, putting 1.0 out of reach entirely (Q-1151). A
strategy still pinned to ``RealizedVolatilityRegime`` v1 on a sub-daily
clock needs its threshold divided by ``sqrt(bars_per_day)``, or the
component upgraded to v2.

Example:
    # Globals(target_timeframe="1d"): PriceDataLoader() serves the daily bars itself
    PriceDataLoader() -> Store("ohlcv") -> ExtractSeries(series_name="close") ->
      RealizedVolatilityRegime(ohlcv_slot="ohlcv", lookback=20) ->
      Store("market_vol")

    # 1.0 = 100% annualized vol: press below it, halve above it
    ... -> EqualWeightSizer(target_leverage=1.0) ->
      MarketRiskScaler(risk_slot="market_vol", low_risk_scale=1.5,
                       high_risk_scale=0.5, risk_threshold=1.0)

components.name: MarketTrendRegimeFilter
components.description:
Detect market-wide bull/bear trend regime using EMA crossover on a market index for portfolio-level decisions.

Use for portfolio-level exposure management. Constructs a market index from
cross-asset price data (trimmed mean or equal weight), then applies EMA crossover
to classify bull/bear/neutral regimes. Output is a Series suitable for leverage
scaling or regime gating. For volatility-based regimes, use VolatilityFilter.

Output:
    Series with +1.0 (bull, fast EMA > slow EMA), -1.0 (bear), or 0.0 (neutral).
    Shifted by 1 bar to prevent look-ahead bias. NaN during EMA warmup.

Formula:
    market_index = trimmed_mean(prices) or equal_weight_mean(prices)
    fast_ema = EMA(market_index, fast_period)
    slow_ema = EMA(market_index, slow_period)
    regime = +1 if fast > slow, -1 if fast < slow, 0 otherwise

Example:
    PriceDataLoader() -> MarketTrendRegimeFilter(fast_period=5, slow_period=17)

components.name: MarketVolumeRegimeFilter
components.description:
Detect market-wide high-volume regime from cross-asset dollar volume for portfolio-level leverage scaling.

Use for portfolio-level decisions when you want to scale leverage based on overall
market volume activity. Averages each asset's DOLLAR VOLUME across assets, then
compares the market mean to a rolling average. Returns a binary Series (1.0 =
high volume regime, 0.0 = normal). For per-asset volume filtering, use
RelativeVolume instead.

Dollar volume is traded notional, ``pv_sum`` (Σ trade price × size) — the 15m
capture's ``volume × close`` before 2025-03-23 — read from the
``DollarVolumeLoader`` output wired into ``dollar_volume_slot`` (version 3,
dollar-volume DV4). It never computes ``volume × close`` and has no fallback to
it. The flow input supplies only the strategy's bars and the assets: an OHLCV
dict (the union of its indexes, its keys) or any T×A frame (its index, its
columns). The slot's frame must be on those bars (a different timeframe or
``bar_offset`` raises; a missing slot raises). Version 2 (``volume × close``
from the OHLCV input) is frozen in ``versions/market_volume_regime_v2.py``.

Output:
    Series with 1.0 (high volume regime) or 0.0 (normal). Shifted by 1 bar
    to prevent look-ahead bias. NaN during warmup (window/2 bars).

NaN semantics:
    An asset with NaN dollar volume at a bar (unobserved), or with no
    dollar-volume column at all (named in a warning), is excluded from that
    bar's cross-asset mean; a bar where every asset is NaN yields NaN market
    dollar volume (regime 0.0 after the shift).

Formula:
    market_dv = mean(dollar_volume across assets)   (NaN-excluding)
    threshold_line = threshold * rolling_mean(market_dv, window)
    regime = 1.0 if market_dv >= threshold_line else 0.0

Example:
    # Globals(target_timeframe="1d")
    DollarVolumeLoader() -> Store("dollar_volume") -> PriceDataLoader()
        -> MarketVolumeRegimeFilter(dollar_volume_slot="dollar_volume",
            threshold=2.0, window=20)

Averages each asset's DOLLAR VOLUME across assets, then compares the market mean to a rolling average. Returns a binary Series (1.0 = high volume regime, 0.0 = normal). For per-asset volume filtering, use RelativeVolume instead.

components.name: MaskAnd
components.description:
Combine boolean masks with AND — True where ALL branches are True.

Use after a Parallel block that produces multiple boolean masks. Requires
all conditions to pass. Common use: combining a trend filter with a
volume filter to require both.

Output:
    Float mask DataFrame (0.0/1.0). 1.0 only where every branch is True.
    NaN in any branch treated as False.

Example:
    {
        "low_trend": [ADX(period=14), BelowThresholdFilter(threshold=25)],
        "high_volume": [NotionalVolumeExtractor(), AboveThresholdFilter(threshold=1e6)],
    } -> MaskAnd()
components.usage_hint: Use after a Parallel block that produces multiple boolean masks. Requires all conditions to pass. Common use: combining a trend filter with a volume filter to require both.

components.name: MaskOr
components.description:
Combine boolean masks with OR — True where ANY branch is True.

Use after a Parallel block that produces multiple boolean masks. Passes
assets matching any condition. Common use: combining multiple threshold
filters into a single "any extreme" mask.

Output:
    Float mask DataFrame (0.0/1.0). 1.0 where at least one branch is True.
    NaN in any branch treated as False.

Example:
    {
        "overbought": [RSI(period=3), AboveThresholdFilter(threshold=90)],
        "oversold": [RSI(period=3), BelowThresholdFilter(threshold=10)],
    } -> MaskOr()

components.name: MeanReversionDistance
components.description:
Compute price displacement from its moving average in ATR units for mean reversion detection.

Use to measure how far price has stretched from its mean in volatility-normalized terms.
Positive values indicate price above the SMA (extended upward), negative indicates below
(extended downward). Extreme values suggest reversion potential. Already vol-normalized
by ATR, so output is comparable across assets without additional normalization. Feed into
QuantileRankTransform for screening or CrossSectionalZScore for signal generation.

Output:
    Unbounded, centered around 0. Positive = price above SMA (overextended long),
    negative = below SMA (overextended short). Typical range [-3, +3] for liquid
    crypto on 4h bars. NaN during warmup (sma_period bars).

Formula:
    MR = (close - SMA(close, sma_period)) / ATR(atr_period)

Example:
    PriceDataLoader() -> MeanReversionDistance(sma_period=20, atr_period=14) -> QuantileRankTransform()
components.usage_hint: Use to measure how far price has stretched from its mean in volatility-normalized terms. Positive values indicate price above the SMA (extended upward), negative indicates below (extended downward). Extreme values suggest reversion potential. Already vol-normalized by ATR, so output is comparable across assets without additional normalization. Feed into QuantileRankTransform for screening or CrossSectionalZScore for signal generation.

components.name: MinMaxNormalize
components.description:
Scale signals to [0, 1] range using rolling min-max normalization.

Use when downstream components require bounded input (e.g., regime classifiers,
threshold-based filters) and you want to preserve the signal's shape. Each asset
is normalized independently against its own rolling history. Prefer
RollingZScoreTransform when you need centering around zero, or SigmoidNormalize
for a stateless bounded transform without lookback.

Output:
    Range [0, 1]. 0 = at rolling minimum, 1 = at rolling maximum.
    NaN during warmup and when rolling min equals rolling max (flat signal).

Formula:
    output = (x - rolling_min(x, window)) / (rolling_max(x, window) - rolling_min(x, window))

Example:
    RSI(period=14) -> MinMaxNormalize(window=60) -> ThresholdCross(upper=0.8, mode="long_only")
components.usage_hint: Use when downstream components require bounded input (e.g., regime classifiers, threshold-based filters) and you want to preserve the signal's shape. Each asset is normalized independently against its own rolling history. Prefer RollingZScoreTransform when you need centering around zero, or SigmoidNormalize for a stateless bounded transform without lookback.

parameters.description: Lookback period in bars for rolling min/max. Shorter (10-20) adapts quickly but compresses range around recent values, longer (60-120) captures broader historical range. Default 20.

parameters.name: min_periods
parameters.description: Minimum observations before producing output. Defaults to window // 2. Lower values produce earlier (noisier) output.

components.name: NATR
components.description:
Compute Normalized Average True Range as a percentage of price for cross-asset volatility comparison.

Use when you need volatility that is comparable across assets with different price levels.
Unlike ATR which returns absolute price units, NATR normalizes by close price so a 2%
NATR means the same relative volatility whether the asset is $100 or $50,000. Ideal as
input to universe filters (exclude low-vol assets) or volatility regime detection.

Output:
    Range [0, inf), in percentage units. Typically 1-5% for liquid crypto on 15-min bars.
    Higher = more volatile. NaN during warmup (period bars).

Formula:
    NATR = ATR(period) / close * 100

Example:
    PriceDataLoader() -> NATR(period=14) -> CrossSectionalZScore()

Negate (multiply by -1) signal values to flip polarity for carry, mean reversion, or directional inversion.

Use when a signal has the opposite polarity from what downstream components
expect. For example, high funding rate naturally means "pay to be long" so
negating converts it to a short signal. Also useful when combining signals
that need opposite-sign alignment before ForecastCombiner.

Output:

Example:

components.name: NotionalVolumeExtractor
components.description:
Turn an OHLCV dict into a per-bar candle-notional frame (volume x close) — the dollar-volume PROXY.

Use for "notional volume", "turnover", "rank the universe by liquidity",
"only trade the liquid names" when the candle approximation is wanted.
Raw ``volume`` is in COIN units and is not comparable across assets — a
million DOGE and a million BTC are not the same trade — so multiplying
by price puts every column in one quote-currency unit, which is the form
a cross-sectional liquidity rank or filter needs.

Dollar volume proper is traded notional (sum of trade price × size):
``DollarVolumeLoader`` serves it (with this candle quantity spliced in
before 2025-03-23), and it is what the dollar-volume components read
from their ``dollar_volume_slot``. This step is the named candle proxy.

This step only produces the measure. Selecting on it is a separate
component: ``TopNAssetSelector`` for a per-bar top-N mask,
``AboveThresholdFilter`` for an absolute floor. For a smoother measure,
put a rolling mean between this and the selector.

Formula (elementwise, per asset i, per bar t):
    notional[t, i] = volume[t, i] * close[t, i]

NaN discipline and alignment (read off the implementation):
    - The product is plain multiplication, so a NaN volume OR a NaN price
      yields NaN — missing liquidity is reported as missing, never as
      zero. That is the right pairing for ``TopNAssetSelector``, which
      excludes both NaN and exactly-zero cells from its ranking.
    - Each symbol is computed on its OWN frame and the results are then
      assembled into one DataFrame, so the output index is the UNION of
      the per-symbol indexes. An asset whose history starts later is NaN
      before its first bar rather than being dropped, and columns come
      out in the OHLCV dict's key order.
    - A symbol whose frame lacks ``volume_column`` or ``price_column``
      RAISES, naming the symbol and the columns it does have — it is
      never silently skipped or filled.

Causality / invariance:
    Purely elementwise on bar t — no window, no state, no cross-sectional
    term. Appending or removing other bars cannot change a bar's value.

Output:
    SignalSeries DataFrame (bar close labels x symbols) in QUOTE-CURRENCY
    units per bar, non-negative wherever both inputs are, NaN where
    either is missing. Unbounded and scale-dependent: the magnitude
    depends on the bar clock (a 1d bar's notional is ~96x a 15min bar's)
    and on the asset, so this is a RANKING input, not something to
    threshold with a number copied from another timeframe.

Example:
    # Globals(target_timeframe="1d", bar_offset="12h"): PriceDataLoader() serves 1d on the 12h grid — no resampler
    Pipeline([
        PriceDataLoader(),
        {
            "momentum": [ROC(period=20)],
            "liquidity": [NotionalVolumeExtractor(), TopNAssetSelector(n=10)],
        },
        ApplyMask(score_signal="momentum", filter_signal="liquidity"),
    ])

Raw ``volume`` is in COIN units and is not comparable across assets — a million DOGE and a million BTC are not the same trade — so multiplying by price puts every column in one quote-currency unit, which is the form a cross-sectional liquidity rank or filter needs.

"open"/"high"/"low" are available for a diagnostic; there is no volume-weighted average price here, so this is an approximation of turnover, not the exact traded notional. A symbol missing this column raises.

components.name: OBV
components.description:
Compute On-Balance Volume to detect buying and selling pressure from cumulative volume flow.

Use to confirm price trends with volume or spot divergences where price moves without
volume support. OBV accumulates raw base-coin volume, so its values are in per-asset
volume units: comparing or ranking raw OBV across assets sorts by token supply, not
money flow. Feed into RollingZScoreTransform (per-asset history) to normalize before
combining with other signals; do not feed raw OBV into CrossSectionalZScore or other
cross-sectional rankers — cross-sectional ranking does not cancel the per-asset unit
scale. Requires volume data in PriceFrame.

Output:
    Unbounded cumulative value. Rising OBV = net buying pressure, falling = net selling.
    Absolute scale is in base-coin volume units — not comparable across assets without
    per-asset normalization. No NaN warmup (starts from first bar).

Formula:
    OBV_t = OBV_{t-1} + volume  (if close > prev_close)
    OBV_t = OBV_{t-1} - volume  (if close < prev_close)
    OBV_t = OBV_{t-1}           (if close == prev_close)

Example:
    PriceDataLoader() -> OBV() -> RollingZScoreTransform(window=60) -> ForecastScaler()
components.usage_hint: Use to confirm price trends with volume or spot divergences where price moves without volume support. OBV accumulates raw base-coin volume, so its values are in per-asset volume units: comparing or ranking raw OBV across assets sorts by token supply, not money flow. Feed into RollingZScoreTransform (per-asset history) to normalize before combining with other signals; do not feed raw OBV into CrossSectionalZScore or other cross-sectional rankers — cross-sectional ranking does not cancel the per-asset unit scale. Requires volume data in PriceFrame.

components.name: OpenInterestLoader
components.description:
Load open interest (OI) data on the strategy's clock for positioning, crowding, and OI delta signals.

Use to measure market positioning: leverage buildup, crowding, OI delta /
open interest change, and liquidation-cascade risk. Rising OI with rising
price suggests a strong trend; rising OI with falling price suggests
potential liquidation cascades. Synonyms: open interest, OI, OI change,
OI delta, positioning, leverage, crowding, contracts outstanding.

UNITS — BASE-COIN OI, not dollars. Values are open interest in the
asset's own base-coin units (BTC-denominated for BTC, DOGE-denominated
for DOGE). Ranking or comparing assets cross-sectionally on raw base OI
units is FORBIDDEN — the units are not comparable across assets. Use
per-asset changes (Difference, SignalROC) or per-asset normalization
first. Dollar (notional) OI requires a causally aligned price join and
is served by composition, not by this loader: multiply this series by a
price branch with ``SignalProduct`` (``{"oi": [OpenInterestLoader(), ...],
"px": [ExtractSeries(series_name="close")]} -> SignalProduct(left_key="oi",
right_key="px")``) — the result is notional OI, comparable across assets.

Timeframe: omit `timeframe` to serve Globals.target_timeframe; pass a
literal for a branch on its OWN clock (multi-timeframe). The series is
stored at ONE MINUTE (market_data.ctx_1m) and served at every platform
clock from 5min up: the minutes are rolled onto the bar grid
(Globals.bar_offset included) with `agg`. Nothing finer than 5min is
declarable, so nothing is refused.

Aggregation (`agg`, default "last"): OI is a point-in-time LEVEL, so a
bar carries the level at its close — the value a strategy acts on, and
the reading the venue's own hourly snapshot always was. A "mean" would
blur the level a breakout or squeeze signal reads; "first", "median" and
"sum" are available and none of them is what the series means.

Output:
    StreamSeries (DataFrame, bar close labels x symbols). Values are open
    interest in base-coin units at each completed bar. If the venue
    published nothing for a bar, the previous bar's value is repeated for
    up to 3 bars; after that the bar is NaN (the coin pauses, and nothing
    is refused). Never interpolated and never zero (a level is never
    zero).

Example:
    # Globals(target_timeframe="1d"): served 1d, the level at each day's close
    OpenInterestLoader() -> Difference() -> CrossSectionalZScore()

    # Globals(target_timeframe="15min"): served 15min, from the minutes
    OpenInterestLoader() -> Difference() -> CrossSectionalZScore()

    # A branch on its own clock, beside a finer strategy clock
    OpenInterestLoader(timeframe="1h") -> Difference() -> TargetSignalProjector()
components.usage_hint: Use to measure market positioning: leverage buildup, crowding, OI delta / open interest change, and liquidation-cascade risk. Rising OI with rising price suggests a strong trend; rising OI with falling price suggests potential liquidation cascades. Synonyms: open interest, OI, OI change, OI delta, positioning, leverage, crowding, contracts outstanding.

parameters.name: timeframe
parameters.description: The grain this loader SERVES. None (default) binds to Globals.target_timeframe; a literal serves that clock explicitly (a multi-timeframe branch). Every platform token from 5min up is served from the 1m ctx partition.

parameters.name: agg
parameters.description: How the ctx minutes are rolled into a bar. None (default) = "last", the level at the bar's close — the family's stored aggregation and the one the node-local ctx ladder holds. "mean" = the average level over the bar; "first"; "median"; "sum". A non-default choice is computed from the same minutes on this loader's own cache entry.
