components.name: OpenInterestRegime
components.description:
Detect market-wide open-interest crowding (or washout) as a binary regime from per-asset OI z-scores.

Use to gate or scale a strategy on POSITIONING state: 1.0 when open
interest across the universe is unusually high versus each asset's own
recent history (leverage buildup / crowded positioning, elevated
liquidation-cascade risk) or unusually low (washed-out, deleveraged
market), 0.0 otherwise. Feed the output into RegimeGate (hard on/off),
RegimeScale (proportional) or RegimeLeverageScaler unchanged — it is a
1-D market-wide GlobalSeries like every regime detector.

UNITS — the design rule. OpenInterestLoader serves OI in BASE-COIN units
(BTC for BTC, DOGE for DOGE), which are not comparable across assets, so
pooling raw OI across the universe is FORBIDDEN: a raw sum or mean is
whichever asset has the largest coin count (Q-0773). This component is
the correct way to read OI market-wide: every asset is normalized
against its OWN rolling history first (rolling z-score over `lookback`
bars), and the market score is the cross-sectional MEDIAN of those
z-scores — unit-free by construction, one vote per asset, robust to a
single outlier. Input is the loader's StreamSeries (timestamps x symbols).

Axes (defaults sized in bars of the loaders' 1h clock grain; OI itself is
served from the ctx_1m family — market_data.ctx_1m at a 1m native grain,
no finer than 5min — not the old hourly market_data.oi_data):
    lookback: z-score window in bars of the input clock — the grain the
        loader SERVES (it follows Globals: hourly under a 1h clock, daily
        under a 1d clock, so 720 is 30 days on 1h and 30 is 30 days on
        1d). Default 720 (30 days of hourly OI) — a positioning regime is a weeks-scale
        state; 168 (7d) reacts to faster leverage swings, 2160 (90d) is
        a slow structural read. Warmup is `lookback - 1` bars (NaN).
    threshold: z-units the market median must exceed. Default 1.5 (~7%
        one-sided tail for a normal score); 1.0 is permissive, 2.0-2.5
        flags only extreme crowding.
    direction: "high" = crowded (median z > threshold); "low" = washed
        out (median z < -threshold); "abs" = either (|median z| >
        threshold). Default "high".

Output:
    GlobalSeries with 1.0 (in regime), 0.0 (not), NaN where the market
    score is undefined. Name "open_interest_regime". Value at bar t uses
    OI through bar t (the completed bar the loader serves) — causal, no
    shift, no repaint: a fixed rolling window never revises a past value.

NaN semantics:
    First `lookback - 1` bars NaN (strict warmup: a window needs
    `lookback` observations). A NaN OI cell blanks that asset's z for
    `lookback` bars — never interpolated — and the asset is EXCLUDED
    from the median (pandas skipna) while blanked; an asset with a
    zero-dispersion window has no z (NaN, never +/-inf). A bar where no
    asset has a z yields NaN (never 0.0). With few assets the median is
    coarse (two assets -> their mean); the detector reads a MARKET, so
    prefer a universe of at least three symbols.

Caveat:
    A regime describes positioning STATE, not direction. High OI is
    fuel for a move either way (a crowded long book can squeeze up or
    cascade down); pair it with a directional signal on the price branch
    rather than trading the regime itself. OpenInterestLoader follows
    Globals down to its 5min served floor (served daily under a 1d clock,
    hourly under a 1h clock, agg last) — it rolls the 1m ctx_1m base, so
    a 5/15/30min clock is served directly and needs no projector.

Example:
    # Globals(target_timeframe="1h"): both loaders serve the hourly bars themselves
    Pipeline([
        {
            "trend": [PriceDataLoader(), EWMA(window=20)],
            "oi_regime": [OpenInterestLoader(), OpenInterestRegime(lookback=720, threshold=1.5, direction="low")],
        },
        RegimeGate(signal_key="trend", index_key="oi_regime", condition="index > 0"),
        EqualWeightSizer(target_leverage=1.0),
    ])
    # trade the trend only into a washed-out (deleveraged) market

Feed the output into RegimeGate (hard on/off), RegimeScale (proportional) or RegimeLeverageScaler unchanged — it is a 1-D market-wide GlobalSeries like every regime detector.

components.name: OrCombinator
components.description:
Combine multiple boolean filter masks with OR logic so any condition being True is sufficient.

Use after a Parallel step producing multiple filter signals when you want to trade
if ANY condition is met (e.g., trade if volume OR momentum is favorable). For AND
logic requiring all conditions, use AndCombinator instead. NaN values are treated
as False.

Every branch must carry the same timestamps and the same symbols; branches
are matched by symbol name, not column position, and a mismatch raises.

Output:
    Float mask DataFrame, values 0.0/1.0 (never bool dtype). 1.0 where ANY input mask is True.
    Same shape as input masks, in the first branch's row and column order.

Example:
    {"vol": [VolatilityFilter(...)], "momentum": [MarketTrendRegimeFilter(...)]}
    -> OrCombinator(signals_list=["vol", "momentum"])

components.name: OrderBlock
components.description:
Track ICT/SMC order blocks — the candle a confirmed impulse originated from — and emit the signed ATR distance to the nearest active block.

Use for the "return to the origin of the move" family of SMC entries: an
order block is the candle a leg came FROM, marked only once the leg has
CONFIRMED itself (a structure break, a displacement, or either). The
component keeps every unmitigated block as an active zone and reports
how far the close is from the nearest one in ATR units, so "price is
back at the order block" is a threshold recipe on this scalar
(RangeSelector / AboveThresholdFilter): inside <= 0, approaching from
outside is a small positive number. Every contested clause below is a
parameter whose options are pinned to the school that uses them
(smc-trader-cohort research/05 §8); Keel does not adjudicate between
them.

THE HEADLINE SPLIT (research/05 §8, R4): ICT canon teaches
`candle_select="last_opposite"` — "a bullish order block is the last
down candle before a strong push up" — while BOTH dominant deployed
implementations (LuxAlgo's Pine, smc.py) mark the EXTREME candle in the
leg instead. Both ship. The default is `"extreme_in_leg"` because it is
what the deployed majority computes, not because it is more correct;
no controlled test of either exists (see the caveat below).

Axes (sourced defaults, spec 01 contract 3):
    direction: "bullish" | "bearish" | "both" (default). Which blocks
        are tracked. A bullish block is demand below price, a bearish
        one supply above it.
    candle_select: "extreme_in_leg" (default — LuxAlgo, smc.py: the
        lowest low / highest high in the confirmed leg) or
        "last_opposite" (ICT canon: the last candle that CLOSED against
        the push). See the headline split above.
    confirm: what makes the candle a block. "structure_break" (default
        — LuxAlgo, smc.py: the first CLOSE beyond the active swing
        level; the leg scanned is the broken swing's bar through the
        breaking bar), "displacement" (the Displacement-Order-Blocks
        school: a body >= 1.5x the ATR reference, no structure break
        needed; the leg scanned is the contiguous same-direction close
        run ending at the impulse, plus the bar that begins it), or
        "either" (a block at every bar that carries one; when a bar
        carries both, the structure-break leg wins).
    zone: the block's bounds. "full_range" (default — LuxAlgo, smc.py:
        the candle's high/low) or "body" (the ICT mirrors: "marked
        using the candle body — not the full candle range").
    mitigation: when a block stops being active. "touch" (default —
        smc.py: the first bar whose low reaches the block top / high
        reaches its bottom), "midpoint" (the ICT mean threshold, 50%)
        or "close_through" (ICT-strict / LuxAlgo removal: only a body
        CLOSE beyond the far edge). Tested from the bar AFTER birth.
    require_fvg: True = the confirming leg must also contain a fair
        value gap completing inside it (DOB / ICT-strict); False
        (default — LuxAlgo, smc.py).
    max_range_atr: LuxAlgo's volatility filter — a candle whose own
        range reaches this many ATR is not eligible to be the block.
        Default 0.0 = OFF (smc.py has no such filter); 2.0 reproduces
        LuxAlgo's `range < threshold * 2`.
    expiry_bars: the single bound on EVERY piece of state this component
        holds (default 200) — an unbroken swing level stops being
        breakable `expiry_bars` bars after it is confirmed, AND a block
        is dropped `expiry_bars` bars after birth whether or not it
        mitigated. One knob, so nothing can outlive it; lowering it far
        enough starves the confirmation itself, which is intended and
        visible (no levels, no blocks). A KEEL CONVENTION, not a
        practitioner one: the surveyed sources cap the DISPLAYED count
        instead (LuxAlgo shows the 5 most recent).
    output: "distance" (default) = signed ATR distance (below); "edge"
        = the nearest active block's invalidation boundary PRICE
        (bottom of a bullish block, top of a bearish one) for an AtEntry(slot=...) structure stop and RiskSizer(distance=...).
        One scalar series either way; "edge" carries price units and is
        not cross-asset comparable.
    detector: pivot rule for `confirm="structure_break"` — "fractal"
        (default, the symmetric window smc.py's swing_length uses) or
        "leg_flip" (LuxAlgo's rolling-extreme state flip). research/05 §1.
    width: swing width in bars for the `confirm="structure_break"`
        pivots (default 5) — the SAME axis the structure family takes,
        spelled the same way. The sourced ladder is 1 (ICT's short-term
        high, "a candle with lower highs on both sides"), 5 (LuxAlgo's
        hardcoded INTERNAL structure) and 50 (its SWING structure, and
        smc.py's `swing_length` default); `structure.TIER_WIDTHS` is
        that named pair. It is ONE CONTINUOUS AXIS (>= 1, typically
        1..100), not two rungs: the two named readings remain reachable
        as the values 5 and 50, and every width between and beyond them
        is now available too. The default follows the internal reading — a
        width-50 fractal must be the strict extreme of a 101-bar window
        and so confirms only a handful of levels per 500 bars, too
        sparse to birth blocks on a normal backtest window.
        research/05 §1, §3.
    atr_period: bars in the ATR reference (default 14). The reference at
        bar t is the simple mean true range of the `atr_period` bars
        ENDING AT t-1, so a leg is never measured against its own range.

UNITS — "distance" is in ATR multiples (unit-free, comparable across
assets); "edge" is in price units. `max_range_atr` is an ATR multiple.

Output:
    SignalSeries (timestamps x symbols), causal, no repaint. "distance":
    > 0 outside every active block (price distance to the nearest
    block's nearest edge / ATR), 0 exactly on an edge, < 0 inside (minus
    the depth to the nearest edge / ATR). Nearest = smallest such value
    across active blocks (an enclosing block wins; ties go to the older
    one). NaN when no block is active.
    THE BAR THAT REACHES A BLOCK REPORTS IT (Q-1020): the output at bar
    t is computed over every block alive at t's close, including the
    one(s) bar t mitigates — so under the default "touch" the first bar
    whose low reaches a bullish block emits its distance (<= 0 when the
    close is inside), and the block is gone from the NEXT bar on. That
    touch bar is the bar-close entry ("price is in the block"); a
    durable in-block mask over several bars needs mitigation="midpoint"
    or "close_through" — the Example below uses "close_through".
    A block is BORN at the close of the CONFIRMING bar — never at the
    block candle's own bar, which is in the past — and is reflected in
    that bar's output; it is tested for mitigation from the next bar on.
    The block candle itself always PRECEDES the confirming bar (Q-1021):
    the candidate range for `candle_select` ends the bar before the
    confirmation, so a displacement candle is never its own block.

NaN semantics:
    A bar with NaN in open/high/low/close emits NaN and neither births
    nor mitigates a block (state untouched; it still ages toward
    expiry), and it can never BE the block candle. A NaN inside the ATR
    window blanks the reference for `atr_period` bars: "distance" is NaN
    over those bars even with active blocks ("edge" still reports), and
    a displacement confirmation cannot be judged there. A flat tape
    (ATR 0) has no reference — NaN, never a division by zero. A
    confirming leg that holds no qualifying candle births NO block
    (undefined, never a default candle). Never zero-filled: NaN means
    "no active block / undefined", not 0.

Caveats (research/05 §8, research/06, R5): the order-block construct has
never been tested in a controlled study — the zone-revisit claim ("price
returns to the origin of the move") carries no published evidence, no
matched-control baseline, and no agreed definition, which is why the two
dominant definitions here disagree. Offered as an interpretation of the
tape, NEVER as a Keel claim that order blocks work. Execution is
bar-close: "at the block" means the CLOSE is at it.

Note: stops, targets, trails and other price-level rules are checked and filled at the bar's close, with no intra-bar measurement or execution, so a fill can be well past the level.

Example:
    # Globals(target_timeframe="1h"): PriceDataLoader() serves the 1h bars itself — no resampler
    Pipeline([
        PriceDataLoader(),
        OrderBlock(direction="bullish", confirm="structure_break",
                   mitigation="close_through"),
        RangeSelector(low_threshold=-10.0, high_threshold=0.0),   # close inside a live bullish block
        EqualWeightSizer(target_leverage=1.0),
    ])
components.usage_hint: Use for the "return to the origin of the move" family of SMC entries: an order block is the candle a leg came FROM, marked only once the leg has CONFIRMED itself (a structure break, a displacement, or either). The component keeps every unmitigated block as an active zone and reports how far the close is from the nearest one in ATR units, so "price is back at the order block" is a threshold recipe on this scalar (RangeSelector / AboveThresholdFilter): inside <= 0, approaching from outside is a small positive number. Every contested clause below is a parameter whose options are pinned to the school that uses them (smc-trader-cohort research/05 §8); Keel does not adjudicate between them.

components.name: ParabolicSAR
components.description:
Compute Parabolic SAR (Stop and Reverse) trailing stop levels for trend-following and exit signals.

Use as a trailing stop or trend reversal detector. Output is a price level that follows
the trend: below price in uptrends, above price in downtrends. Comparing SAR to close
gives a direction signal. Requires high/low data. Since output is in absolute price units,
it must be transformed (e.g., (close - SAR) / close) before cross-asset comparison.
Prefer SuperTrend over ParabolicSAR when you want a pre-computed direction signal
rather than raw stop levels.

Output:
    In price units (absolute levels). Tracks below price during uptrends and
    above price during downtrends. NaN for the first bar only (minimal warmup).
    Not directly comparable across assets without normalization.

Formula:
    SAR_t = SAR_{t-1} + AF * (EP - SAR_{t-1})
    where AF starts at `acceleration`, increments by `acceleration` on new extremes,
    capped at `maximum`. EP = extreme point (highest high or lowest low in trend).

Note: stops, targets, trails and other price-level rules are checked and filled at the bar's close, with no intra-bar measurement or execution, so a fill can be well past the level.

Example:
    ParabolicSAR(acceleration=0.02, maximum=0.2)
    -> PercentageNormalizationTransform(ohlcv_slot="ohlcv") -> ForecastScaler()
components.usage_hint: Use as a trailing stop or trend reversal detector. Output is a price level that follows the trend: below price in uptrends, above price in downtrends. Comparing SAR to close gives a direction signal. Requires high/low data. Since output is in absolute price units, it must be transformed (e.g., (close - SAR) / close) before cross-asset comparison. Prefer SuperTrend over ParabolicSAR when you want a pre-computed direction signal rather than raw stop levels.

parameters.name: acceleration
parameters.description: Starting and increment value for the acceleration factor (AF). Smaller (0.01) = slower trailing, larger (0.03-0.04) = faster trailing that stays closer to price. Default 0.02 is standard.

parameters.name: maximum
parameters.description: Cap for the acceleration factor. Limits how aggressively the SAR trails price. Default 0.2. Reducing to 0.1 makes the indicator less responsive to new extremes; increasing to 0.3 makes it tighter but more prone to whipsaw.

components.name: PeakPrice
components.description:
The best close since this trade's entry (highest for a long, lowest for a short): the
high-water mark a trailing stop measures from.

Position layer: TradeManager turns entry signals into a Position; each rule is a reader, then
ordinary components, then an action (Exit, Reduce, ScaleIn, AllowEntry). The peak is updated
on a bar before any comparison on that bar; bars with no price are skipped.

Note: stops, targets, trails and other price-level rules are checked and filled at the bar's close, with no intra-bar measurement or execution, so a fill can be well past the level.

Example:
    TradeManager(entries="entries", prices="ohlcv") ->
      {"ran_25pct": [{"numerator": [PeakPrice()], "denominator": [EntryPrice()]}, SignalRatio(),
        AboveThresholdFilter(threshold=1.25, inclusive=True), Reduce(fraction=0.5)]} ->
      Exposure() -> FixedWeightSizer(weight_per_position=0.1)
components.usage_hint: Position layer: TradeManager turns entry signals into a Position; each rule is a reader, then ordinary components, then an action (Exit, Reduce, ScaleIn, AllowEntry). The peak is updated on a bar before any comparison on that bar; bars with no price are skipped.

components.name: PercentageNormalizationTransform
components.description:
Normalize indicator values by price to create percentage-based measures for cross-asset comparison.

Use to convert absolute indicators (ATR, Bollinger bandwidth, spread) into
price-relative percentages so assets at different price levels are comparable.
Requires an OHLCV slot for price data. Commonly placed after ATR or similar
absolute indicators and before CrossSectionalZScore or a ranking transform.

Output:
    Non-negative, unbounded. Represents indicator as a percentage of price
    (e.g., ATR of $500 on a $50,000 asset = 1.0%). NaN where price is zero.

Formula:
    output = (indicator / price) * multiplier
    where multiplier defaults to 100 for percentage

Example:
    ATR(period=14) -> PercentageNormalizationTransform(ohlcv_slot="ohlcv") -> CrossSectionalZScore()

components.name: PortfolioMarginCap
components.description:
Cap projected maintenance-margin consumption (fraction of equity) for cross-margin venues.

Hyperliquid cross-margin liquidates when equity falls below the sum of
per-position maintenance margins, where each asset's maintenance-margin
fraction is 1/(2 x maxLeverage). This component bounds that sum at the
TARGET-WEIGHT level: mm(t) = sum_i |w_i(t)| x 1/(2 x maxLeverage_i).

Two one-sided controls, both scaling the whole row proportionally:
- soft_limit: trim toward it when exceeded (the active control).
- hard_limit: absolute bound applied after the soft trim (the declared
  guarantee — with a gross LeverageCap L in the stack, it licenses
  "liquidation buffer >= (1 - hard_limit)/L at rebalance stamps, always",
  independent of vol estimates, correlations, or the sample).

Per-asset maxLeverage arrives via the Universe declaration
(`universe.max_leverages`) — resolved from the platform's instrument
registry alongside the symbol list by universe resolution, baked into the
compiled blob (identical in live and backtest; nothing is loaded at
runtime). Symbols absent from the map use `default_max_leverage`
(conservative low tier => high margin assumption).

Output:
    WeightSeries (DataFrame, same shape as input). Projected MM per row
    <= hard_limit; rows already below the limits pass through unchanged.

Formula:
    mm(t)   = sum_i |w_i| / (2 x maxLev_i)
    w      *= min(1, soft_limit / mm)          [if soft_limit]
    w      *= min(1, hard_limit / mm')         [if hard_limit; mm' after soft]

Example:
    ... -> LeverageCap(max_leverage=4.5, max_asset_weight=1.0)
        -> PortfolioMarginCap(soft_limit=0.30, hard_limit=0.35)
components.usage_hint: Hyperliquid cross-margin liquidates when equity falls below the sum of per-position maintenance margins, where each asset's maintenance-margin fraction is 1/(2 x maxLeverage). This component bounds that sum at the TARGET-WEIGHT level: mm(t) = sum_i |w_i(t)| x 1/(2 x maxLeverage_i).

parameters.description: Projected-MM fraction above which the book is trimmed toward the limit (one-sided). None disables. Default 0.30.

parameters.name: hard_limit
parameters.description: Absolute projected-MM bound applied after the soft trim — the guarantee level. None disables. Default 0.35.

parameters.name: default_max_leverage
parameters.description: maxLeverage assumed for symbols missing from the universe.max_leverages map. Default 3.0 (the most conservative HL tier: 16.67% maintenance margin).

parameters.description: Log fire count + min multiplier at INFO when True.

parameters.name: entry_slot
parameters.description: Slot holding the entry channel — a BinarySignal where +1 opens long, -1 opens short and 0 means no entry. Values outside {-1, 0, +1} RAISE (NaN allowed, and NaN poisons the state forward — see the class docstring). This frame's index and columns become the output's. Required; must match a Store() upstream. The pipeline input is NOT read.

parameters.name: exit_slot
parameters.description: Slot holding the exit channel, also guarded as a BinarySignal. How its values are read depends entirely on ``exit_mode``. Required; must match a Store() upstream.

parameters.name: exit_mode
parameters.description: How an exit value is interpreted. "scalar" (default): the exit fires on EXACTLY 1.0, whatever the position's direction — an exit of -1 does nothing at all. This is the mode for one-sided boolean exits (TimeBasedExitFilter, ValueStopExitFilter), and the one to pick when the exit channel means "get out" rather than "the signal has turned". "directional": the exit fires when it OPPOSES the position (``exit × state < 0``), so ThresholdCross(upper=0, lower=0) emits +1 above zero (closing shorts) and -1 below it (closing longs). Pick this for "enter at the extreme, exit at the mean", where the same continuous signal drives both ends of the trade. Any other value raises.

components.name: PredictedFundingLoader
components.description:
Load the PREDICTED funding rate — what the next settlement is expected to charge — on the strategy's clock.

PREDICTED IS NOT SETTLED. This loader serves the venue's forecast: the
value at a bar is the last prediction the venue published inside that
bar, for the settlement at the end of the current funding hour. The
venue refines it until the tick, and the final pre-tick value IS the
settled rate. For the SETTLED hourly funding rate actually charged (the
carry that was paid or received) use FundingDataLoader, which reads
funding_data.funding_rate. Never read one series as the other: a
backtest that uses this loader as "the funding paid" is wrong, and one
that uses FundingDataLoader as "the funding expected" has lookahead.

Use for funding-carry entry timing and anticipation signals: the
expected cost of holding a perp through the next settlement, the
cross-sectional spread of expected funding across coins (where carry is
about to be richest), and predicted-minus-settled as a measure of how
much the venue's forecast moved within the hour.

Timeframe: omit `timeframe` to serve Globals.target_timeframe; pass a
literal for a branch on its OWN clock (multi-timeframe). The series is
stored at ONE MINUTE (market_data.ctx_1m) and served at every platform
clock from 5min up. LOOKAHEAD, read this: v1 served the value known at
the TOP of the hour — the least-informed forecast of the hour. v2 on a
sub-hourly clock serves a LATER, better-informed forecast of the SAME
settlement, which is still causal (a bar only ever carries observations
inside it) but is not the same statistic. A branch that wants v1's
reading asks for it: timeframe="1h" with the hour's last observation is
the forecast as the hour closed; a 5min branch is twelve refinements
per hour.

Aggregation (`agg`, default "last"): the prediction is a point-in-time
forecast, so a bar carries the last one inside it. "mean" averages the
forecasts over the bar; "first" is the earliest (v1's reading, at 1h);
"median"; "sum".

Output:
    StreamSeries (DataFrame, bar close labels x symbols). Values are the
    predicted hourly funding rate as decimals (e.g. 0.0001 = 1 bp per
    hour), read from ctx_1m.predicted_funding. If the venue published
    nothing for a bar, the previous bar's value is repeated for up to 3
    bars; after that the bar is NaN (the coin pauses, and nothing is
    refused). Never interpolated, and there is no REST fallback because
    the venue exposes the prediction as current-only.

Example:
    # Globals(target_timeframe="1d")
    PredictedFundingLoader() -> CrossSectionalZScore()

    # Globals(target_timeframe="15min"): a branch on the funding hour beside
    # a finer strategy clock — the projector carries each completed hour
    # onto the 15min grid (coarse → fine only)
    PredictedFundingLoader(timeframe="1h") -> CrossSectionalZScore() -> TargetSignalProjector()
components.usage_hint: PREDICTED IS NOT SETTLED. This loader serves the venue's forecast: the value at a bar is the last prediction the venue published inside that bar, for the settlement at the end of the current funding hour. The venue refines it until the tick, and the final pre-tick value IS the settled rate. For the SETTLED hourly funding rate actually charged (the carry that was paid or received) use FundingDataLoader, which reads funding_data.funding_rate. Never read one series as the other: a backtest that uses this loader as "the funding paid" is wrong, and one that uses FundingDataLoader as "the funding expected" has lookahead.

components.name: PremiumDiscount
components.description:
Where the close sits in the current dealing range, as a RANGE COORDINATE — 0 at the low, 1 at the high.

Use as the SMC "am I buying cheap or expensive" gate, the least contested
idea in the family: equilibrium is the 50% of the dealing range, above it
is PREMIUM (where the schools teach you sell) and below it DISCOUNT (where
you buy). Because it is one scalar in range coordinates, every threshold
recipe reads directly off it — `BelowThresholdFilter(threshold=0.5)` is
"in discount" and `AboveThresholdFilter(threshold=0.5)` is "in premium".
Reach for those ONE-SIDED filters, never a two-sided band pinned at 0 or
1: the coordinate keeps going past both ends of the range (see Output), so
`RangeSelector(0.0, 0.5)` written for "in discount" throws away exactly
the bars deepest IN discount — measured a 36% shortfall against the
one-sided filter on the same bars (Q-1025). It composes with the crowding
regimes for the spec 01 §4 "crowded premium" recipe. Two anchors ship,
each pinned to the school that uses it (smc-trader-cohort research/05 §6).

Axes (sourced defaults, spec 01 contract 3):
    range_anchor: WHAT the dealing range is.
        "swing_pair" (default) = ICT's dealing range, "the most recent
        established high and low on your trade timeframe": the last
        CONFIRMED swing high and the last CONFIRMED swing low, each held
        until superseded or expired. It is the default as the more common
        sourced teaching; the two sources disagree here, so nothing is
        blessed. The range only exists once BOTH sides have confirmed, and
        it is a pair of levels, not a window — so price can and does trade
        outside it (see Output).
        "trailing_extremes" = LuxAlgo's trailing structural extremes: from
        the pivot bar of the most recent confirmed swing (either side) to
        the current bar, the running high and running low, re-anchored
        whenever a newer pivot confirms. This one contains the close by
        construction, so it is the anchor to pick when you want a strictly
        bounded [0, 1] reading.
    detector: "fractal" (default, ICT's symmetric shape / smc.py) or
        "leg_flip" (LuxAlgo's rolling-extreme state flip, which is NOT a
        fractal — research/05 §1 V3). See `SwingPivot` for the contract.
    width: swing width in bars (default 5). The sourced ladder is 1 (ICT's
        short-term high), 5 (LuxAlgo's internal tier) and 50 (LuxAlgo's
        swing tier / smc.py's `swing_length` default); a width-50 fractal
        confirms only a handful of levels per 500 bars, which is why the
        default is the internal tier.
    expiry_bars: safety bound — a range side goes stale `expiry_bars` bars
        after its confirmation if nothing supersedes it (default 200). A
        KEEL CONVENTION, not a practitioner one: no surveyed source
        expires a dealing range by bar count.

UNITS — a range COORDINATE (unit-free), NOT price and NOT a percentage:
0.0 is the range low, 0.5 equilibrium, 1.0 the range high, and the axis
continues past both ends. A reading of 1.5 is "half a range width ABOVE
the range high"; -0.5 is "half a range width BELOW the range low". It is
the same coordinate the sourced cohort quotes its extension targets on —
ICT's -0.27 / -0.62 are points on this axis, not a different scale.
Comparable across assets, so it pools directly. Scale-invariant.

Output:
    SignalSeries (timestamps x symbols), causal, no repaint:
    `(close - range_low) / (range_high - range_low)`.

    LEAVING [0, 1] IS ORDINARY, NOT EXCEPTIONAL — size every consumer for
    it. Under "swing_pair" the range is a PAIR OF LEVELS, not a window, so
    price trades outside it routinely: a close above the last confirmed
    swing high reads > 1, one below the last confirmed swing low reads
    < 0. That reading IS the measurement: it says how far BEYOND the range
    price has travelled, counted in range widths. The expansion state is a
    different market condition from "at the range edge" and is reported as
    one. Measured at the shipped defaults (swing_pair, fractal, width=5,
    expiry_bars=200) over two years of hourly bars for eight majors, 33%
    of the 142,069 finite readings sit outside [0, 1] and the readings
    themselves run from -42 to +1669; on the random-walk fixture in the
    test file it is 44%, running -5.4 to +21.7. The magnitude is unbounded
    in both directions, and the large values are exact arithmetic on a
    genuinely narrow range rather than numerical noise (see the
    tick-wide-range note under NaN semantics). Pick "trailing_extremes"
    when a bounded reading is what you want: its
    running extremes include the current bar, so the coordinate is inside
    [0, 1] by construction — 0% outside, pinned by
    `TestExpansionIsNotClipped`.

    Spec 01 §2 describes the output as [0, 1]. The unbounded axis is the
    one deliberate widening, and it is a SUPERSET: a ONE-SIDED threshold
    written against [0, 1] behaves identically on it, which is why the
    recipes above are one-sided. A TWO-SIDED `RangeSelector(0.0, 0.5)`
    does not — it excludes every < 0 reading, precisely the deepest
    discount, and measured a 36% shortfall against
    `BelowThresholdFilter(threshold=0.5)` on the same bars (Q-1025).
    Bound a band at 0 or 1 only when you positively mean to EXCLUDE the
    expansion state, and say so where you build it.

    The OTE convention, which users will ask for by name: the 0.62-0.79
    retracement band with its 0.705 sweet spot, invalidation at 1.0 and
    extension targets at -0.27 / -0.62 (liquidityhunters,
    innercircletrader.net). Measured from a range LOW those map to
    0.38-0.21 on this scalar (a bullish OTE is a discount-side band); from
    a range HIGH they read 0.62-0.79 directly. Expressed as
    `RangeSelector(low_threshold=0.21, high_threshold=0.38)` or the mirror.
    Note that the extension targets are NEGATIVE coordinates: the sourced
    vocabulary already lives outside [0, 1], which is a second reason the
    axis is not bounded there.

NaN semantics:
    NaN until a range exists — under "swing_pair" that means until BOTH a
    swing high and a swing low have confirmed, so at least `2 * width`
    bars and usually more; under "trailing_extremes" until the first pivot
    confirms. NaN on any bar with a NaN in high/low/close (an unobserved
    bar has no position, and the range state persists across it). NaN when
    the range has no width — a degenerate range (high == low) or an
    INVERTED one (the last confirmed swing high sitting below the last
    confirmed swing low, which happens in a fast trend) is not a range,
    and reports NaN rather than dividing by zero or by a negative span.
    Never zero-filled: 0.0 means "at the range low", not "no data".

    A range that is merely NARROW is still a range and still reports. The
    two confirmed pivots can land a tick apart — equal highs and equal
    lows are a sourced structure, not an artifact — and the coordinate is
    then exact but enormous: measured on the tape above, ETH's confirmed
    pair sat at [3906.6, 3906.7] for six hours in 2025-10, reading up to
    1669. Only an EXACTLY zero span is NaN'd (10 bars of 142,754). If a
    consumer divides by, ranks on, or sizes from this scalar rather than
    thresholding it, bound it yourself.

Caveats (research/06 §2.4, R5 — BINDING): the range-position idea has
partial support and the fib machinery on top of it does not. Short-horizon
reversal is a documented regularity (Jegadeesh 1990, Lehmann 1990) and
Osler (2000) found published support/resistance levels predicted intraday
trend interruptions, so "buy low in the range, sell high" is a folk
phrasing of effects that exist — the 50% midpoint as a RANGE POSITION is
innocuous. But the specific OTE machinery is CONTRADICTED where tested:
Batchelor & Ramyar (2006), "Magic Numbers in the Dow" (Cass), found trend
lengths and durations cluster at Fibonacci ratios no more than chance
given the number of tests. The 0.62-0.79 band inherits a literature that,
at its only rigorous examination, found nothing. The constants above are
documented because users ask for them, never because Keel claims they
work; the thresholds are the user's interpretation.

Example:
    # Globals(target_timeframe="1h"): PriceDataLoader() serves the 1h bars itself — no resampler
    Pipeline([
        PriceDataLoader(),
        PremiumDiscount(range_anchor="swing_pair", width=5),
        BelowThresholdFilter(threshold=0.5),  # in discount; one-sided, so < 0 bars are kept
        EqualWeightSizer(target_leverage=1.0),
    ])

components.name: PremiumLoader
components.description:
Load perp-vs-oracle premium data on the strategy's clock for crowding, basis, and funding-pressure signals.

Use for crowding and basis signals: the premium of the perpetual's mark
price over the oracle (spot) price. A persistently positive premium
means perps trade rich to spot (long crowding / contango-like pressure,
and upward pressure on the next funding rate); a negative premium means
perps trade cheap (short crowding / backwardation). Distinct from
FundingDataLoader, which serves the SETTLED hourly funding rate actually
charged. Synonyms: premium, mark-oracle premium, perp premium, basis,
perp-spot spread, funding pressure, crowding.

Timeframe: omit `timeframe` to serve Globals.target_timeframe; pass a
literal for a branch on its OWN clock (multi-timeframe). The series is
stored at ONE MINUTE (market_data.ctx_1m) and served at every platform
clock from 5min up: the minutes are rolled onto the bar grid
(Globals.bar_offset included) with `agg`. Nothing finer than 5min is
declarable, so nothing is refused.

Aggregation (`agg`, default "last"): the premium is an instantaneous
sample, so a bar carries the LAST sample inside it — the reading the
venue's hourly snapshot always was, now at minute resolution. "mean" is
the average premium over the bar, computed from the minutes (a different
and strictly better-sampled quantity than the hourly-sample average this
loader used to default to — see the module docstring); "first";
"median"; "sum".

Output:
    StreamSeries (DataFrame, bar close labels x symbols). Values are the
    perp-vs-oracle premium as decimals (e.g. 0.0005 = 5 bps above oracle),
    read from ctx_1m.premium. If the venue published nothing for a bar,
    the previous bar's value is repeated for up to 3 bars; after that the
    bar is NaN (the coin pauses, and nothing is refused). Never
    interpolated and never zero (the venue sends a null premium for an
    untraded coin, and a null is not a zero basis).

Example:
    # Globals(target_timeframe="1d"): served 1d, the premium at each day's close
    PremiumLoader() -> RollingZScoreTransform(window=30) -> CrossSectionalZScore()

    # Globals(target_timeframe="15min"): served 15min, from the minutes
    PremiumLoader() -> RollingZScoreTransform(window=96) -> CrossSectionalZScore()

    # The day's average premium instead of its close
    PremiumLoader(agg="mean")

Distinct from FundingDataLoader, which serves the SETTLED hourly funding rate actually charged. Synonyms: premium, mark-oracle premium, perp premium, basis, perp-spot spread, funding pressure, crowding.

parameters.name: agg
parameters.description: How the ctx minutes are rolled into a bar. None (default) = "last", the sample at the bar's close — the family's stored aggregation and the one the node-local ctx ladder holds. "mean" = the average premium over the bar; "first"; "median"; "sum". A non-default choice is computed from the same minutes on this loader's own cache entry.

components.name: PremiumRegime
components.description:
Detect market-wide perp-premium crowding (rich or cheap to oracle) as a binary regime from per-asset premium z-scores.

Use to gate or scale a strategy on CROWDING state read from the
perpetual's mark-vs-oracle premium: 1.0 when perps across the universe
trade unusually rich to spot versus their own recent history (long
crowding, contango-like pressure, upward pressure on the next funding
settlement) or unusually cheap (short crowding / backwardation), 0.0
otherwise. Feed the output into RegimeGate, RegimeScale or
RegimeLeverageScaler unchanged — a 1-D market-wide GlobalSeries. Distinct
from FundingLevelRegime, which reads the SETTLED funding actually
charged; premium is the instantaneous pressure before settlement.

UNITS — premium is a dimensionless rate (0.0005 = 5 bps above oracle), so
it is comparable across assets on its own; this component still
normalizes each asset against its OWN rolling history first (rolling
z-score over `lookback` bars) and takes the cross-sectional MEDIAN of the
z-scores — the same shape as OpenInterestRegime, so the two read
identically, and one dislocated instrument is one vote rather than the
market. Input is the loader's StreamSeries (timestamps x symbols).

Axes (defaults sized in bars of the loaders' 1h clock grain; premium itself
is served from the ctx_1m family — market_data.ctx_1m at a 1m native grain,
no finer than 5min — not the old hourly market_data.premium_data):
    lookback: z-score window in bars of the input clock — the grain the
        loader SERVES (it follows Globals: hourly under a 1h clock, daily
        under a 1d clock, so 168 is 7 days on 1h and 7 is 7 days on 1d).
        Default 168 (7 days of hourly premium) — premium mean-reverts within days, so a
        week is the natural crowding horizon; 72 (3d) is a fast read, 720
        (30d) a slow one. Warmup is `lookback - 1` bars (NaN).
    threshold: z-units the market median must exceed. Default 1.5; 1.0 is
        permissive, 2.0-2.5 flags only extreme dislocations.
    direction: "high" = perps rich / long crowding (median z >
        threshold); "low" = perps cheap / short crowding (median z <
        -threshold); "abs" = either. Default "high".

Output:
    GlobalSeries with 1.0 (in regime), 0.0 (not), NaN where the market
    score is undefined. Name "premium_regime". Value at bar t uses premium
    through bar t (the completed bar the loader serves) — causal, no
    shift, no repaint: a fixed rolling window never revises a past value.

NaN semantics:
    First `lookback - 1` bars NaN (strict warmup). A NaN premium cell
    blanks that asset's z for `lookback` bars — never interpolated — and
    the asset is EXCLUDED from the median while blanked; a
    zero-dispersion window has no z (NaN, never +/-inf). A bar where no
    asset has a z yields NaN (never 0.0). Prefer a universe of at least
    three symbols — with two the median is their mean.

Caveat:
    A regime describes crowding STATE, not direction. Rich perps mean the
    long side is paying to stay long — that is fuel for a squeeze in
    either direction, not a forecast; pair the regime with a directional
    signal on the price branch. PremiumLoader follows Globals down to its
    5min served floor (served daily under a 1d clock, hourly under a 1h
    clock, agg last since the ctx move) — it rolls the 1m ctx_1m base, so
    a 5/15/30min clock is served directly and needs no projector.

Example:
    # Globals(target_timeframe="1h"): both loaders serve the hourly bars themselves
    Pipeline([
        {
            "carry": [PriceDataLoader(), EWMA(window=20)],
            "crowding": [PremiumLoader(), PremiumRegime(lookback=168, threshold=1.5, direction="high")],
        },
        RegimeGate(signal_key="carry", index_key="crowding", condition="index < 1"),
        EqualWeightSizer(target_leverage=1.0),
    ])
    # stand down while the long side is crowded (regime 1.0 gates the branch off)

Feed the output into RegimeGate, RegimeScale or RegimeLeverageScaler unchanged — a 1-D market-wide GlobalSeries. components.name: PriceDataLoader
components.description:
Load OHLCV price data for all universe symbols at the timeframe the strategy executes on.

Use as the first component in any pipeline that needs price data. With no
arguments the loader serves the strategy's own clock: it reads
`Globals(target_timeframe=...)` for the bar size and `Globals(bar_offset=...)`
for the bar boundary, and delivers bars ready to compute on — no
TargetTimeframeResampler needed. Bars are rolled from the venue's 15-minute
capture with the platform's one resampling semantics (closed-right bars
labeled by close, incomplete trailing bar dropped, the offset grid when
Globals declares one).

Pass `timeframe=` only for a branch that needs its OWN bar size — a 1h
momentum branch inside a 1d strategy, say. An explicit timeframe is a
branch clock, not a default: bring that branch back to the strategy clock
with TargetSignalResampler() when it is finer, or TargetSignalProjector()
when it is coarser. The bar offset lives in Globals and nowhere else. Load
each clock you need with its own PriceDataLoader rather than resampling a
15-minute load with TargetTimeframeResampler(): that is a second
aggregation whose open/high/low differ from this loader's own roll on bars
that begin without a trade.

Without `Globals(target_timeframe=...)` and without `timeframe=` there is
no bar size to serve and the loader refuses to run — it never assumes one.
A timeframe FINER than the venue capture (5min) can only be served where the
environment's price source supports it (see :func:`served_floor`).

Absent quiet bars that the ingestion completeness ledger verified as no-trade
windows are materialized as true empty bars on the source before any roll-up;
small unverified internal gaps are filled heuristically (max_gap_fill).

Output:
    OHLCVDict mapping symbol names to DataFrames with lowercase OHLCV columns
    and DatetimeIndex at the served timeframe, on the declared bar_offset
    grid. NaN for unverified gaps larger than max_gap_fill.

Example:
    # Globals(target_timeframe="1d", bar_offset="12h"): the canonical
    # opening — the bound loader serves 1d on the 12h grid, no resampler
    PriceDataLoader() -> Store("ohlcv_1d")

    # Globals(target_timeframe="1d"): a branch on its OWN 1h clock — the
    # explicit timeframe= is the override; put it back on the strategy
    # clock with TargetSignalResampler (a finer branch) / TargetSignalProjector (a coarser one)
    PriceDataLoader(timeframe="1h") -> EWMA(window=20) -> TargetSignalResampler(method="last")

components.name: QuantileRangeSelector
components.description:
Mask in the assets whose percentile rank sits inside a 0-100 band.

Use for "top quartile by momentum", "the strongest 20%", "bottom decile
for mean reversion", "the middle of the pack", "trade only the leaders".
It turns a cross-sectional RANK into a tradeable mask, which is the step
between "score everything" and "act on some of it".

It does NOT compute a quantile:
    The thresholds are compared against the incoming values DIRECTLY,
    with no normalisation, so the input must already be on the 0-100
    percentile scale — which is exactly what ``QuantileRankTransform``
    emits (``rank(pct=True) * 100``, cross-sectional, per bar). Handed a
    raw indicator instead, ``low_quantile=75`` silently means "value >=
    75" in that indicator's own units, and on a z-score or a return that
    selects almost nothing. Rank first.

    (The input is declared ``SignalSeries`` rather than ``RankSignal``
    because ``RankSignal`` denotes [0, 1], which contradicts this
    component's own 0-100 validation.)

Formula (elementwise, per cell):
    keep = (x >= low_quantile) and (x <= high_quantile)
    out  = 1.0 if keep else 0.0

    Both bounds are INCLUSIVE and there is no exclusivity switch — use
    ``RangeSelector`` if you need one. An unset bound is simply not
    applied, so ``low_quantile=80`` alone means "the top 20%".

Granularity to expect:
    Percentile ranks of N assets land on multiples of 100/N, so with 20
    assets a band of width 4 can be empty on some bars and hold one asset
    on others. Ties share a rank. Pick bands wider than 100/N unless a
    variable-width selection is what you want; for an exact count per bar
    use ``TopNAssetSelector`` instead.

NaN discipline:
    NaN fails both comparisons, so a missing rank emits 0.0 — "not
    selected", never NaN and never carried forward (the declared
    ``neutral_on_missing`` contract). Since ``QuantileRankTransform``
    preserves NaN, an asset with no data is excluded automatically, and
    it never displaces a real asset from the band.

Causality / invariance:
    This step is elementwise on bar t — no window, no state — so it adds
    no time dependence of its own. Note that the RANK it consumes is
    cross-sectional (every asset at that bar influences every other),
    which is a property of the upstream ranker, not of this mask.

Output:
    BinarySignal DataFrame of float 0.0/1.0 (never bool, never NaN), same
    index and columns as the input. Feeds ``ApplyMask`` (gate a score),
    ``MaskAnd``/``MaskOr`` (combine with other conditions), or a
    ``Store`` for a component that names a mask slot.

Example:
    # Globals(target_timeframe="1d", bar_offset="12h"): PriceDataLoader() serves 1d on the 12h grid — no resampler
    Pipeline([
        PriceDataLoader(),
        {
            "momentum": [ROC(period=20)],
            "leaders": [ROC(period=20), QuantileRankTransform(),
                        QuantileRangeSelector(low_quantile=80, high_quantile=100)],
        },
        ApplyMask(score_signal="momentum", filter_signal="leaders"),
    ])
components.usage_hint: Use for "top quartile by momentum", "the strongest 20%", "bottom decile for mean reversion", "the middle of the pack", "trade only the leaders". It turns a cross-sectional RANK into a tradeable mask, which is the step between "score everything" and "act on some of it".

parameters.name: low_quantile
parameters.description: Inclusive lower bound in PERCENTILE units, 0-100 (not 0-1). None (default) applies no lower bound. 80 = the top fifth, 75 = the top quartile, 50 = at or above the median. Values outside 0-100 raise.

parameters.name: high_quantile
parameters.description: Inclusive upper bound in PERCENTILE units, 0-100. None (default) applies no upper bound; pair it with ``low_quantile`` for a band and use 100 for "and everything above". 25 = the bottom quartile, 20 = the bottom fifth. Must be >= ``low_quantile``, and values outside 0-100 raise.

components.name: QuantileRankTransform
components.description:
Rank assets cross-sectionally into 0-100 percentiles for comparable quantile-based filtering.

Use to convert any raw indicator into cross-sectional percentile ranks so that
different indicators share a common [0, 100] scale. Parameter-free and suitable
for universe filtering (e.g., "top 20% by momentum"). Prefer CrossSectionalZScore
when you need unbounded z-scores for forecast scaling, or RankTransform when you
need ordinal ranks (1 to N) rather than percentiles.

Output:
    Range [0, 100] — NOT the [0, 1] of the ``RankSignal`` convention: this
    emits ``rank(pct=True) * 100``, so downstream thresholds are calibrated
    in PERCENTILE units (e.g. 80 = the 80th percentile), which is what
    QuantileRangeSelector's 0-100 params expect. 100 = highest-ranked asset,
    0 = lowest. NaN preserved from input. Cross-sectional: ranks are
    relative to other assets at each bar.

Example:
    ROC(period=10) -> QuantileRankTransform()
    -> QuantileRangeSelector(low_quantile=20, high_quantile=80)
components.usage_hint: Use to convert any raw indicator into cross-sectional percentile ranks so that different indicators share a common [0, 100] scale. Parameter-free and suitable for universe filtering (e.g., "top 20% by momentum"). Prefer CrossSectionalZScore when you need unbounded z-scores for forecast scaling, or RankTransform when you need ordinal ranks (1 to N) rather than percentiles.

components.name: ROC
components.description:
Compute rate of change (percentage return) over a lookback period as a momentum signal.

Use as a momentum or mean reversion input signal. For momentum strategies, feed into
ForecastScaler directly. For mean reversion, pipe through CrossSectionalZScore then
WingsTransform to fade extreme moves. Differs from MOM by outputting percentage change
rather than absolute price difference, making it comparable across assets.

Output:
    Percentage change, unbounded. Typically [-30, +30] for 15-min crypto bars
    with period=14. Positive = price rising, negative = price falling.
    NaN for the first `period` bars (warmup).

Formula:
    ROC = ((close - close[t-period]) / close[t-period]) * 100

Example:
    ROC(period=10) -> CrossSectionalZScore() -> ForecastScaler()
components.usage_hint: Use as a momentum or mean reversion input signal. For momentum strategies, feed into ForecastScaler directly. For mean reversion, pipe through CrossSectionalZScore then WingsTransform to fade extreme moves. Differs from MOM by outputting percentage change rather than absolute price difference, making it comparable across assets.

parameters.name: period
parameters.description: Lookback in bars for return calculation. Shorter (2-8) captures fast momentum, longer (14-32) captures medium-term trends. Common values: 4 (fast MR), 10 (standard), 20 (slow trend).

components.name: RSI
components.description:
Compute Relative Strength Index (RSI), a bounded momentum oscillator measuring overbought and oversold conditions.

Use as a mean reversion signal when assets reach extremes (>70 overbought, <30 oversold),
or as a trend-confirmation filter (midline 50 crossover). Typically followed by
CrossSectionalZScore or a threshold-based transform like WingsTransform. Prefer RSI over
CMO when you want a bounded [0, 100] oscillator; CMO provides a similar signal on [-100, 100].

Output:
    Range [0, 100]. Values > 70 = overbought (potential short), < 30 = oversold
    (potential long), ~50 = neutral. NaN during warmup (`period` bars).

Formula:
    RS = avg_gain(period) / avg_loss(period)
    RSI = 100 - 100 / (1 + RS)

Example:
    RSI(period=14) -> CrossSectionalZScore() -> WingsTransform(threshold=1.0)
components.usage_hint: Use as a mean reversion signal when assets reach extremes (>70 overbought, <30 oversold), or as a trend-confirmation filter (midline 50 crossover). Typically followed by CrossSectionalZScore or a threshold-based transform like WingsTransform. Prefer RSI over CMO when you want a bounded [0, 100] oscillator; CMO provides a similar signal on [-100, 100].

Select values within a numeric range, converting continuous signals to binary entry/exit filters.

Use after any continuous indicator or quantile ranking to create a binary mask

components.name: RankTransform
components.description:
Rank assets cross-sectionally from 1 to N for ordinal signal comparison and portfolio construction.

Use when portfolio construction requires ordinal ranks (e.g., "go long top 5, short
bottom 5"). More configurable than QuantileRankTransform with control over sort
direction, tie handling, and percentage mode. Prefer QuantileRankTransform for
simple percentile-based filtering, or CrossSectionalZScore for continuous z-scores.

    with the universe and is not the [0, 1] of the ``RankSignal``
    convention), or [0, 1] when pct=True. NaN preserved from input.
    Cross-sectional: ranks computed across assets at each timestamp.

    ROC(period=10) -> RankTransform(ascending=False)
    -> TopNAssetSelector(n=5, method="smallest")  # rank 1 = strongest

components.name: RealizedPnL
components.description:
Realized return (a fraction, TradeReturn units) of this asset's partial sells and closes in
the window (a UTC day by default): the reader for a per-asset daily loss limit.

Position layer: TradeManager turns entry signals into a Position; each rule is a reader, then
ordinary components, then an action (Exit, Reduce, ScaleIn, AllowEntry). A daily loss limit
of 2% is RealizedPnL(window="1d") above -0.02, ending in AllowEntry().

Example:
    TradeManager(entries="entries", prices="ohlcv") ->
      {"daily_loss": [RealizedPnL(window="1d"), AboveThresholdFilter(threshold=-0.02), AllowEntry()]} ->
      Exposure() -> FixedWeightSizer(weight_per_position=0.1)

Note: per asset; a limit across the whole book is not expressible yet.

components.name: RealizedVolCap
components.description:
Cap portfolio weights by recent realized portfolio vol.

Computes per-bar portfolio P&L from lagged weights × per-asset returns,
measures rolling stdev over `recent_window`, and scales weights down
proportionally if the annualized recent vol exceeds `target_vol × ratio`.

Use as a final risk overlay when you want positions to respect a realized-
vol budget. Common pairing: VolTargetWeightConverter sets intended vol →
IDM aggregation may push above → RealizedVolCap pulls back to target if
the strategy's recent realized vol drifts above the ceiling.

Output:
    WeightSeries (same shape as input). Per-bar weights scaled by M ≤ 1.
    Logs fire count + average M at INFO when log_fires=True.

Formula:
    pnl[t]      = Σ w_lag[t-1, i] × r[t, i]
    recent_vol  = rolling_std(pnl, recent_window) × √bars_per_year
    M[t]        = clip(target_vol × ratio / recent_vol[t], 0, 1)
    capped      = weights × M

Causality:
    weights.shift(1) before computing portfolio P&L — no lookahead. Rolling
    stdev uses past-only window. M[t] is bar-t value applied to bar-t
    weights (correct under right-labeled bars / decision-at-close[t]).

Tuning:
    ratio=1.0 binds at exactly the target_vol — strict cap, fires often.
    ratio=2.0 fires only when recent vol exceeds 2× target — looser.
    For the v1 strategy, ratio=2.0 with target_vol=0.50 (50% annualized)
    gives Carver-orthodox tail-only firing (~2% of bars).

Example:
    VolTargetWeightConverter(return_vol_slot="return_vol")
    → IDMPortfolioAggregator(forecast_slot="forecast", ohlcv_slot="ohlcv",
                             return_vol_slot="return_vol")
      → RealizedVolCap(target_vol=0.50, ratio=2.0, recent_window=30)
      → AdverseVolCap(target_vol=0.50, ratio=6.5)
      → LeverageCap(max_leverage=5)

components.name: RealizedVolatility
components.description:
Measure each target bar's realized volatility from the finer-frequency bars inside it.

A MEASUREMENT, not an estimator — the conceptual counterpart of
ReturnVolatility. ReturnVolatility ESTIMATES the current volatility
level by pooling returns ACROSS many same-frame bars (EWM window,
memory, lag: "what is the vol level now?"). RealizedVolatility looks
INSIDE one bar and measures the volatility that actually occurred
there — sqrt of the sum of squared sub-bar returns, the standard
realized-volatility quantity from the high-frequency literature
("how much vol did this bar contain?"). No window across bars, no
memory, no model. To build a smoothed vol ESTIMATE from these
measurements, compose a downstream smoother (e.g.
EWMATransform(window=36)) — each day's measurement here carries ~96
observations (15m bars in a day) where a squared daily return
carries one.

Frame-general: the source frequency is DETECTED from the input's
index, and the output frame comes from the strategy's
Globals(target_timeframe, bar_offset) declaration. A 1d strategy fed
15m bars gets daily RV; a 1h strategy fed 15m bars gets hourly RV.
Raises if the input is not finer than the target frame, and equally if
the source cadence cannot be detected at all (irregular index) — the
detected frequency IS the coverage denominator, so there is no correct
value to fall back to.

Output:
    SignalSeries on the target-timeframe clock (per-target-bar vol,
    NOT annualized — downstream consumers annualize, e.g.
    AdverseVolCap's bars_per_year). Target bars with insufficient
    source coverage (< min_coverage of the expected sub-bar count:
    the in-progress trailing bar, an asset's partial first day,
    data-gap days) emit NaN.

    The output index is a function of the input's SPAN, never of where
    the gaps fall inside it (Q-0694): the leading/trailing empty bins
    are trimmed, and every bin in between is emitted — as NaN when the
    gap swallowed it. A downstream `pd.concat`/reindex against a
    sibling signal therefore sees an explicit NaN for a data-hole bar
    instead of silently ffilling or dropping it.

Formula:
    r = sub-bar returns ("pct" or "log")
    rv[T] = sqrt( sum r² over source bars inside target bar T )
    rv[T] = NaN where count(r in T) < min_coverage × expected

    A sub-bar return is r[t] = close[t] / close[t-1] - 1 where t-1 is
    exactly ONE source bar before t. A return across a data gap is not a
    sub-bar return and is excluded, whether the gap arrives as NaN rows or
    as absent rows (Q-2245) — so the coverage count is the number of
    observed one-bar returns, and the measurement does not depend on the
    serving path or on which other assets share the frame.

Example:
    # Globals(target_timeframe="1d"): the strategy clock. This branch loads
    # 15min on its OWN clock — the explicit timeframe= is the override (a
    # bare PriceDataLoader() would serve the 1d target itself, which is not
    # finer) — so RV can measure inside each daily bar.
    PriceDataLoader(timeframe="15min") -> Store("ohlcv_15m") ...
    Load("ohlcv_15m") -> RealizedVolatility() -> EWMATransform(window=36) -> Store("rv_intra")

ReturnVolatility ESTIMATES the current volatility level by pooling returns ACROSS many same-frame bars (EWM window, memory, lag: "what is the vol level now?"). RealizedVolatility looks INSIDE one bar and measures the volatility that actually occurred there — sqrt of the sum of squared sub-bar returns, the standard realized-volatility quantity from the high-frequency literature ("how much vol did this bar contain?"). No window across bars, no memory, no model. To build a smoothed vol ESTIMATE from these measurements, compose a downstream smoother (e.g. EWMATransform(window=36)) — each day's measurement here carries ~96 observations (15m bars in a day) where a squared daily return carries one.

parameters.description: Minimum fraction of the expected sub-bar count a target bar needs to emit a value (default 0.9). Below it the bar is NaN — this one rule handles the in-progress trailing bar, an asset's partial first day, and data-gap days, at any frame pair.

components.name: RealizedVolatilityRegime
components.description:
Compute annualized realized volatility averaged across the universe as a volatility regime indicator.

Use to detect high-volatility regimes where strategies may need position scaling
or risk reduction. Feed into RegimeGate to disable momentum strategies during
vol spikes, or into RegimeScale to reduce forecast intensity. For a
multi-factor read, combine it in a Parallel branch with a funding or
open-interest regime rather than reaching for a single composite.

The annualisation factor is derived from the strategy's declared
``Globals(target_timeframe=...)``, so the emitted number means the same
thing on every clock: **1.0 is 100% annualized vol at 1d, at 4h and at
15min alike.** An absolute threshold you pick on one clock therefore keeps
its meaning on another. (Before v2 the factor was a hardcoded
``sqrt(365)`` — the count of calendar DAYS in a crypto year, which is the
bars-per-year count only when one bar is one day. On a 15min clock that
understated the emitted value by ``sqrt(96) = 9.80x``, so the documented
``index < 1.0`` gate could not fire at all. See Q-1151.)

This is a SAME-CLOCK detector: it annualises the returns of the bars it is
given, so its slot must carry bars on the declared target clock. To measure
volatility from bars FINER than the target frame, use ``RealizedVolatility``
instead — feeding sub-target bars here is refused rather than silently
mis-annualised.

Output:
    Scalar GlobalSeries, non-negative (annualized vol). Higher values indicate
    elevated market-wide volatility. 1.0 = 100% annualized vol on every clock.
    NaN during warmup (lookback // 2 bars) or when fewer than 2 instruments
    are available.

Formula:
    bars_per_year = minutes_per_year / minutes(target_timeframe)
    vol_i = rolling_std(returns_i, lookback) * sqrt(bars_per_year)
    signal = mean(vol_i) across instruments

Example:
    Globals(target_timeframe='1d') -> PriceDataLoader() -> Store('ohlcv') -> {
        "vol": [ExtractSeries(series_name='close'),
                RealizedVolatilityRegime(ohlcv_slot='ohlcv', lookback=20)],
        "momentum": [ROC(period=20), ForecastScaler()],
    } -> RegimeGate(index_key='vol', signal_key='momentum', condition='index < 1.0')
components.usage_hint: Use to detect high-volatility regimes where strategies may need position scaling or risk reduction. Feed into RegimeGate to disable momentum strategies during vol spikes, or into RegimeScale to reduce forecast intensity. For a multi-factor read, combine it in a Parallel branch with a funding or open-interest regime rather than reaching for a single composite.

Output is UNCHANGED on a 1d clock and larger on every finer one; absolute thresholds tuned against v1 on a sub-daily clock must be divided by sqrt(bars_per_day). Also refuses, rather than mis-annualising, when the slot's bars are not on the declared clock.

components.name: Reduce
components.description:
Sells a fraction of the INITIAL size once per trade, on the first bar its mask is 1: the
action for take-half-off, scale-out and partial take-profit rules.

Position layer: TradeManager turns entry signals into a Position; each rule is a reader, then
ordinary components, then an action (Exit, Reduce, ScaleIn, AllowEntry). Partials firing on
one bar are summed; a sum that reaches the units held closes the trade.

Example:
    TradeManager(entries="entries", prices="ohlcv") ->
      {"tp1": [TradeReturn(), AboveThresholdFilter(threshold=0.05, inclusive=True), Reduce(fraction=0.5)],
       "stop": [TradeReturn(), BelowThresholdFilter(threshold=-0.05, inclusive=True), Exit()]} ->
      Exposure() -> FixedWeightSizer(weight_per_position=0.1)

Note: stops, targets, trails and other price-level rules are checked and filled at the bar's close, with no intra-bar measurement or execution, so a fill can be well past the level.
Note: after adds, fraction=0.5 sells half of the initial size, not half the position.
Note: fraction=1.0 sells one initial unit.

components.name: RegimeLeverageScaler
components.description:
Renormalize the book's gross exposure to a regime's leverage target, decaying a stale regime to neutral.

Use for the same ask as ``MarketLeverageScaler`` — "lever up in a bull
regime", "trade smaller when the regime turns" — when the regime series
runs on a SLOWER clock than the book and a carried-forward value must
expire rather than persist. Handed the same already-aligned regime series
and the same parameters, the two components produce the same weights by the
same arithmetic; they differ only in the staleness bound below and in what
each accepts as regime input.

Like ``MarketLeverageScaler`` this RESCALES rather than multiplies: the
incoming gross is divided out and replaced by the regime's target, so a
book arriving at 0.2 gross and one arriving at 2.0 gross both leave at
exactly ``base_leverage`` in a neutral regime.

Formula (long_only=True — one target for the whole book):
    L[t]     = regime_leverage  if regime[t] == +1
             = base_leverage    otherwise (bearish, neutral, expired, NaN)
    G[t]     = Σ_i |w_i[t]|                        (NaN cells skipped)
    out_i[t] = w_i[t] × L[t] / G[t],   and 0 where G[t] == 0

Formula (long_only=False — the two sides are rescaled independently):
    bullish → longs to regime_leverage, shorts to base_leverage
    bearish → longs to base_leverage,   shorts to regime_leverage
    neutral/expired/NaN → both sides to base_leverage
    out_i[t] = w_i[t] × target_side[t] / Σ(that side's |w|)

Staleness — read this before choosing between the two scalers:
    ``max_stale_bars`` is applied ONLY on the alignment path. When the
    regime's index differs from the weights' index the regime is reindexed
    onto the weights with ``ffill(limit=max_stale_bars)`` and whatever is
    still missing is filled with 0.0 (neutral), so a regime that stops
    publishing decays back to ``base_leverage`` after that many bars. When
    the regime ALREADY shares the weights' index, no reindex happens, no
    limit is applied, and no expiry can occur — a value that an upstream
    component itself carried forward is indistinguishable from a fresh one
    here. The bound protects against a regime that stops arriving, not
    against a regime that arrives stale.

Regime input contract:
    A Series, or a DataFrame whose FIRST COLUMN is taken as the regime (a
    zero-column DataFrame raises; extra columns are silently ignored — this
    is looser than ``MarketLeverageScaler``, which refuses a multi-column
    frame). Only exactly +1 (within 1e-6) is bullish and exactly -1
    bearish; every other value, NaN included, is neutral.

NaN discipline (the two modes differ, and the difference is load-bearing):
    - Regime NaN ⇒ neutral ⇒ ``base_leverage``, whether it arrived NaN or
      aged out of the staleness window.
    - long_only=True: a NaN weight cell stays NaN in the output and is
      skipped by the gross sum, so the REMAINING names absorb the entire
      leverage target.
    - long_only=False: a NaN weight cell becomes 0.0 (the side masks send
      NaN to zero), i.e. the output is densified.
    - An all-zero (or all-NaN) row scales to 0.0 rather than dividing by
      zero.

Causality / invariance:
    Every step is per-bar — a row-wise gross sum, a row-wise regime lookup,
    and a multiply — and the only cross-bar operation is a BACKWARD forward
    fill of the regime, bounded by ``max_stale_bars``. Bar t therefore
    reads bars <= t only, so appending or removing FUTURE bars cannot
    change a past value. (Removing PAST bars can, if the dropped bars held
    the regime observation the ffill was carrying.)

Output:
    WeightSeries with the input's index and columns. Gross exposure per bar
    is exactly ``base_leverage`` or ``regime_leverage`` (per side when
    ``long_only=False``), or 0.0 on a flat row. Signs are preserved.

Example:
    # Globals(target_timeframe="1h"): PriceDataLoader() serves the 1h bars itself — no resampler
    PriceDataLoader() ->
      MarketTrendRegimeFilter(fast_period=5, slow_period=17) ->
      Store("regime_filter")

    ... -> EqualWeightSizer(target_leverage=1.0) ->
      RegimeLeverageScaler(base_leverage=1.0, regime_leverage=5.0,
                           regime_slot="regime_filter", max_stale_bars=5)
components.usage_hint: Use for the same ask as ``MarketLeverageScaler`` — "lever up in a bull regime", "trade smaller when the regime turns" — when the regime series runs on a SLOWER clock than the book and a carried-forward value must expire rather than persist. Handed the same already-aligned regime series and the same parameters, the two components produce the same weights by the same arithmetic; they differ only in the staleness bound below and in what each accepts as regime input.

Raise it for a deliberately slow regime — a daily regime under 1h bars needs at least 24 — and lower it when acting on a stale label is worse than acting on none. components.name: RegimeScale
components.description:
Continuously scale a forecast signal proportional to a regime index for soft regime conditioning.

Use when you want proportional exposure adjustment rather than binary on/off gating.
Receives signal and index from a preceding Parallel step. For hard on/off gating,
use RegimeGate instead. The "linear" method is the standard choice; "inverse" and
"sigmoid" are experimental alternatives.

Output:
    Same units as input signal, multiplied by a scaling factor in clip_range
    (default [0.0, 2.0]). NaN where index is NaN. Factor of 1.0 means
    no change, 0.0 means fully suppressed, 2.0 means doubled.

Formula:
    linear:  factor = clip(1 - index/3, clip_range)
    inverse: factor = clip(1 / (1 + |index|), clip_range)
    sigmoid: factor = clip(sigmoid(-index), clip_range)

Example:
    {"momentum": ..., "regime": ...} -> RegimeScale(signal_key="momentum", index_key="regime", scale_method="linear")

For hard on/off gating, use RegimeGate instead. The "linear" method is the standard choice; "inverse" and "sigmoid" are experimental alternatives.

components.name: RegimeWeightedBlender
components.description:
Blend two forecast signals with dynamic weights driven by a regime signal for adaptive allocation.

Use to smoothly shift allocation between two strategies based on a regime indicator
(e.g., favor momentum in trending markets, mean reversion in ranging). Unlike
DispersionWeightedCombinator which uses return dispersion, this uses an arbitrary
regime signal. For binary gating instead of blending, use RegimeGate.

Output:
    Same scale as input forecasts (weighted blend). NaN during regime signal
    burn-in (~20 bars). Weight for signal_a is in [min_weight_a, max_weight_a].

Formula:
    z = expanding_zscore(regime_signal)
    w_a = sigmoid(regime_coeff * z) * (max_w_a - min_w_a) + min_w_a
    w_b = 1 - w_a
    blended = w_a * signal_a + w_b * signal_b

Example:
    {"mr": ..., "momentum": ..., "regime": ...} -> RegimeWeightedBlender(signal_a_key="mr", signal_b_key="momentum", regime_key="regime")

components.name: RelativeVolume
components.description:
Compute relative volume as a ratio of current volume to its rolling average.

Use to identify unusual volume activity — values above 1.0 indicate higher-than-normal
participation, below 1.0 indicates quiet trading. Feed into CrossSectionalZScore for
cross-sectional comparison or use as a filter dimension (Z axis in screening).

components.name: ResidualMomentum
components.description:
Cross-sectional residual momentum after stripping out N named benchmark factors.

For each bar t, fits OLS of each asset's returns on benchmark returns over a
strictly past window [t-bw, t-1] (EXCLUDES bar t). Applies that β to compute
a strict out-of-sample residual ε_t at bar t, then cumulates ε over
`momentum_window` bars to produce a momentum-style signal that is orthogonal
to the named benchmarks.

Use as the signal source for cross-sectional residual-momentum strategies on
a universe with one or more obvious common factors (e.g., crypto with
BTC/ETH/SOL representing the systematic component). The output ranks alts by
their idiosyncratic outperformance, NOT by their direction relative to the
market — by construction, MOM weights on the benchmarks themselves are
forced to zero (their residual against themselves is degenerate).

Output:
    SignalSeries (T × A) of cumulative residuals over the past
    `momentum_window` bars. Positive = outperformed its β-implied move.
    Benchmark columns are exactly zero. NaN during warmup (β fit needs at
    least max(N+5, beta_window/2) past observations; cumulation needs at
    least momentum_window/2 valid residuals).

Causality:
    β-fit window [t-bw, t-1] is STRICTLY past — does not include bar t.
    Residual at bar t uses bar-t benchmark and asset returns (both
    observable at close[t] under right-labeled bars). Cumulation uses
    rolling window [t-W+1, t] — past-only ending at t.

    Verified bit-exact against hand-OLS in research (Phase III.2 audit
    diff = 0.00e+00). Causality also independently confirmed by end-date
    stability test (Phase III.1) — 0 differences across 80K+ cells when
    re-run with three different end dates.

Performance:
    Implementation batches `np.linalg.lstsq` across "fully-valid" assets
    per bar (one OLS solve per bar instead of one per (bar, asset) pair),
    with a per-asset fallback for partial-NaN columns. ~11× faster than
    the naive per-asset loop on a 600-bar / 50-asset universe (~0.04s per
    call vs ~0.45s). Bit-equivalent to the per-asset path within machine
    epsilon (max diff observed 4.44e-16).

Slot pattern:
    Source-like component: ignores upstream `current` and reads OHLCV
    from a named slot. `input_type` is overridden to `None` so the type
    validator skips the upstream-shape check.

Example:
    ResidualMomentum(momentum_window=21, beta_window=90, benchmarks=["BTC", "ETH", "SOL"])
    -> VolAttenuator(return_vol_slot="return_vol")
    -> CrossSectionalZScore()

components.name: ReturnFromAverage
components.description:
This trade's return from its average entry after adds, as a fraction: the reader for a
take-profit target "X% above the average entry".

Position layer: TradeManager turns entry signals into a Position; each rule is a reader, then
ordinary components, then an action (Exit, Reduce, ScaleIn, AllowEntry). Value at row k:
direction × (close / average entry − 1). It is the exit side of a DCA or safety-order ladder
whose adds are ScaleIn.

Note: stops, targets, trails and other price-level rules are checked and filled at the bar's close, with no intra-bar measurement or execution, so a fill can be well past the level.

      {"safety": [ReturnSinceLastFill(), BelowThresholdFilter(threshold=-0.02, inclusive=True), ScaleIn(units=1.0, times=4)],
       "take": [ReturnFromAverage(), AboveThresholdFilter(threshold=0.02, inclusive=True), Exit()]} ->
      Exposure() -> FixedWeightSizer(weight_per_position=0.04)
